explanation.summary: Operative vaginal birth (vacuum or forceps) is indicated for prolonged second stage, fetal compromise, or maternal exhaustion when cervix is fully dilated, head at +2 station or lower, and position known. Pre-requisites (mnemonic ABCDEFGHIJ): Address patient/Adequate analgesia, Bladder empty, Cervix fully dilated, Determine position, Equipment, Fetal presentation/Adequate maternal pelvis, Gentle traction, Halt at no descent, Incision (episiotomy if needed), Jaw (delivery of head before shoulders). Vacuum (Kiwi OmniCup) is preferred over forceps when both suitable: less maternal trauma but higher fetal scalp injury; abandon if 3 detachments, 20 minutes, no progress with 3 pulls, or 3 contractions. Forceps (Wrigley outlet, Neville-Barnes mid-cavity) used for non-cephalic positions, vacuum failure, fetal distress requiring rapid delivery, or vacuum-contraindicated (prematurity <34 weeks, fetal bleeding disorders). Sequential use of both instruments roughly triples third-stage trauma and is avoided.
key_points: Pre-requisites ABCDEFGHIJ for operative vaginal birth
Vacuum first if both suitable - less maternal trauma
Vacuum abandon: 3 detachments, 20 minutes, no progress
Forceps for vacuum failure, non-cephalic, <34 weeks, fetal bleed risk
Sequential use of both instruments substantially increases trauma
explanation.pearls: Vacuum delivery carries about 10% incidence of cephalohaematoma and a small risk of subgaleal haemorrhage (about 0.06%); subgaleal bleed presents with progressive scalp swelling crossing suture lines and may cause neonatal shock.

options.rationale: Pathological CTG with recurrent late decelerations mandates expedited delivery; continued pushing is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Operative Vaginal Birth)

OA position, head visible without parting labia, +2 station, cooperative pushing maternal effort all favour vacuum; Kiwi OmniCup is the standard Australian device; 3 detachments or 20 minutes are the abandon-criteria. (Source: RANZCOG Operative Vaginal Birth)

At +2 station OA with visible vertex, vacuum is safer and faster than caesarean; caesarean from this point carries higher maternal morbidity and is reserved for failed operative vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Operative Vaginal Birth)

Forceps are appropriate but not first-choice over vacuum when both are suitable; vacuum has lower maternal trauma though slightly higher fetal scalp injury risk. (Source: RANZCOG Operative Vaginal Birth)
Augmentation in the setting of pathological CTG worsens hypoxia and is unsafe; expedited delivery is required. (Source: RANZCOG Operative Vaginal Birth)

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum pituitary necrosis from hypovolaemic shock during or after major obstetric haemorrhage; the gravid anterior pituitary is enlarged and uniquely vulnerable to ischaemia. Presentation can be acute (within days, with cardiovascular collapse, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia) or chronic (months to years, with progressive panhypopituitarism). Classic features are failure of lactation (agalactia, prolactin deficiency), failure to resume menses (LH/FSH deficiency), fatigue and weight loss (ACTH/cortisol deficiency), cold intolerance and bradycardia (TSH/thyroid deficiency), and growth hormone deficiency. Replacement priority is glucocorticoid FIRST (IV hydrocortisone then oral 15 to 25 mg daily in divided doses), then thyroxine 24 to 48 hours later (starting thyroxine first precipitates adrenal crisis by accelerating cortisol clearance), then oestrogen-progestogen for women who do not desire pregnancy, with GH and fertility-related FSH/LH as needed. MRI shows empty sella in long-standing disease.
key_points: Sheehan: postpartum pituitary necrosis after massive PPH
Agalactia + amenorrhoea + cortisol deficiency + hypothyroid = classic
Treat glucocorticoid FIRST, then thyroxine 24-48 hours later
Secondary (low ACTH) so no fludrocortisone needed
MRI: empty sella in chronic disease
explanation.pearls: Sheehan syndrome is the commonest cause of hypopituitarism in lower-income countries but is now rare in Australia (incidence about 1 in 100,000 live births); the postpartum failure of lactation, which can otherwise be missed, is the earliest and most specific clinical clue.

options.rationale: Starting thyroxine before glucocorticoid in panhypopituitarism precipitates adrenal crisis; cortisol replacement must come first or be given concurrently. (Source: Endocrine Society Hypopituitarism Guideline)

Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis after massive PPH) presents with adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, agalactia, amenorrhoea; secondary adrenal crisis is life-threatening and IV hydrocortisone must be given FIRST, with thyroxine added 24 to 48 hours later. (Source: Endocrine Society Hypopituitarism Guideline)

Sheehan syndrome causes SECONDARY adrenal insufficiency (low ACTH); mineralocorticoid axis is intact (controlled by renin-angiotensin); fludrocortisone is not required. (Source: Endocrine Society Hypopituitarism Guideline)

GH deficiency may co-exist but does not address immediate adrenal crisis risk; replacement priority is glucocorticoid > thyroid > sex steroid > GH. (Source: Endocrine Society Hypopituitarism Guideline)
MRI confirms pituitary infarct/empty sella but delaying treatment risks fatal adrenal crisis; MRI does not change immediate management. (Source: Endocrine Society Hypopituitarism Guideline)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is heart failure with LVEF <45% developing in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum, in the absence of other identifiable cause. Australian incidence is approximately 1 in 1,500 live births, higher in older mothers, hypertensive disorders, multiple pregnancy, and African ancestry. Pathophysiology involves a prolactin-derived 16 kDa fragment causing endothelial dysfunction, hence bromocriptine (prolactin inhibitor) may accelerate recovery. Management is heart failure GDMT: loop diuretic for congestion; beta blocker (bisoprolol or metoprolol succinate); ACE inhibitor (enalapril or captopril, breastfeeding-compatible) - or ARB if not breastfeeding; aldosterone antagonist; LMWH anticoagulation when LVEF <35% (high thrombotic risk especially around delivery); device therapy (CRT, ICD) considered after 6 months recovery period. About 50% recover to LVEF >50%; relapse risk in subsequent pregnancy is 30 to 50% if recovery incomplete, hence contraception counselling.
key_points: PPCM: LVEF <45% last month of pregnancy or up to 5 months postpartum
GDMT: loop diuretic + beta blocker + ACE inhibitor (enalapril/captopril breastfeeding-OK)
LMWH if LVEF <35%
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg BD adjunctive - accelerates LV recovery (ESC)
Recurrence 30-50% if LVEF not recovered to >50%
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks then daily for 6 weeks in peripartum cardiomyopathy improved LVEF and reduced mortality in the IPAC and PPCM-bromocriptine trials, and is supported by ESC 2018 guidelines as an adjunct alongside standard heart failure therapy.

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in breastfeeding mothers postpartum if breastfeeding continues (captopril and enalapril are exceptions with caution); ramipril is not first-line in breastfeeding. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)

Spironolactone and digoxin are second-line or add-on therapies; first-line is loop diuretic + beta blocker + ACE inhibitor (Australian heart failure standard) plus PPCM-specific bromocriptine and anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure)

Postpartum cardiomyopathy with LVEF <35% has high thromboembolic risk; LMWH is indicated unless active bleeding; postpartum status is not a contraindication. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)

Mechanical circulatory support is reserved for cardiogenic shock refractory to medical therapy; she is stable on room air with maintained BP and warrants medical therapy first. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy)

Peripartum cardiomyopathy is treated with standard heart failure therapy (loop diuretic, beta blocker, ACE inhibitor - enalapril/captopril safe in breastfeeding); LMWH anticoagulation when LVEF <35% (high thromboembolic risk); bromocriptine (prolactin inhibition) is emerging Australian and ESC-supported therapy that may accelerate LV recovery. (Source: ESC Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy; CSANZ)

explanation.summary: PMDD affects 3-8% of women of reproductive age and is characterised by severe mood and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase with complete resolution after menses. Diagnosis requires prospective symptom charting over at least 2 consecutive cycles. SSRIs are first-line treatment, and uniquely for PMDD, luteal-phase-only dosing is effective, distinguishing the neuropharmacology from MDD where continuous dosing is required. This rapid SSRI effect in PMDD is thought to relate to neurosteroid modulation rather than serotonin reuptake inhibition alone.
key_points: Prospective daily symptom charting for at least 2 cycles is required for PMDD diagnosis
SSRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy with luteal-phase dosing as effective as continuous dosing
The rapid SSRI response in PMDD (within 1-2 days) differs from the 2-4 week onset in MDD
COCPs with extended cycling are second-line; GnRH agonists are reserved for refractory cases
explanation.pearls: SSRIs work within 24-48 hours for PMDD symptoms due to rapid enhancement of allopregnanolone (a neurosteroid) rather than the delayed serotonergic remodelling that mediates their effect in MDD, which is why luteal-phase-only dosing is effective.

options.rationale: COCPs can improve PMDD symptoms through ovulation suppression, but they are considered second-line to SSRIs for PMDD. The cyclical hormone-free interval can trigger symptom recurrence. Evidence for SSRIs in PMDD is stronger and more consistent. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome)

Progesterone supplementation has not shown consistent benefit for PMDD in randomised controlled trials despite the historical assumption that progesterone deficiency causes PMS. Current evidence does not support its use as first-line therapy. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome)

Calcium supplementation and vitamin B6 have modest evidence for mild PMS symptoms but are insufficient for PMDD with significant functional impairment. They are appropriate for mild PMS as lifestyle adjuncts but not as first-line pharmacotherapy for PMDD. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome)

SSRIs are first-line pharmacotherapy for PMDD, with strong evidence from multiple RCTs. Luteal-phase dosing (from ovulation to menses) is as effective as continuous dosing for PMDD specifically, offering the advantage of reduced total SSRI exposure and side effects. Sertraline and fluoxetine have the strongest evidence base. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome)

GnRH agonists effectively suppress ovulation and eliminate PMDD symptoms, but significant side effects including bone density loss limit them to refractory cases. They are third-line therapy, used only when SSRIs and COCPs have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is characterised by ectopic endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, causing a diffusely enlarged uterus, heavy menstrual bleeding, and dysmenorrhoea. Transvaginal ultrasound features include a globular uterus, heterogeneous myometrium, myometrial cysts, and a poorly defined endometrial-myometrial junction. The LNG-IUS is the preferred first-line medical treatment, reducing menstrual blood loss by up to 90% and significantly improving dysmenorrhoea. Hysterectomy is definitive but reserved for medical therapy failure.
key_points: Ultrasound features of adenomyosis include myometrial cysts, heterogeneity, and blurred endometrial-myometrial junction
LNG-IUS is first-line medical therapy for adenomyosis-related bleeding and pain
Iron deficiency anaemia should be treated concurrently
Hysterectomy is definitive but should follow failed medical management
explanation.pearls: MRI has higher sensitivity than ultrasound for adenomyosis diagnosis, with junctional zone thickness greater than 12 mm being diagnostic; however, transvaginal ultrasound in experienced hands approaches MRI accuracy and is the recommended first-line imaging modality.

options.rationale: The LNG-IUS is first-line medical management for adenomyosis-related heavy menstrual bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. It provides local progestogenic effect causing endometrial and ectopic endometrial tissue atrophy, reducing both bleeding and pain. Concurrent iron replacement is essential given this patient's iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual blood loss by 40-50% and NSAIDs help with dysmenorrhoea, but this combination is symptomatic only and does not address the underlying adenomyosis. It is less effective than the LNG-IUS for heavy bleeding associated with adenomyosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

COCPs can reduce menstrual bleeding and pain but are less effective than the LNG-IUS for adenomyosis specifically. They are a reasonable second-line option if the LNG-IUS is contraindicated or declined. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

GnRH agonists effectively shrink adenomyotic tissue but are limited to 6-month courses due to bone density loss, and symptoms typically recur after cessation. They are reserved for short-term use before surgery or when other medical options have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology)

While hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for adenomyosis, it should not be offered as the initial management without first trialling appropriate medical therapy. The LNG-IUS should be offered first as it avoids surgical morbidity and is highly effective. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as loss of ovarian function before age 40 with elevated FSH (>25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart) and hypoestrogenism. It affects approximately 1% of women under 40. HRT is the cornerstone of management, providing bone and cardiovascular protection until the average age of natural menopause. Unlike early natural menopause, HRT in POI does not carry the same risk profile as post-menopausal HRT use. Spontaneous pregnancy occurs in 5-10% of cases, and cyclical progesterone rather than continuous COCPs is preferred when fertility is desired.
key_points: POI requires two elevated FSH measurements at least 4 weeks apart in a woman under 40
HRT should be continued until the average age of natural menopause (51 years)
Cyclical progesterone is preferred over COCPs when fertility is desired to preserve spontaneous ovulation potential
Karyotype and autoimmune screening (thyroid, adrenal antibodies) are part of the aetiological workup
explanation.pearls: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) is the earliest marker to decline in diminishing ovarian reserve and becomes undetectable in established POI; however, AMH alone should not be used to diagnose POI as FSH elevation on two occasions remains the diagnostic standard.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency

options.rationale: Clomifene citrate works by blocking oestrogen negative feedback to stimulate FSH release, but in premature ovarian insufficiency the FSH is already markedly elevated and the ovaries are unresponsive. Clomifene will not be effective in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency)

HRT is essential in premature ovarian insufficiency to manage vasomotor symptoms, prevent bone density loss, and reduce cardiovascular risk from premature oestrogen deficiency. HRT should be continued until the average age of natural menopause (51 years). Cyclical progesterone preserves the option of spontaneous pregnancy, as 5-10% of women with POI conceive spontaneously. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency)

While COCPs provide oestrogen replacement, they suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and may mask spontaneous ovarian activity. HRT with cyclical progesterone is preferred over COCPs in POI when fertility is desired, as it does not suppress potential ovulation. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency)

While donor oocyte IVF is ultimately the most effective fertility treatment for POI, it should not be the immediate first step. HRT should be commenced for bone and cardiovascular protection, and the patient should be counselled that 5-10% of women with POI conceive spontaneously. Donor oocyte discussion is appropriate but alongside HRT initiation. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency)

While bone density assessment is important, calcium supplementation alone is insufficient to prevent the accelerated bone loss seen with premature oestrogen deficiency. HRT is the cornerstone of bone protection in young women with POI and should not be withheld. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is chronic vulvar pain without an identifiable cause, persisting for at least 3 months. Provoked vestibulodynia is the most common subtype, characterised by pain elicited by touch or pressure at the vulvar vestibule. Diagnosis is clinical, based on a positive cotton-swab test after excluding infectious, dermatological, and neoplastic causes. First-line management is multimodal: topical anaesthetics, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and psychosexual support. Second-line options include tricyclic antidepressants and gabapentinoids. Vestibulectomy is reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: Cotton-swab test eliciting vestibular pain with normal examination is characteristic of provoked vestibulodynia
Multimodal first-line management includes topical lidocaine, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and psychosexual support
Empiric antifungal use without microbiological evidence should be discontinued
Vestibulectomy is effective but reserved for cases refractory to conservative management
explanation.pearls: Pelvic floor electromyography in provoked vestibulodynia typically shows elevated resting tone and poor relaxation; pelvic floor physiotherapy targeting voluntary relaxation and desensitisation achieves symptom improvement in 50-70% of women within 12 weeks.

options.rationale: Multiple antifungal courses have already failed and swabs confirm no candida. Continuing empiric antifungal therapy without microbiological evidence of infection is inappropriate and delays proper diagnosis and management. (Source: ISSVD: Vulvodynia Guidelines)

Potent topical corticosteroids are indicated for vulvar dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus and lichen planus. The absence of visible skin changes and the provoked vestibular pain pattern point to vulvodynia rather than a dermatological condition. (Source: ISSVD: Vulvodynia Guidelines)

Provoked vestibulodynia is the most common subtype of vulvodynia. First-line management is multimodal: topical lidocaine for pain relief, pelvic floor physiotherapy to address associated pelvic floor hypertonicity, and psychosexual counselling. This approach addresses both the peripheral sensitisation and the muscular dysfunction that perpetuate the condition. (Source: ISSVD: Vulvodynia Guidelines)

Tricyclic antidepressants are used for vulvodynia but are typically second-line, reserved for patients who have not responded to topical measures and physiotherapy. Starting with systemic medication before non-invasive first-line approaches is not recommended. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual Health)

Vestibulectomy has high success rates (60-90%) for provoked vestibulodynia but is reserved as a last-line option after failure of conservative management including topical therapy, physiotherapy, and pharmacological agents. Surgery should not be offered before conservative measures are exhausted. (Source: ISSVD: Vulvodynia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Fetal growth restriction below the 3rd centile with asymmetric growth (elevated HC:AC ratio) suggests placental insufficiency. Umbilical artery Doppler is central to surveillance: elevated pulsatility index with present end-diastolic flow warrants increased monitoring and corticosteroids; absent end-diastolic flow requires admission and consideration of delivery; reversed end-diastolic flow is an indication for delivery after corticosteroids. Delivery timing depends on gestational age and Doppler findings, typically aiming for 37 weeks if stable but earlier with deterioration.
key_points: EFW below the 3rd centile requires heightened surveillance regardless of Doppler findings
Umbilical artery Doppler progression: elevated PI, then absent end-diastolic flow, then reversed end-diastolic flow
Antenatal corticosteroids should be given when preterm delivery is likely within the next 7 days
Ductus venosus Doppler and computerised CTG provide additional surveillance in severe early-onset FGR
explanation.pearls: The middle cerebral artery to umbilical artery cerebroplacental ratio (CPR) below the 5th centile is an earlier marker of fetal redistribution than abnormal umbilical artery Doppler alone and identifies at-risk fetuses who may benefit from closer surveillance even with normal UA Doppler.

options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 32 weeks is not indicated when umbilical artery end-diastolic flow is still present, as the risks of prematurity outweigh the benefits. Delivery is indicated urgently when absent or reversed end-diastolic flow is detected, or when other features suggest imminent fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction)

A 4-week interval is too long for a fetus with EFW below the 3rd centile and abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. This level of growth restriction requires more frequent surveillance with Doppler assessment at least twice weekly to detect deterioration before fetal compromise occurs. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction)

Low-dose aspirin is a preventive measure started before 16 weeks for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia and growth restriction. Starting aspirin at 32 weeks with established growth restriction is too late to be beneficial. Active surveillance rather than prevention is needed. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction)

With EFW below the 3rd centile and elevated umbilical artery pulsatility index but present end-diastolic flow, management includes antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity (as preterm delivery is likely), twice-weekly umbilical artery Doppler surveillance, and delivery planning around 37 weeks or earlier if Doppler deteriorates to absent or reversed end-diastolic flow. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction)

Bed rest has not been shown to improve outcomes in fetal growth restriction and may increase VTE risk. Biophysical profile alone without Doppler surveillance is inadequate, as umbilical artery Doppler changes precede biophysical profile abnormalities in the deterioration sequence. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction)

explanation.summary: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy requires immediate cessation of ACE inhibitors and ARBs due to teratogenicity (renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia). First-line alternatives include labetalol, modified-release nifedipine, and methyldopa. The CHAP trial (2022) established that targeting BP below 140/90 mmHg reduces pre-eclampsia and adverse outcomes compared to the previous threshold of 160/110 mmHg. Low-dose aspirin 150 mg nightly should be commenced before 16 weeks in women with chronic hypertension to reduce pre-eclampsia risk.
key_points: ACE inhibitors and ARBs must be ceased immediately upon confirmation of pregnancy
Labetalol, nifedipine MR, and methyldopa are first-line pregnancy antihypertensives
BP target in pregnancy with chronic hypertension is below 140/90 mmHg per CHAP trial evidence
Aspirin 150 mg at bedtime should start before 16 weeks for pre-eclampsia prevention
explanation.pearls: The CHAP trial enrolled 2408 women with chronic hypertension and showed that a treatment target of <140/90 mmHg reduced pre-eclampsia with severe features by 20% compared to the reserving-treatment-for-severe approach, without increasing small-for-gestational-age births.

options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated throughout pregnancy due to teratogenicity including renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, and fetal death. Ramipril must be ceased immediately regardless of blood pressure control. Aspirin is appropriate but not with continued ACE inhibitor use. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Atenolol is associated with fetal growth restriction when used in pregnancy, particularly in early gestation, and is not a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy. Labetalol, nifedipine, or methyldopa are the recommended alternatives. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

While amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker, nifedipine (modified-release) is the preferred dihydropyridine in pregnancy as it has substantially more safety data. Aspirin 150 mg daily should be commenced before 16 weeks in this woman with chronic hypertension, a significant risk factor for pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

The CHAP trial demonstrated that treating chronic hypertension to a target below 140/90 mmHg in pregnancy (rather than waiting until severe hypertension) reduces pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and adverse perinatal outcomes. A step-down approach withholding treatment until severe hypertension is no longer recommended. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Ramipril must be ceased immediately due to ACE inhibitor teratogenicity. Labetalol is a first-line pregnancy-safe antihypertensive with extensive safety data. Aspirin 150 mg daily should be commenced before 16 weeks gestation in women with chronic hypertension to reduce pre-eclampsia risk. Target BP in pregnancy is below 140/90 mmHg. (Source: SOMANZ: Hypertension in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Thyroid function in pregnancy requires trimester-specific reference ranges, with the first-trimester TSH upper limit approximately 4.0 mIU/L (or institution-specific). Subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal free T4) with positive TPO antibodies is associated with increased miscarriage, preterm birth, and impaired neurodevelopment. Treatment with levothyroxine is recommended in this setting. Women on levothyroxine pre-pregnancy typically need a 30-50% dose increase, and those newly diagnosed should start at 50 microg with regular monitoring.
key_points: First-trimester TSH upper limit is approximately 4.0 mIU/L in pregnancy
TPO antibody positivity increases the risk of adverse outcomes and strengthens the indication for treatment
Levothyroxine dose should maintain TSH in the lower half of the trimester-specific range
TSH should be monitored every 4 weeks during pregnancy with dose adjustments as needed
explanation.pearls: Women already on levothyroxine who become pregnant should increase their dose by approximately 30% immediately upon confirmation of pregnancy (a practical approach is to take two extra tablets per week) and have TSH checked within 2 weeks.

options.rationale: A threshold of 10 mIU/L is the treatment threshold for overt hypothyroidism detection but is too conservative for pregnancy. In the first trimester with positive TPO antibodies, subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH above the pregnancy-specific upper limit should be treated to reduce miscarriage and preterm birth risk. (Source: Endocrine Society: Thyroid and Pregnancy)

The TSH is elevated, not suppressed. This is subclinical hypothyroidism, not thyrotoxicosis. Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism and is teratogenic in the first trimester (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia). (Source: AMH: Antithyroid Drugs)

While the TSH elevation is modest, the presence of positive TPO antibodies significantly changes management. TPO-positive women with subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy have higher rates of miscarriage and preterm birth, and levothyroxine treatment is recommended when TSH exceeds the trimester-specific upper limit. (Source: Endocrine Society: Thyroid and Pregnancy)

While adequate iodine intake is important in pregnancy (220 microg/day), this patient has positive TPO antibodies indicating autoimmune thyroiditis as the cause of elevated TSH, not iodine deficiency. Levothyroxine replacement rather than iodine supplementation is the appropriate treatment. (Source: NHMRC: Iodine Supplementation in Pregnancy)

In pregnancy, subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH above trimester-specific upper limit with normal free T4) with positive TPO antibodies should be treated with levothyroxine. A starting dose of 50 microg daily is appropriate. TSH should be monitored every 4 weeks with dose titration to keep TSH in the lower half of the trimester-specific reference range. (Source: Endocrine Society: Thyroid and Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Dichorionic diamniotic twins have separate placentas and membranes, identified by the lambda sign in the first trimester. While they carry lower risks than monochorionic twins (no TTTS or TAPS risk), they still require enhanced surveillance compared to singletons. Growth scans every 4 weeks from 20 weeks monitor for discordant growth (>20% EFW difference). Planned delivery at 37 weeks reduces the risk of late stillbirth without significant prematurity-related morbidity. Monochorionic twins, by contrast, require fortnightly scans from 16 weeks and delivery at 36 weeks.
key_points: DCDA twins are identified by the lambda sign or thick dividing membrane in the first trimester
Growth scans every 4 weeks from 20 weeks with delivery at 37 weeks is the standard DCDA schedule
Discordant growth exceeding 20% EFW difference requires increased surveillance
Monochorionic twins require more intensive monitoring with fortnightly scans from 16 weeks
explanation.pearls: The lambda (twin peak) sign is most reliable before 14 weeks gestation; after this, membrane thickness becomes less reliable for determining chorionicity, which is why first-trimester dating and chorionicity assessment is critical in all twin pregnancies.

options.rationale: Monthly scanning is insufficient for twin pregnancies, and delivery at 40 weeks carries increased risk of stillbirth in twins. DCDA twins should have growth scans every 4 weeks from 20 weeks with planned delivery at 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

Fortnightly scanning from 16 weeks is the schedule for monochorionic twins, not dichorionic twins. DCDA twins have a lower complication rate due to separate placentas and do not require the intensive monitoring needed for shared-placenta pregnancies. Delivery at 36 weeks is also too early for uncomplicated DCDA twins. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

All twin pregnancies require more intensive surveillance than singletons due to higher rates of fetal growth restriction, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, and discordant growth. Singleton antenatal schedules are insufficient for twins regardless of chorionicity. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

Weekly Doppler surveillance is excessive for uncomplicated DCDA twins and is reserved for complicated pregnancies with growth restriction or discordance. Delivery at 34 weeks is too early without an indication, exposing both babies to unnecessary prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

DCDA twins should have growth ultrasounds every 4 weeks from 20 weeks gestation to monitor for discordant growth (>20% EFW difference) and growth restriction. Planned delivery at 37 weeks is recommended to balance the risks of late stillbirth against prematurity. Low-dose aspirin should be commenced for pre-eclampsia prevention. (Source: RANZCOG: Multiple Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea (absent menses for 3-6 months in a previously menstruating woman) requires systematic investigation. After excluding pregnancy, the initial workup includes TSH, prolactin, FSH, LH, and oestradiol. The pattern of results guides further testing: elevated FSH suggests ovarian failure, elevated prolactin warrants pituitary imaging, and normal FSH with androgen excess points toward PCOS. PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria requiring two of three features: oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology.
key_points: Always exclude pregnancy first in secondary amenorrhoea regardless of reported sexual activity
LH:FSH ratio >2:1 with normal FSH is suggestive of PCOS
Rotterdam criteria require two of three: oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound
DHEAS and 17-hydroxyprogesterone should be measured to exclude adrenal causes of hyperandrogenism
explanation.pearls: Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound is defined as 12 or more follicles of 2-9 mm per ovary or ovarian volume exceeding 10 mL; this criterion alone without anovulation or hyperandrogenism does not diagnose PCOS, as up to 20% of normal women have polycystic ovarian morphology.

options.rationale: Prolactin is within normal limits at 220 mIU/L, making a prolactinoma unlikely. Pituitary MRI is indicated when prolactin exceeds 1000 mIU/L or when there are visual field defects. The clinical picture with obesity, hirsutism, and elevated LH:FSH ratio points elsewhere. (Source: RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)

Turner syndrome typically presents with primary amenorrhoea or premature ovarian insufficiency with elevated FSH. This patient has low-normal FSH, secondary amenorrhoea, and signs of androgen excess, making Turner syndrome very unlikely. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Secondary Amenorrhoea)

While Cushing syndrome can cause obesity and oligomenorrhoea, it is rare and should be suspected only when specific features are present (striae, proximal myopathy, easy bruising, buffalo hump). The clinical picture is more consistent with PCOS, which should be investigated first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

AMH is useful for assessing ovarian reserve but is not the key diagnostic investigation here. The FSH is not elevated, excluding premature ovarian insufficiency. AMH is often elevated in PCOS but is not part of the standard diagnostic criteria. (Source: RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)

The combination of oligomenorrhoea, clinical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), obesity, and elevated LH:FSH ratio strongly suggests PCOS. Per the Rotterdam criteria, two of three features are needed: oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical), and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. Total testosterone confirms biochemical hyperandrogenism and pelvic ultrasound assesses ovarian morphology. (Source: RANZCOG: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Uterine fibroids are the most common pelvic tumours in women, with submucosal fibroids causing the most significant menstrual bleeding. When LNG-IUS placement fails due to cavity distortion, medical options include oral GnRH antagonist combination therapy (relugolix with add-back), which allows long-term use unlike GnRH agonists. Procedural options include uterine artery embolisation, myomectomy, and hysterectomy. Management should be individualised based on fibroid location, patient symptoms, fertility wishes, and treatment preferences.
key_points: Submucosal fibroids cause disproportionate bleeding relative to their size and may prevent LNG-IUS retention
GnRH antagonist combination therapy with add-back allows extended medical management beyond 6 months
GnRH agonists without add-back are limited to 6 months and fibroids regrow after cessation
Iron deficiency anaemia should be corrected with IV iron infusion when oral iron is insufficient
explanation.pearls: The FIGO fibroid classification system (types 0-8) guides treatment selection: types 0-2 (submucosal) are amenable to hysteroscopic resection, while types 3-5 (intramural) typically require laparoscopic or open myomectomy or medical management.

options.rationale: Oral GnRH antagonist combination therapy (relugolix with add-back oestradiol and norethindrone) is a long-term medical option for fibroid-related heavy menstrual bleeding when LNG-IUS has failed. It suppresses fibroid growth while add-back therapy prevents bone loss and menopausal symptoms, allowing extended use beyond the 6-month limit of GnRH agonists alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology)

GnRH agonists are limited to 6 months of use without add-back therapy due to bone density loss. Fibroids regrow rapidly after cessation, so GnRH agonists alone are not definitive treatment. They are primarily used as short-term preoperative therapy to shrink fibroids and improve haemoglobin before surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology)

Tranexamic acid can reduce menstrual blood loss but does not address the fibroid burden. With LNG-IUS failure and significant anaemia from two fibroids including a cavity-distorting submucosal fibroid, more definitive fibroid-directed therapy is needed. IV iron addresses the anaemia symptomatically but not the underlying cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology)

Uterine artery embolisation is an effective minimally invasive option but the patient has requested to avoid procedural interventions. UAE outcomes are less predictable for submucosal fibroids and carry a risk of IUS expulsion if future LNG-IUS placement is considered. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

Hysteroscopic myomectomy is appropriate for the submucosal fibroid but cannot address the 6 cm intramural fibroid. A combined hysteroscopic and laparoscopic approach would be needed, which is a significant surgical procedure the patient wishes to avoid. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine Fibroids)

explanation.summary: Uterine inversion occurs when the uterine fundus collapses into or through the cervix. It presents with severe pain, haemorrhagic shock (often disproportionate to visible blood loss due to vagal stimulation), and an absent fundal contour on abdominal palpation. Immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) is critical before a cervical constriction ring forms. Key management principles include replacing the uterus before removing the placenta, withholding uterotonics until after replacement, and using uterine relaxants only if a constriction ring prevents manual repositioning.
key_points: Absent uterine fundus on abdominal palpation with a mass at or through the cervix is diagnostic
Manual replacement should be attempted immediately before a constriction ring forms
The placenta should not be removed until after the uterus is successfully replaced
Uterotonics are given only after replacement to maintain uterine position and tone
explanation.pearls: Neurogenic shock from parasympathetic stimulation of the stretched uterine ligaments contributes to the cardiovascular collapse seen in uterine inversion, causing bradycardia and hypotension that may be disproportionate to the measured blood loss.

options.rationale: Uterotonics should be withheld until the uterus is replaced, as contracting an inverted uterus will make repositioning more difficult by forming a constriction ring. Bimanual compression is ineffective on an inverted uterus. The absent fundus on abdominal palpation distinguishes this from simple uterine atony. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric Emergencies)

Acute uterine inversion requires immediate manual replacement (Johnson manoeuvre) before a constriction ring forms. The inverted fundus is pushed back through the cervix with the palm applying upward pressure. Simultaneous IV fluid resuscitation addresses the haemorrhagic shock. Uterotonic agents should be given only after successful replacement to maintain uterine tone. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric Emergencies)

Hysterectomy is a last resort for uterine inversion, reserved for cases where manual and surgical replacement attempts fail. The vast majority of inversions can be corrected with manual replacement, especially when performed promptly before a constriction ring develops. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric Emergencies)

Uterine relaxants (terbutaline, glyceryl trinitrate, or general anaesthesia with volatile agents) are used when a constriction ring prevents manual replacement. In acute inversion presenting immediately, manual replacement should be attempted first before pharmacological relaxation, as delay increases the chance of ring formation. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric Emergencies)

If the placenta is still attached to the inverted uterus, it should not be removed before replacement as this will worsen haemorrhage by disrupting the placental bed. The uterus should be replaced with the placenta in situ, and the placenta removed only after the uterus is repositioned and uterotonics are given. (Source: RANZCOG: Obstetric Emergencies)

explanation.summary: Asherman syndrome refers to intrauterine adhesions (synechiae) causing partial or complete obliteration of the uterine cavity, typically following uterine instrumentation. The strongest risk factor is curettage for pregnancy-related complications, particularly when repeated. The classic presentation is secondary amenorrhoea or hypomenorrhoea with cyclical pain (suggesting trapped endometrium), normal hormonal profile, and failed progesterone withdrawal. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the therapeutic modality for adhesiolysis.
key_points: Repeated curettage for retained products is the highest risk factor for intrauterine adhesion formation
Cyclical pain with amenorrhoea after uterine instrumentation strongly suggests Asherman syndrome
Normal FSH, LH, and oestradiol with failed progesterone withdrawal points to an outflow problem
Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis followed by oestrogen therapy and IUD placement reduces recurrence
explanation.pearls: A combined oestrogen-progesterone withdrawal test that also fails after a failed progesterone-only test confirms an outflow tract or endometrial cause rather than anovulation, as adequate oestrogen priming should produce a decidualised endometrium capable of shedding.

options.rationale: While MRI can show a thin or obliterated endometrial stripe, it cannot reliably confirm intrauterine adhesions or determine their extent. Hysteroscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic, making it the preferred investigation when Asherman syndrome is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine Adhesions)

Saline infusion sonography can suggest intrauterine adhesions when the cavity fails to distend or shows filling defects, but it lacks the sensitivity and therapeutic capability of hysteroscopy. In this clinical scenario with high pre-test probability, proceeding directly to hysteroscopy is more appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine Adhesions)

The history of amenorrhoea after repeated curettage with cyclical pain, normal hormonal profile, and failed progesterone withdrawal strongly suggests Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions). Hysteroscopy is the gold-standard investigation, allowing direct visualisation of adhesions and simultaneous adhesiolysis. The normal oestradiol confirms functioning ovaries, and cyclical pain suggests endometrium is present but outflow is obstructed. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine Adhesions)

Hysterosalpingogram can identify filling defects suggesting adhesions but involves radiation exposure and cannot treat the adhesions. It is more appropriate for infertility workup when tubal assessment is needed. Hysteroscopy provides superior diagnostic accuracy and offers simultaneous treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine Adhesions)

Endometrial biopsy may be technically difficult or impossible when adhesions obliterate the cavity. The normal oestradiol level already confirms adequate ovarian oestrogen production. Direct visualisation of the cavity is needed to diagnose and manage the adhesions. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine Adhesions)

explanation.summary: Rh alloimmunisation occurs when a Rh-negative mother develops anti-D antibodies after exposure to Rh-positive fetal red cells. Serial antibody titres guide surveillance intensity, with critical titre (typically 1:16 or 1:32) triggering MCA Doppler monitoring. MCA peak systolic velocity above 1.5 MoM indicates moderate-to-severe fetal anaemia with high sensitivity and specificity, replacing amniocentesis for Liley zone assessment. Intrauterine transfusion is the standard treatment for fetal anaemia before 34-36 weeks gestation.
key_points: Anti-D titre above the critical threshold triggers MCA Doppler surveillance
MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM has >95% sensitivity for moderate-severe fetal anaemia
Intrauterine transfusion is the treatment of choice for fetal anaemia remote from term
Cell-free fetal DNA can non-invasively determine fetal Rh status from maternal blood
explanation.pearls: After intrauterine transfusion, MCA-PSV becomes unreliable for monitoring subsequent anaemia because the transfused adult haemoglobin has different oxygen-carrying characteristics; subsequent IUT timing relies on predicted haemoglobin decline (approximately 1 g/dL per day of estimated fetal blood volume).

options.rationale: With MCA-PSV already at 1.6 MoM, exceeding the 1.5 MoM threshold indicating moderate-to-severe fetal anaemia, expectant management with repeat Doppler alone risks fetal hydrops and death. The fetus requires urgent assessment for anaemia with likely need for transfusion. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh Disease Management)

At 26 weeks, delivery carries extreme prematurity risks. Intrauterine transfusion is the standard intervention for fetal anaemia remote from term, allowing the pregnancy to continue while correcting the anaemia. Delivery is reserved for gestations beyond 34-36 weeks or when IUT is technically impossible. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh Disease Management)

Plasmapheresis can reduce antibody levels but is used as an adjunct in severe early-onset disease before IUT is technically feasible (typically before 20 weeks). At 26 weeks with evidence of fetal anaemia, direct fetal treatment via intrauterine transfusion is the standard approach. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Rh Isoimmunisation)

MCA-PSV exceeding 1.5 MoM indicates moderate-to-severe fetal anaemia requiring intervention. Cordocentesis (fetal blood sampling) confirms the fetal haemoglobin and haematocrit, and intrauterine transfusion of irradiated, CMV-negative, Rh-negative packed red cells corrects the anaemia. This procedure can be repeated as needed until a gestational age suitable for delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh Disease Management)

IVIG has been used in some protocols for alloimmunisation but evidence for its efficacy is limited and it does not reliably prevent fetal anaemia when MCA-PSV already indicates established anaemia. Direct fetal transfusion is the evidence-based intervention at this stage. (Source: RANZCOG: Rh Disease Management)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing lupus nephritis from pre-eclampsia in pregnancy is one of the most challenging clinical discriminations in obstetric medicine. Both conditions cause hypertension, proteinuria, and renal impairment. The key distinguishing features are complement levels (consumed and low in active lupus, normal or elevated in pre-eclampsia), anti-dsDNA titres (rising in lupus flare), active urinary sediment with red cell casts (lupus nephritis), and urate levels (typically elevated in pre-eclampsia, normal in lupus). Treatment differs fundamentally: lupus nephritis requires immunosuppression while pre-eclampsia requires delivery.
key_points: Low C3 and C4 with rising anti-dsDNA strongly favours lupus nephritis over pre-eclampsia
Urate is typically elevated in pre-eclampsia but normal in lupus nephritis
Active urinary sediment with red cell casts suggests glomerulonephritis rather than pre-eclampsia
The two conditions can coexist, making serial monitoring and multidisciplinary input essential
explanation.pearls: Hydroxychloroquine should be continued throughout pregnancy in women with SLE as discontinuation doubles the lupus flare rate; it also reduces the risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro positive mothers by approximately 50%.

options.rationale: Rising creatinine and proteinuria occur in both lupus nephritis and pre-eclampsia, making these findings non-discriminatory. Both conditions can cause progressive renal impairment in pregnancy and this feature alone cannot distinguish them. (Source: SOMANZ: Lupus in Pregnancy)

New hypertension after 20 weeks can occur in both conditions. Pre-eclampsia classically develops after 20 weeks, but lupus nephritis can also first present or flare at any gestation. This is not a distinguishing feature. (Source: SOMANZ: Lupus in Pregnancy)

While thrombocytopenia and elevated LFTs are features of severe pre-eclampsia and HELLP, normal platelets and LFTs can occur in mild pre-eclampsia. This finding makes severe pre-eclampsia less likely but does not specifically discriminate between the two diagnoses. (Source: SOMANZ: Lupus in Pregnancy)

Oedema and weight gain from fluid retention are common to both conditions and also occur in normal pregnancy. This is not a discriminating feature between lupus nephritis and pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ: Lupus in Pregnancy)

Active lupus nephritis consumes complement, causing low C3 and C4, with rising anti-dsDNA antibody titres reflecting disease activity. In pre-eclampsia, complement levels are typically normal or elevated (complement is an acute-phase reactant in pregnancy). This combination of falling complement with rising anti-dsDNA is the most reliable discriminator between lupus nephritis and pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ: Lupus in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Fetal macrosomia (EFW >4.0 kg) in diabetic pregnancies carries increased risks of shoulder dystocia, brachial plexus injury, and emergency caesarean section. When EFW exceeds 4.5 kg in a diabetic pregnancy, delivery planning must balance these risks against prematurity. Induction of labour at 38-39 weeks is appropriate for insulin-requiring GDM with macrosomia, with the mode of delivery influenced by estimated fetal weight, previous obstetric history, and cervical favourability. Elective caesarean should be discussed when EFW exceeds 4.5-5.0 kg.
key_points: Insulin-requiring GDM with macrosomia warrants delivery at 38-39 weeks
EFW above 4.5 kg in diabetic pregnancy significantly increases shoulder dystocia risk
Previous vaginal delivery and favourable Bishop score support a trial of labour
Shared decision-making about mode of delivery is essential when macrosomia is present
explanation.pearls: Ultrasound estimation of fetal weight has a margin of error of 10-15% at term; when EFW is at the macrosomic threshold, this uncertainty means clinical counselling should present both induction and caesarean as reasonable options rather than mandating one approach.

options.rationale: With GDM requiring insulin, suboptimal glycaemic control, and EFW exceeding 4.5 kg, the balance of risks favours delivery at 38-39 weeks. Induction of labour is appropriate given the favourable Bishop score and prior vaginal delivery, but with a lower threshold for caesarean section if labour does not progress or if shoulder dystocia risk factors are present. (Source: ADIPS: GDM Management)

While elective caesarean may be offered when EFW exceeds 4.5-5.0 kg in a diabetic pregnancy, this woman has a favourable Bishop score and previous vaginal delivery. A trial of labour with early caesarean recourse is a reasonable first option, with the final decision made in shared discussion with the patient. (Source: ADIPS: GDM Management)

Continuing expectant management with insulin-requiring GDM and macrosomia increases the risk of stillbirth, shoulder dystocia, and birth trauma. Insulin-requiring GDM guidelines recommend delivery by 38-39 weeks, and earlier when there are complications such as macrosomia or poor glycaemic control. (Source: ADIPS: GDM Management)

While glycaemic optimisation should continue, delaying delivery to 40 weeks with macrosomia and suboptimal control increases the risk of adverse outcomes. Fetal macrosomia in the setting of GDM is unlikely to resolve with improved glycaemic control at this advanced gestation, and delivery timing should not be delayed. (Source: ADIPS: GDM Management)

While EFW is concerning, the AFI of 24 cm is at the upper limit of normal rather than true polyhydramnios (AFI >25 cm). There is no acute fetal compromise requiring emergency delivery. Planned delivery at 38-39 weeks allows adequate preparation and counselling. (Source: RANZCOG: Macrosomia)

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture complicates approximately 0.5% of trials of labour after caesarean section and is a time-critical emergency. The classic presentation includes sudden fetal bradycardia, acute abdominal pain, cessation of contractions, presenting part recession, and maternal haemodynamic instability. Risk factors include previous classical or T-incision, short inter-delivery interval (<18 months), oxytocin augmentation, and multiple previous caesarean sections. Decision-to-delivery time directly influences neonatal outcome, with delays beyond 18 minutes associated with increasing hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy risk.
key_points: Fetal bradycardia with presenting part recession in the setting of previous caesarean is uterine rupture until proven otherwise
Loss of uterine contractions occurs when the myometrium ruptures and cannot generate coordinated contraction
Category 1 caesarean must proceed within minutes as fetal outcome depends on delivery speed
Previous lower-segment caesarean carries a 0.5% rupture risk during TOLAC compared to 2-5% for classical scars
explanation.pearls: Epidural analgesia does not mask the pain of uterine rupture in most cases; studies show that 90% of women with rupture report breakthrough abdominal pain despite effective epidural, though the character changes from contraction-related to constant scar-site pain.

options.rationale: While abruption can cause fetal bradycardia and pain, the combination of presenting part recession, loss of contractions, and previous caesarean scar is more consistent with uterine rupture. In abruption, the uterus typically remains contracted and tense rather than losing contractility, and the presenting part does not recede. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC Guidelines)

The clinical triad of prolonged fetal bradycardia, acute abdominal pain with loss of contractions, and presenting part recession in the setting of previous caesarean section is diagnostic of uterine rupture until proven otherwise. Category 1 caesarean with laparotomy must be performed within minutes. Time from decision to delivery must be minimised as fetal survival depends on rapid delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC Guidelines)

Cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia but would not explain the cessation of contractions, lower segment tenderness, or presenting part recession. In cord prolapse, the cord is typically palpable on vaginal examination and management involves elevating the presenting part. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Intrapartum Emergencies)

Scar dehiscence (incomplete rupture with intact serosa) is typically an incidental finding and does not present with this degree of haemodynamic compromise and fetal distress. The clinical severity with fetal bradycardia, presenting part recession, and maternal shock indicates complete uterine rupture requiring immediate surgical intervention, not conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC Guidelines)

Uterine hyperstimulation causes excessive contractions, not cessation of contractions. The presenting part recession and lower segment tenderness are not features of hyperstimulation. This patient is in spontaneous labour without oxytocin augmentation. (Source: RANZCOG: VBAC Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Cervical cancer in pregnancy is rare but requires careful multidisciplinary management balancing maternal oncological outcomes with fetal wellbeing. For early-stage disease (stage IA-IB1 with tumour <2 cm), treatment can be safely deferred until after delivery with serial colposcopic and MRI surveillance without worsening maternal survival. Delivery is planned at 34-37 weeks via caesarean section, with concurrent radical hysterectomy or radical trachelectomy performed at the time of delivery. For more advanced stages, neoadjuvant chemotherapy during pregnancy or pregnancy termination for definitive treatment may be necessary.
key_points: Stage IB1 cervical cancer with tumour <2 cm in pregnancy can be safely monitored with deferred treatment
Serial colposcopy and MRI every 6-8 weeks monitor for progression during pregnancy
Caesarean delivery at 34-37 weeks with concurrent radical hysterectomy is the standard approach
Pelvic radiation is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Vaginal delivery through a cervix with invasive cancer has been associated with rare case reports of tumour dissemination and episiotomy-site implantation; caesarean section is therefore universally recommended for delivery in women with cervical cancer.

options.rationale: While radical hysterectomy is standard treatment for stage IB1 cervical cancer in non-pregnant women, performing it at 14 weeks gestation would terminate the pregnancy. For stage IB1 at this gestation, treatment can be safely deferred until fetal viability or maturity with close surveillance, without worsening maternal oncological outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG: Gynaecological Cancer in Pregnancy)

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy during pregnancy is considered for bulky stage IB2-IIB cancers to control disease while awaiting fetal maturity. For stage IB1 with a small tumour, the risks of chemotherapy to the fetus generally outweigh the benefits, as treatment can be safely deferred with surveillance. (Source: RANZCOG: Gynaecological Cancer in Pregnancy)

For stage IB1 cervical cancer diagnosed early in pregnancy, evidence supports deferring definitive treatment until after delivery when the tumour is small (less than 2 cm) and confined to the cervix without lymph node involvement. Serial colposcopic and MRI surveillance every 6-8 weeks monitors for progression. Delivery is typically planned at 34-37 weeks via caesarean section with concurrent radical hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Gynaecological Cancer in Pregnancy)

LLETZ or cone biopsy in pregnancy carries significant risks of haemorrhage, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, and preterm delivery. For confirmed invasive cancer, excisional procedures during pregnancy are generally avoided as they do not provide adequate surgical margins for invasive disease and carry procedural risks. (Source: RANZCOG: Gynaecological Cancer in Pregnancy)

Pelvic radiation is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy due to lethal fetal effects. Chemoradiation is the standard treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer in non-pregnant women but cannot be delivered during a continuing pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: Gynaecological Cancer in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: A retained placenta is defined as non-delivery of the placenta within 30 minutes of birth with active management (or 60 minutes with physiological management). It complicates 1-3% of vaginal deliveries. Manual removal under anaesthesia in theatre is the standard management. Risk factors include preterm birth, previous retained placenta, and previous uterine surgery. If manual removal encounters a plane of cleavage that cannot be established, placenta accreta spectrum should be suspected and senior obstetric involvement is essential.
key_points: Retained placenta is defined as non-delivery within 30 minutes with active management
Manual removal in theatre under anaesthesia is the standard treatment
Ongoing bleeding with a retained placenta constitutes PPH and requires concurrent resuscitation
If no cleavage plane is found during manual removal, placenta accreta should be suspected
explanation.pearls: Trapped placenta (separated but retained behind a closing cervix) can be distinguished from unseparated placenta by cord lengthening and a gush of blood suggesting separation has occurred; sublingual GTN 400 microg may relax the cervix sufficiently to allow delivery without theatre in this specific scenario.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour

options.rationale: The third stage has already exceeded 30 minutes with active management, which defines a retained placenta. The uterus is already well-contracted, so additional oxytocin is unlikely to aid placental separation. Continuing conservative management risks increasing blood loss without achieving delivery. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour

options.rationale: Umbilical vein injection (intra-umbilical oxytocin) has been studied but evidence for its effectiveness is inconsistent. With 45 minutes elapsed and ongoing bleeding of 500 mL, definitive management in theatre is more appropriate than further conservative measures. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour

options.rationale: Ultrasound is not routinely required before manual removal of a retained placenta. The clinical diagnosis is established by the failure of placental delivery after 30 minutes with active management. Ultrasound may delay definitive treatment and increase blood loss. (Source: RANZCOG: Third Stage of Labour)

After 30 minutes of active management without placental delivery, the placenta is retained and manual removal in theatre is indicated. This is performed under spinal, epidural top-up, or general anaesthesia. The uterine cavity is explored manually to ensure complete removal, followed by uterotonics and antibiotics. Proceeding to theatre is particularly important with ongoing bleeding of 500 mL. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour

options.rationale: GTN can relax a contracted cervix trapping a separated placenta, but this patient has a well-contracted uterus suggesting the placenta may be morbidly adherent (placenta accreta spectrum) or simply not yet separated. GTN without anaesthesia support risks uncontrolled uterine relaxation and haemorrhage. Manual removal in theatre remains the standard approach. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Third Stage of Labour

explanation.summary: Peripartum thrombotic microangiopathy requires discrimination between TTP, HELLP syndrome, and atypical HUS. TTP features severe thrombocytopenia (often <20 x10^9/L), neurological symptoms, MAHA, and relatively preserved renal function, with ADAMTS13 activity <10% being diagnostic. HELLP syndrome features elevated liver transaminases and typically less severe thrombocytopenia. Atypical HUS predominates postpartum with severe renal impairment. ADAMTS13 activity must be drawn before plasma exchange as the treatment replaces the deficient enzyme and normalises levels. Plasma exchange should begin urgently without waiting for results, as untreated TTP has >90% mortality.
key_points: ADAMTS13 activity <10% confirms TTP; the sample must be drawn before plasma exchange
Normal liver transaminases and coagulation studies distinguish TTP from HELLP and DIC
TTP features neurological predominance while aHUS features renal predominance
Plasma exchange is the cornerstone treatment and should not be delayed for ADAMTS13 results
explanation.pearls: The PLASMIC score (Platelet count <30, combined haemolysis variables, no active cancer, no solid organ transplant, MCV <90, INR <1.5, creatinine <177) has >90% positive predictive value for severe ADAMTS13 deficiency when the score is 6-7, allowing pre-test probability assessment while awaiting ADAMTS13 results.

options.rationale: While complement-mediated aHUS is an important differential, it typically presents postpartum and features more prominent renal impairment. In this case, the predominant features are severe thrombocytopenia with neurological symptoms and relatively preserved renal function, making TTP the more urgent consideration. Complement testing takes days to return and should not delay management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Normal liver transaminases make HELLP syndrome and hepatic pathology unlikely. The clinical picture with profound thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, and normal LFTs points away from a hepatic cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

The normal fibrinogen and INR effectively exclude DIC. Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS) are characterised by consumptive thrombocytopenia without coagulation factor consumption, distinguishing them from DIC where fibrinogen is low and INR prolonged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Renal biopsy is contraindicated with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 18 x10^9/L) due to unacceptable bleeding risk. The histological appearances of TTP and HUS overlap, and the clinical distinction relies on ADAMTS13 activity levels rather than tissue diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

ADAMTS13 activity below 10% is diagnostic of TTP, caused by acquired inhibitory antibodies against the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease. This must be sent urgently before initiating plasma exchange (which replaces ADAMTS13 and confounds the result). The clinical picture of severe thrombocytopenia, neurological symptoms, MAHA with normal LFTs and coagulation, and relatively preserved renal function is classic for TTP. Plasma exchange should not be delayed for the result but the sample must be drawn first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: After one ectopic pregnancy the risk of another is roughly 10 per cent, which is about ten times the background rate, and it is higher still with tubal damage, previous pelvic inflammatory disease, smoking or assisted conception. Fertility after unilateral salpingectomy with a healthy contralateral tube is close to normal, so conception can be attempted once she feels ready and hCG has resolved. The practical advice is an early transvaginal ultrasound at six to seven weeks in any future pregnancy to establish the location, and prompt presentation for pain or bleeding rather than waiting for a routine scan. In context, an intrauterine device or progestogen implant does not raise the absolute risk of ectopic pregnancy, but any pregnancy that occurs with one in place is more likely to be ectopic.
key_points: Recurrence risk is about 10 per cent after one ectopic pregnancy.
Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound at six to seven weeks next pregnancy.
Fertility is near normal with one healthy remaining tube.
Smoking cessation lowers the risk of a further ectopic pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Give her a plan in writing: a positive test, then a scan at six to seven weeks, and earlier review for pain, bleeding or shoulder tip discomfort.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Recurrence runs at roughly one in ten, so an early scan to confirm the pregnancy is inside the uterus is the one thing that changes, and she should present promptly with pain or bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Assisted reproduction is the route when both tubes are absent or damaged, or after a reasonable period of infertility, not when one healthy tube and both ovaries remain. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Tubal patency testing belongs in the work-up of infertility after about twelve months of trying, or where pelvic inflammatory disease or adhesions are suspected. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: A previous ectopic is the strongest single risk factor for the next one, so telling her the risk is unchanged removes the reason for the early scan. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: A defined delay is needed after methotrexate, where conception is avoided for three months, and after molar pregnancy while hCG is monitored, but not after surgical treatment with a resolved hCG. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Tissue lodged at the cervical os is a gynaecological emergency that requires immediate manual removal. The tissue mechanically prevents cervical closure and impairs myometrial contraction, leading to ongoing haemorrhage. Removal with sponge forceps or ring forceps can be performed at the bedside and often produces immediate relief. Definitive surgical evacuation should follow to ensure complete uterine emptying. Rh-negative patients require anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours of any pregnancy loss event beyond 10 weeks or with surgical intervention.
key_points: Tissue at the cervical os is a mechanical cause of ongoing haemorrhage requiring immediate removal
Cervical shock (bradycardia and hypotension from cervical distension) may occur and resolves with tissue removal
Anti-D immunoglobulin is indicated for Rh-negative women after miscarriage events
Surgical evacuation is preferred over medical management when bleeding is heavy and haemoglobin is falling
explanation.pearls: In Rh-negative women, anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU before 12 weeks, 625 IU at or after 12 weeks) should be given within 72 hours of miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or any uterine instrumentation.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Management of Early Pregnancy Loss

options.rationale: Medical management with mifepristone-misoprostol is appropriate for missed or incomplete miscarriage when the patient is haemodynamically stable without tissue at the os. With active heavy bleeding and visible tissue at the cervical os, immediate removal of the tissue is required to allow the cervix to close and stop bleeding. (Source: Queensland Health - Early Pregnancy Loss)

Tissue lodged at the cervical os causes cervical shock (vasovagal from cervical distension) and prevents uterine contraction, perpetuating bleeding. Immediate removal of cervical os tissue with sponge forceps is the priority, followed by definitive surgical evacuation (suction curettage) given the heavy ongoing bleeding. Anti-D immunoglobulin is also required given her Rh-negative status. (Source: RANZCOG - Management of Early Pregnancy Loss)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Management of Early Pregnancy Loss

options.rationale: While IV access and fluid resuscitation are appropriate concurrent steps, delaying removal of tissue at the os to obtain an ultrasound is not indicated. The clinical picture is clear: open os with visible tissue and heavy bleeding. The immediate priority is removing the obstructing tissue. (Source: Queensland Health - Early Pregnancy Loss)

Oxytocin may assist uterine contraction but does not address the immediate problem of tissue at the cervical os preventing cervical closure. Waiting for spontaneous expulsion risks worsening haemorrhage and haemodynamic compromise. Active removal is required. (Source: RANZCOG - Management of Early Pregnancy Loss)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Management of Early Pregnancy Loss

options.rationale: While tranexamic acid reduces bleeding in various settings, it does not address the mechanical cause of ongoing haemorrhage - tissue at the cervical os preventing uterine contraction. Sublingual misoprostol alone is insufficient when tissue is obstructing the os. (Source: Queensland Health - Early Pregnancy Loss)

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. In women with an intact uterus, oestrogen must always be combined with a progestogen for endometrial protection. Transdermal oestradiol is preferred over oral preparations due to lower VTE and stroke risk. A first-degree relative with breast cancer diagnosed after age 60 does not contraindicate HRT but warrants informed discussion. The choice between cyclical and continuous progestogen depends on menopausal stage - cyclical is used in early menopause and continuous after 12 months of amenorrhoea or 2 years of cyclical HRT.
key_points: Unopposed oestrogen is contraindicated in women with an intact uterus due to endometrial cancer risk
Transdermal oestradiol carries lower VTE risk than oral oestrogen
Micronised progesterone has a more favourable safety profile than synthetic progestins
A family history of breast cancer diagnosed after age 60 is not an absolute contraindication to HRT
explanation.pearls: Transdermal oestradiol at standard doses (25-50 mcg/day) does not significantly increase VTE risk, unlike oral oestrogens which increase VTE risk 2-fold through hepatic first-pass prothrombotic protein synthesis.

options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with an intact uterus significantly increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. A progestogen must be added for endometrial protection. Oestrogen-only therapy is reserved for women who have had a hysterectomy. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society - HRT Guideline)

While combined oral HRT provides both oestrogen and endometrial protection, oral oestrogens carry a higher risk of VTE compared with transdermal delivery due to first-pass hepatic metabolism and prothrombotic effects. Current Australian guidance favours transdermal oestradiol as the preferred route. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society - HRT Guideline)

Transdermal oestradiol is preferred over oral oestrogen as it avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and carries lower VTE risk. In a woman with an intact uterus, a progestogen is mandatory for endometrial protection. Cyclical progesterone (12-14 days per cycle) is appropriate in the perimenopausal transition and early menopause. Micronised progesterone has a favourable metabolic and breast safety profile compared with synthetic progestins. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society - HRT Guideline)

Tibolone is a synthetic steroid with oestrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic activity that can treat menopausal symptoms and provides endometrial protection. However, it is generally reserved for women who are at least 12 months postmenopausal and is associated with increased stroke risk in older women. It is not typically first-line for initial HRT. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

Vaginal oestrogen effectively treats urogenital symptoms (dryness, dyspareunia) but has minimal systemic absorption and does not adequately treat vasomotor symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats. Systemic HRT is needed for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society - HRT Guideline)

explanation.summary: Australia's renewed National Cervical Screening Program uses primary HPV testing every 5 years for women aged 25-74, replacing the previous 2-yearly Pap smear program. Since July 2022, self-collection has been available to all eligible participants, improving access and participation rates. If HPV is detected, reflex liquid-based cytology is performed on the same clinician-collected sample or a subsequent clinician-collected sample if the initial test was self-collected. HPV vaccination reduces but does not eliminate cervical cancer risk, and vaccinated individuals follow the same screening schedule.
key_points: NCSP uses primary HPV testing every 5 years from age 25 to 74
Self-collection is available to all eligible participants since July 2022
HPV vaccination does not alter the screening interval or method
Positive HPV results require reflex cytology from a clinician-collected sample
explanation.pearls: Self-collected vaginal HPV samples have sensitivity above 90% for detecting CIN2+ when using PCR-based assays, making them clinically equivalent to clinician-collected samples for primary HPV screening.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program
Australian Government - National Cervical Screening Program

options.rationale: Under the renewed NCSP, the screening interval is 5 years for HPV-based testing, not 3 years. At 5 years since her last negative HPV test, she is due now, not overdue. The 3-year interval was from the old Pap smear-based program. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program

options.rationale: She is exactly 5 years from her last negative HPV test, so she is due for screening now. There is no age-based deferral to 30 under the current NCSP. Screening commences from age 25 (or 2 years after first sexual activity in unvaccinated individuals) and continues 5-yearly. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program

options.rationale: The renewed NCSP replaced cytology-based screening with primary HPV testing in December 2017. Conventional cytology (Pap smear) is no longer the primary screening modality in Australia. HPV vaccination does not change the screening method, only the expected prevalence of high-risk HPV types. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program

options.rationale: Under the renewed NCSP, she is due at 5 years from her last negative HPV test. Since 1 July 2022, all eligible screening participants in Australia can choose self-collection as an alternative to clinician-collected samples. Both methods use PCR-based HPV testing with equivalent sensitivity for detecting high-risk HPV types. If HPV is detected on self-collection, reflex liquid-based cytology requires a clinician-collected sample. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program

options.rationale: HPV vaccination does not alter the recommended screening interval under the NCSP. The vaccine covers the most common oncogenic HPV types (16 and 18) but does not protect against all high-risk types. The 5-yearly screening interval applies regardless of vaccination status. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - National Cervical Screening Program

explanation.summary: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam criteria when two of three features are present: oligo-ovulation or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (12 or more antral follicles per ovary or ovarian volume greater than 10 mL). This patient meets all three criteria. Management depends on whether pregnancy is desired. For women not seeking pregnancy, the combined oral contraceptive pill is first-line for menstrual regulation, endometrial protection, and androgen suppression. Lifestyle modification targeting 5-10% weight loss significantly improves metabolic and reproductive outcomes.
key_points: Rotterdam criteria require 2 of 3: oligo-anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology
COCP is first-line for menstrual regulation and endometrial protection when pregnancy is not desired
