Anti-androgens such as spironolactone require reliable contraception due to teratogenicity
5-10% weight loss improves ovulatory function, insulin sensitivity, and androgen levels
explanation.pearls: Free androgen index (FAI = total testosterone/SHBG x 100) above 5 is the most sensitive biochemical marker for hyperandrogenism in PCOS, often elevated even when total testosterone is within the normal range.

sources.label: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash

options.rationale: While metformin has a role in PCOS for metabolic and ovulatory benefits, it is not first-line for menstrual regulation in women not seeking pregnancy. The combined oral contraceptive pill is first-line for cycle regulation, acne management, and endometrial protection when contraception is desired. Metformin may be added as adjunctive therapy. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash

options.rationale: Spironolactone is an effective anti-androgen for hirsutism and acne in PCOS but requires reliable contraception due to teratogenicity (feminisation of male fetus). It is not first-line monotherapy and is typically added after or alongside the combined oral contraceptive pill. It does not address menstrual irregularity or endometrial protection. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash

options.rationale: Clomifene citrate is an ovulation induction agent used when pregnancy is desired. This patient is not seeking pregnancy, so ovulation induction is inappropriate. Clomifene also carries risks of multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation that are unnecessary in this context. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash

options.rationale: High-dose cyproterone acetate monotherapy is not recommended as first-line due to hepatotoxicity risk and thrombotic potential without consistent cycle regulation. Low-dose cyproterone acetate is available as a component of certain combined oral contraceptive pills, which is a more appropriate vehicle. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Dermatology)

The combined oral contraceptive pill is first-line for menstrual regulation, endometrial protection, acne management, and contraception in PCOS when pregnancy is not desired. A formulation containing cyproterone acetate has additional anti-androgenic benefit for acne. Lifestyle modification (structured exercise and dietary counselling) is a cornerstone of PCOS management, particularly with elevated BMI. (Source: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash)
source_refs: International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS - Monash

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes management follows a stepwise approach: lifestyle modification (medical nutrition therapy and structured physical activity) for 1-2 weeks, followed by pharmacotherapy if glycaemic targets are not met. ADIPS targets are fasting BSL below 5.0 mmol/L, 1-hour postprandial below 7.4 mmol/L, and 2-hour postprandial below 6.7 mmol/L. Metformin is an acceptable first-line oral agent when diet fails, with insulin added if metformin alone is insufficient. Ongoing fetal surveillance with serial growth ultrasounds is essential given the risk of macrosomia and related complications.
key_points: ADIPS diagnostic criteria for GDM on 75 g OGTT - fasting 5.1 or above, 1-hour 10.0 or above, 2-hour 8.5 or above mmol/L
ADIPS treatment targets - fasting below 5.0, 1-hour postprandial below 7.4, 2-hour postprandial below 6.7 mmol/L
Lifestyle modification trial of 1-2 weeks before pharmacotherapy is recommended
Metformin is an appropriate first-line pharmacological option when lifestyle measures are insufficient
explanation.pearls: Metformin crosses the placenta but long-term follow-up studies of children exposed to metformin in utero (MiG TOFU trial) show no adverse developmental effects at 2 years, though children may have slightly higher subcutaneous fat.

options.rationale: This patient has failed to achieve glycaemic targets after 1-2 weeks of lifestyle modification. The ADIPS targets are fasting BSL below 5.0 mmol/L and 1-hour postprandial below 7.4 mmol/L. Her fasting and postprandial values are consistently above target. Metformin is an appropriate first-line pharmacological agent for GDM in Australia, particularly when fasting hyperglycaemia predominates. (Source: ADIPS - GDM Management Guidelines)

The standard trial of lifestyle modification for GDM is 1-2 weeks. After 2 weeks with consistently elevated fasting and postprandial glucose, continuing diet alone delays achievement of glycaemic targets and risks adverse fetal outcomes including macrosomia. Pharmacotherapy should be initiated. (Source: ADIPS - GDM Management Guidelines)

While insulin is effective and safe in GDM, ADIPS guidelines support metformin as an appropriate first-line pharmacological option when lifestyle measures fail. Insulin is preferred when metformin is contraindicated or insufficient, or in certain clinical scenarios such as very high glucose levels. Metformin should be trialled first. (Source: ADIPS - GDM Management Guidelines)

Glibenclamide (glibenclamide) crosses the placenta and is associated with higher rates of neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia compared with metformin and insulin. It is not recommended as first-line pharmacotherapy for GDM in current Australian guidelines. (Source: ADIPS - GDM Management Guidelines)

GDM alone is not an indication for elective caesarean section. The mode of delivery depends on glycaemic control, estimated fetal weight, and obstetric factors. With appropriate treatment, most women with GDM can aim for vaginal birth. Induction of labour at 38-39 weeks may be considered if control is suboptimal. (Source: RANZCOG - GDM Guideline)

explanation.summary: Rh-negative women require anti-D immunoglobulin after any potential sensitising event to prevent Rh isoimmunisation. Sensitising events include abdominal trauma, vaginal bleeding, invasive procedures, miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy. The dose depends on gestational age: 250 IU before 12 weeks, 625 IU at or after 12 weeks. Kleihauer-Betke testing or flow cytometry is performed after events at or beyond 12 weeks to detect large fetomaternal haemorrhage requiring additional anti-D. Anti-D should be given within 72 hours of the event.
key_points: Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event requiring anti-D regardless of vaginal bleeding
Anti-D dose is 250 IU before 12 weeks and 625 IU at or after 12 weeks gestation
Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage to determine if additional anti-D is needed
Standard 625 IU dose covers approximately 6 mL of fetal red cells
explanation.pearls: Anti-D immunoglobulin should be given within 72 hours of a sensitising event, but if missed, administration up to 10 days later may still provide some protection and should not be withheld.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines
RANZCOG - Guidelines on the Use of Anti-D

options.rationale: Abdominal trauma is a recognised sensitising event regardless of whether vaginal bleeding is present, as fetomaternal haemorrhage can occur without external signs. Anti-D immunoglobulin is indicated after any potential sensitising event in Rh-negative women with no pre-existing anti-D antibodies. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines

options.rationale: At 18 weeks (beyond 12 weeks gestation), the recommended dose of anti-D is 625 IU intramuscularly. A Kleihauer-Betke test (or flow cytometry) should be performed to quantify fetomaternal haemorrhage, as large-volume bleeds after trauma may require additional doses of anti-D. The standard 625 IU dose covers approximately 6 mL of fetal red cells. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines

options.rationale: The 250 IU dose of anti-D is appropriate for sensitising events before 12 weeks gestation. At 18 weeks gestation, the dose is 625 IU because the volume of fetal blood in the fetoplacental circulation is larger. Kleihauer-Betke testing is needed to detect large fetomaternal haemorrhage. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines

options.rationale: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 weeks does not replace the need for event-based anti-D administration. Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event requiring prompt anti-D regardless of scheduled prophylaxis timing. Waiting until 28 weeks risks sensitisation from a fetomaternal haemorrhage occurring now. (Source: RANZCOG - Guidelines on the Use of Anti-D)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Guidelines on the Use of Anti-D

options.rationale: Anti-D should be administered as soon as possible after the sensitising event (ideally within 72 hours) and should not be withheld pending Kleihauer-Betke results. The Kleihauer test determines whether additional anti-D is needed beyond the standard dose, not whether anti-D should be given at all. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood - Anti-D Guidelines

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is diagnosed by characteristic pruritus (often palmoplantar, worse at night) combined with elevated serum bile acids above 19 micromol/L. It carries risk of sudden fetal death, the mechanism of which likely involves bile acid-mediated cardiac arrhythmia in the fetus. Risk stratification by bile acid level guides management: mild (19-39 micromol/L) with delivery at 38 weeks, moderate (40-99 micromol/L) with delivery at 37 weeks, and severe (100 micromol/L or above) with individualised earlier delivery. Ursodeoxycholic acid remains first-line treatment despite the PITCHES trial showing limited effect on perinatal outcomes.
key_points: Bile acids above 19 micromol/L with pruritus confirm ICP diagnosis
Risk of stillbirth increases significantly with bile acids above 40 micromol/L
UDCA 10-15 mg/kg/day is first-line treatment for symptom relief
Delivery timing is stratified by bile acid level - 37 weeks for levels 40-99 micromol/L
explanation.pearls: Bile acid levels above 100 micromol/L carry a stillbirth risk of approximately 3.4% - these patients may require inpatient monitoring with CTG and consideration of delivery as early as 34-36 weeks depending on trajectory.

options.rationale: Pruritus gravidarum (benign pruritus of pregnancy) is a diagnosis of exclusion. Elevated bile acids above 14 micromol/L confirm intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP), which carries significant fetal risks including stillbirth. Simple emollients and antihistamines are insufficient. (Source: RANZCOG - Obstetric Cholestasis)

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP) typically presents with urticarial papules and plaques within striae, not isolated palmoplantar pruritus without rash. The elevated bile acids and transaminases confirm ICP. Systemic corticosteroids are not indicated for ICP. (Source: RANZCOG - Obstetric Cholestasis)

ICP with bile acids between 40 and 99 micromol/L carries increased risk of adverse perinatal outcomes. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is the first-line treatment for symptom relief and may reduce bile acid levels. Weekly monitoring of bile acids and liver function is recommended. Current Australian practice recommends planned delivery at 37 weeks for bile acids 40-99 micromol/L to reduce stillbirth risk. (Source: RANZCOG - Obstetric Cholestasis)

Colestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant that may provide symptom relief but impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamins including vitamin K, potentially worsening coagulopathy risk. It is less effective than UDCA and not first-line. Delivery at 39 weeks is too late for bile acids of 48 micromol/L - delivery at 37 weeks is recommended. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Gastroenterology)

The UDCA dose is subtherapeutic at 500 mg daily for moderate ICP - the recommended dose is 10-15 mg/kg/day, typically 1000-1500 mg daily in divided doses. Fortnightly monitoring is insufficient for bile acids in the 40-99 range, and delivery should be planned at 37 weeks, not 38 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG - Obstetric Cholestasis)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by persistent vomiting in pregnancy associated with weight loss exceeding 5%, dehydration, and ketonuria. Admission criteria include inability to tolerate oral intake, significant dehydration or electrolyte derangement, and weight loss exceeding 5% of pre-pregnancy weight. Thiamine must be given before any dextrose-containing IV fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Gestational thyrotoxicosis from hCG cross-reactivity occurs in up to 60% of hyperemesis cases and does not require antithyroid treatment. The metabolic alkalosis with hypokalaemia and hypochloraemia results from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid.
key_points: Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede dextrose-containing fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
Gestational thyrotoxicosis from hCG cross-reactivity resolves spontaneously and does not require antithyroid drugs
Hypokalaemic hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis is the typical electrolyte pattern in hyperemesis
Admission is indicated for weight loss above 5%, inability to tolerate oral intake, or electrolyte derangement
explanation.pearls: Wernicke encephalopathy from hyperemesis gravidarum can present atypically without the classic triad - any patient with prolonged vomiting in pregnancy should receive IV thiamine 100 mg before glucose-containing fluids.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: This patient has clinical signs of significant dehydration (postural hypotension, ketonuria) and has been unable to tolerate any oral intake for 48 hours. Attempting oral therapy is inadequate - she requires intravenous fluid resuscitation and parenteral antiemetics. (Source: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis that has not responded to first-line and second-line antiemetics. They should be avoided before 10 weeks gestation due to association with orofacial clefts. While this patient is at 10 weeks, corticosteroids should only be considered after failure of standard antiemetics, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction. (Source: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Thiamine supplementation is important to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, but this patient's degree of dehydration (postural hypotension, 48 hours nil orally, significant ketonuria) and electrolyte derangement (hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis) require inpatient management, not outpatient infusions. (Source: Queensland Health - Hyperemesis Gravidarum)

This patient meets criteria for admission: significant dehydration with postural hypotension, inability to tolerate oral intake for 48 hours, greater than 5% weight loss, ketonuria 3+, and electrolyte derangement. Management priorities are IV fluid resuscitation with potassium correction, thiamine supplementation before dextrose-containing fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and parenteral antiemetic therapy. The suppressed TSH and elevated free T4 represent gestational thyrotoxicosis from hCG cross-reactivity, which resolves with treatment of hyperemesis. (Source: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy

options.rationale: The suppressed TSH and mildly elevated free T4 in this context represent gestational thyrotoxicosis caused by hCG cross-reactivity with the TSH receptor. This is a self-limiting condition that resolves as hCG levels decline in the second trimester. Antithyroid drugs are not indicated and could cause hypothyroidism. True hyperthyroidism should be suspected only if TSH receptor antibodies are positive or there are features of Graves disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic disease requires structured post-evacuation surveillance through the Australian and New Zealand GTD registry. Complete hydatidiform moles carry a 15-20% risk of malignant transformation to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Serial weekly beta-hCG levels are monitored until normalisation, followed by monthly levels for 6 months for complete moles. Reliable contraception is mandatory throughout surveillance to avoid pregnancy confounding beta-hCG interpretation. Indications for chemotherapy include plateauing or rising beta-hCG, histological evidence of choriocarcinoma, or metastatic disease.
key_points: Complete moles carry 15-20% risk of developing GTN requiring chemotherapy
Weekly beta-hCG monitoring until normalisation, then monthly for 6 months post-normalisation
Reliable contraception is essential throughout the surveillance period
Rising or plateauing beta-hCG mandates further investigation and likely chemotherapy
explanation.pearls: The surveillance period after partial mole is 12 months post-normalisation of beta-hCG (compared with 6 months for complete mole), reflecting the lower but not negligible risk of malignant transformation (approximately 0.5-5%).

options.rationale: The monitoring interval after normalisation is too long and the total surveillance duration is not aligned with Australian GTD registry protocols. For a complete mole, once beta-hCG normalises, monthly monitoring is required, and the total surveillance period after normalisation depends on whether the decline was spontaneous. (Source: ANZGOG - GTD Management Guidelines)

A declining beta-hCG does not exclude subsequent malignant transformation to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). Complete moles have approximately 15-20% risk of developing GTN. Serial monitoring to confirm normalisation and maintained normalisation is mandatory. (Source: ANZGOG - GTD Management Guidelines)

Registration with the GTD registry is appropriate, but chemotherapy is not indicated with a declining beta-hCG. Chemotherapy for GTN is indicated when beta-hCG plateaus (less than 10% decline over 3 consecutive weekly values), rises, or remains elevated beyond 6 months post-evacuation. This patient's level is declining appropriately. (Source: ANZGOG - GTD Management Guidelines)

Repeat curettage is not routinely indicated after molar evacuation unless there is significant retained tissue causing haemorrhage, and carries risk of uterine perforation and Asherman syndrome. The COCP is recommended during the surveillance period for contraception, but a second curettage is not appropriate here with beta-hCG declining. (Source: ANZGOG - GTD Management Guidelines)

Complete mole management requires registration with the Australian and New Zealand GTD registry for centralised monitoring. Weekly beta-hCG is measured until normalisation, then monthly levels for 6 months post-normalisation for complete moles (12 months for partial moles). Reliable contraception is essential throughout surveillance as pregnancy would confound beta-hCG monitoring and could mask GTN. Conception can be attempted after completing the surveillance period. (Source: ANZGOG - GTD Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Simple ovarian cysts in premenopausal women are overwhelmingly benign, most commonly functional (follicular or corpus luteum) cysts. The IOTA simple rules and Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) help stratify risk. Features suggesting malignancy include solid components, papillary projections, thick irregular septae, ascites, bilateral involvement, and elevated CA-125. Simple unilocular cysts up to 7 cm can be managed expectantly with repeat imaging. Surgery is indicated for persistent cysts, complex features, enlarging cysts, or symptomatic torsion. In postmenopausal women, the threshold for intervention is lower as functional cysts are no longer expected.
key_points: Simple unilocular ovarian cysts up to 7 cm in premenopausal women are almost always benign
IOTA simple rules help classify benign versus malignant features on ultrasound
Oral contraceptives do not accelerate resolution of existing functional cysts
Postmenopausal women with ovarian cysts require more aggressive investigation due to higher malignancy risk
explanation.pearls: CA-125 has poor specificity in premenopausal women as it is elevated in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, and during menstruation - it is most useful in postmenopausal women where the Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI = ultrasound score x menopausal status x CA-125) above 200 warrants gynaecological oncology referral.

sources.label: Cochrane - Oral Contraceptives for Functional Ovarian Cysts
RCOG - Management of Suspected Ovarian Masses in Premenopausal Women

options.rationale: Simple ovarian cysts up to 7 cm in premenopausal women are almost always benign (functional cysts). International Ovarian Tumour Analysis (IOTA) simple rules classify this as a benign pattern (unilocular, smooth walls, no solid components, no Doppler flow). For cysts 5-7 cm, repeat imaging in 8-12 weeks is appropriate to confirm resolution, as most functional cysts resolve spontaneously within 2-3 cycles. CA-125 is normal, further supporting benign aetiology. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Cysts)

This cyst has all features of a simple benign cyst: unilocular, thin-walled, no solid components, no septae, no Doppler flow, and a normal CA-125. Gynaecological oncology referral is indicated for complex cysts with features suggesting malignancy (solid components, papillary projections, irregular septae, ascites, elevated CA-125). (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Cysts)

Surgical intervention is not indicated for a simple cyst that may resolve spontaneously. Surgery carries risks of reduced ovarian reserve, adhesions, and anaesthetic complications. Torsion risk is present but does not mandate prophylactic surgery for a simple cyst. Surgery is considered if the cyst persists beyond 2-3 cycles or is enlarging. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Cysts)

The combined oral contraceptive pill does not accelerate resolution of existing ovarian cysts, although it may reduce the formation of new functional cysts. A Cochrane review found no benefit of oral contraceptives for expectant management of functional ovarian cysts. (Source: Cochrane - Oral Contraceptives for Functional Ovarian Cysts)
source_refs: Cochrane - Oral Contraceptives for Functional Ovarian Cysts

options.rationale: CT is inferior to transvaginal ultrasound for ovarian cyst characterisation and adds unnecessary radiation exposure. Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice for assessing ovarian cysts. MRI may be considered for indeterminate lesions on ultrasound, but CT is not the appropriate next step. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Cysts)

explanation.summary: Interstitial ectopic pregnancy implants within the intramural portion of the fallopian tube where it traverses the myometrium. It is particularly dangerous because the thick myometrial wall allows the pregnancy to grow larger before rupture, leading to massive haemorrhage from the uterine and ovarian vessels. The interstitial line sign on ultrasound (an echogenic line extending from the endometrial cavity to the ectopic mass) helps distinguish it from an angular pregnancy. Previous ipsilateral salpingectomy is a risk factor. Surgical management by an experienced operator is preferred for most cases, particularly with higher beta-hCG levels and visible embryonic structures.
key_points: Interstitial ectopic accounts for 2-4% of ectopics but has 2-2.5 times higher mortality than tubal ectopics
The interstitial line sign is a key ultrasound diagnostic feature
Previous ipsilateral salpingectomy is a risk factor for interstitial ectopic
Laparoscopic cornuostomy or cornual wedge resection is the surgical approach of choice
explanation.pearls: The interstitial portion of the tube can expand to 3-5 cm before rupture, which may not occur until 8-16 weeks gestation - later than typical tubal ectopics, making high clinical suspicion essential in women with prior salpingectomy.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: While methotrexate can be used for interstitial ectopic pregnancy, single-dose methotrexate has significantly lower success rates for interstitial ectopics (50-65%) compared with tubal ectopics. The higher beta-hCG level and vascularity of the interstitial segment increase rupture risk. Multi-dose protocols or direct injection may be considered, but many centres prefer surgical management. (Source: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancy is a high-risk variant accounting for 2-4% of ectopic pregnancies, with mortality 2-2.5 times higher than tubal ectopics due to the rich myometrial blood supply and potential for catastrophic haemorrhage at rupture. With a beta-hCG of 12,800, visible gestational sac with yolk sac, and thin overlying myometrium (less than 5 mm), surgical management by laparoscopic cornuostomy or cornual wedge resection by an experienced operator is the safest approach. (Source: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Expectant management is inappropriate for interstitial ectopic pregnancy with a rising or high beta-hCG and a visible gestational sac. The interstitial segment can expand to accommodate the pregnancy before catastrophic rupture at 8-16 weeks, with massive intraperitoneal haemorrhage. Active intervention is required. (Source: KEMH Clinical Guidelines - Ectopic Pregnancy)

Emergency laparotomy is indicated for ruptured interstitial ectopic with haemodynamic instability. This patient is currently stable with no signs of rupture. A planned laparoscopic approach by an experienced surgeon is appropriate and avoids the morbidity of laparotomy. Hysterectomy is rarely necessary when resection is performed before rupture. (Source: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Local methotrexate injection is a technique used at some centres for interstitial ectopic but requires interventional radiology expertise and is not widely available. When available, it can be effective but carries risk of incomplete treatment. Laparoscopic surgical management remains the standard approach when the diagnosis is clear. (Source: BMJ Best Practice - Ectopic Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency managed using the HELPERR mnemonic: Help (call for assistance), Episiotomy (if needed for access), Legs (McRoberts positioning), Pressure (suprapubic), Enter (internal rotational manoeuvres), Remove posterior arm, Roll (Gaskin manoeuvre). After McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail, the critical next step is internal manoeuvres - either rotational manoeuvres (Rubin II, Wood's screw) or delivery of the posterior arm. Fundal pressure and excessive lateral traction are absolutely contraindicated. The entire sequence should ideally be completed within 5 minutes of head delivery to minimise fetal hypoxia.
key_points: Fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated - it worsens impaction and causes injury
McRoberts with suprapubic pressure resolves approximately 50% of shoulder dystocia cases
Internal rotational manoeuvres or posterior arm delivery follow if McRoberts fails
Excessive lateral traction on the fetal head is the primary cause of brachial plexus injury
explanation.pearls: Delivery of the posterior arm has the highest single-manoeuvre success rate (approximately 85%) in shoulder dystocia but is technically demanding - the operator reaches along the posterior arm, flexes the elbow, sweeps the forearm across the chest, and delivers the hand and arm.

options.rationale: Fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated in shoulder dystocia as it further impacts the anterior shoulder behind the symphysis and significantly increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture. This is a critical safety point - fundal pressure worsens the impaction. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia)

Excessive traction on the fetal head is the primary cause of brachial plexus injury in shoulder dystocia. Lateral traction stretches the brachial plexus over the impacted shoulder. Only gentle axial traction should be used, and further pulling when the shoulder is impacted will not resolve the dystocia. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia)

An episiotomy alone does not resolve shoulder dystocia because the obstruction is bony (shoulder against symphysis), not soft tissue. An episiotomy may be performed to facilitate internal manoeuvres (posterior arm delivery, rotational manoeuvres) but is not itself a treatment for the bony impaction. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia)

After McRoberts with suprapubic pressure has failed, internal manoeuvres are the next step. The Rubin II manoeuvre involves reaching behind the posterior shoulder and rotating the fetal shoulders into an oblique diameter, disimpacting the anterior shoulder from behind the symphysis. Wood's screw manoeuvre (pressure on the anterior surface of the posterior shoulder) can also rotate the baby. If rotation fails, delivery of the posterior arm should be attempted. These internal manoeuvres have high success rates. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia)

The Gaskin (all-fours) manoeuvre can be effective by changing the pelvic dimensions and using gravity to disimpact the posterior shoulder. However, in the HELPERR mnemonic sequence, internal manoeuvres (rotation and posterior arm delivery) are attempted before changing position to all fours when McRoberts and suprapubic pressure have failed. All-fours may be attempted if internal manoeuvres fail. (Source: RANZCOG - Shoulder Dystocia)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency with mortality rates of 20-60%. The classic presentation involves sudden cardiovascular collapse, acute respiratory failure, seizures, and DIC occurring during or shortly after labour and delivery. The pathophysiology involves an abnormal maternal immune response to fetal antigens entering the maternal circulation, triggering complement activation and consumptive coagulopathy. Management is entirely supportive: aggressive cardiopulmonary resuscitation, massive transfusion with early fibrinogen replacement, and consideration of perimortem caesarean if undelivered. There is no specific treatment.
key_points: AFE classically presents with the triad of cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and DIC
Fibrinogen is the earliest coagulation factor to fall in obstetric DIC and should be replaced early
Target fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage using cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate
AFE is a diagnosis of exclusion supported by the classic clinical syndrome
explanation.pearls: In obstetric DIC, fibrinogen below 2.0 g/L has a positive predictive value above 90% for severe postpartum haemorrhage - it falls earlier and more precipitously than other coagulation parameters and should be the primary monitoring target.

sources.label: NBA - Patient Blood Management Guideline: Obstetrics

options.rationale: This presentation is classic amniotic fluid embolism (AFE): sudden cardiovascular collapse, acute hypoxia, seizures, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with coagulopathic haemorrhage shortly after delivery. The critically low fibrinogen of 0.6 g/L confirms consumptive coagulopathy. Management is supportive: aggressive resuscitation, massive transfusion protocol activation, and early replacement of fibrinogen (target above 2.0 g/L) with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. (Source: ANZCA - Obstetric Anaesthesia Guidelines)

While acute PE can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse and hypoxia, the combination of seizures and immediate-onset DIC with coagulopathic haemorrhage is not typical of PE. Commencing anticoagulation in the context of active postpartum haemorrhage and DIC would be catastrophic. The temporal relationship to delivery and the coagulopathy pattern point to AFE. (Source: RANZCOG - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Eclampsia typically presents with hypertension and proteinuria, and postpartum eclampsia is usually not associated with acute cardiovascular collapse, cyanosis, or DIC with hypofibrinogenaemia. This patient's BP is profoundly low, not elevated. The degree of hypoxia and coagulopathy is not explained by eclampsia alone. (Source: RANZCOG - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Air embolism is extremely rare in vaginal delivery and typically occurs during caesarean section or uterine manipulation. There are no features here suggesting air entry. The seizures, acute DIC, and pattern of collapse are characteristic of AFE rather than air embolism. (Source: RANZCOG - Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

Septic shock from chorioamnionitis develops gradually with fever and tachycardia, not with sudden cardiovascular collapse seconds to minutes after delivery. The acute onset of hypoxia, seizures, and immediate DIC is not consistent with sepsis. The normal temperature further argues against this diagnosis. (Source: ANZCA - Obstetric Anaesthesia Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis is defined as endometriotic lesions penetrating more than 5 mm below the peritoneal surface, commonly involving the uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, and bowel wall. The combination of dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, cyclical dyschezia with rectal bleeding, and a fixed retroverted uterus with rectovaginal nodularity is highly suggestive of DIE with bowel involvement. Management should occur at a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre with advanced laparoscopic and colorectal surgical expertise. Surgical excision improves both pain and fertility outcomes. AMH should be measured before endometrioma surgery as cystectomy can reduce ovarian reserve.
key_points: Cyclical dyschezia with rectal bleeding strongly suggests bowel endometriosis
DIE requires surgical management at a multidisciplinary centre with colorectal surgical support
Surgical excision of moderate-severe endometriosis improves natural conception rates
AMH measurement before endometrioma cystectomy helps counsel about ovarian reserve risk
explanation.pearls: Endometrioma cystectomy (stripping technique) removes 1-6 mL of normal ovarian cortex with each procedure, potentially reducing AMH by 30-40% - bilateral cystectomy should only be performed by experienced surgeons with ovarian reserve implications discussed preoperatively.

options.rationale: While hormonal suppression improves symptoms, there is no evidence that a period of hormonal suppression prior to attempting conception improves subsequent fertility. This patient has been trying to conceive for 18 months and hormonal treatment further delays fertility investigation and treatment. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

This patient has deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) with evidence of rectovaginal and uterosacral involvement, an ovarian endometrioma, cyclical bowel symptoms suggesting bowel wall involvement, and 18 months of unexplained infertility. Management requires referral to a multidisciplinary endometriosis centre with advanced laparoscopic skills and colorectal surgical support. Surgical excision of DIE and cystectomy of the endometrioma can improve pain symptoms and natural conception rates. Concurrent fertility planning with reproductive medicine input is appropriate given her subfertility. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

GnRH agonist therapy suppresses endometriosis but does not improve fertility and further delays conception. A 4 cm endometrioma may also impair oocyte retrieval and ovarian response during IVF. Surgical treatment of the endometrioma before IVF is generally recommended when endometriomas are 4 cm or above. (Source: ESHRE - Endometriosis Guideline)

While IVF may ultimately be needed, proceeding directly without addressing the 4 cm endometrioma and deep infiltrating disease is suboptimal. Endometriomas 4 cm or larger can impair oocyte retrieval, and surgical excision of moderate-severe endometriosis has been shown to improve natural conception rates. A planned surgical approach with concurrent fertility planning optimises outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG - Endometriosis)

Dienogest is an effective progestogen for endometriosis symptom control but is an oral progestogen that inhibits ovulation and is used as a contraceptive. Concurrent use while trying to conceive is contradictory. Hormonal treatments for endometriosis are not compatible with active fertility attempts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines - Gynaecology)

explanation.summary: Ovarian torsion in pregnancy most commonly occurs in the first trimester and early second trimester, particularly in the context of ovarian hyperstimulation from IVF or large ovarian cysts. The classic presentation is sudden-onset colicky pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting. Ultrasound findings of an enlarged ovary with absent or reduced venous flow on Doppler support the diagnosis. Urgent laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is the treatment of choice - oophorectomy is almost never necessary and the ovary has remarkable recovery potential. In early pregnancy, loss of the corpus luteum-bearing ovary before 10-12 weeks may precipitate miscarriage unless exogenous progesterone is supplemented.
key_points: IVF-stimulated ovaries and large cysts are major risk factors for torsion in pregnancy
Absent venous flow on Doppler in a symptomatic patient is highly suggestive of torsion
Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is standard regardless of ovarian appearance
Ovarian recovery rates after detorsion exceed 90% even when the ovary appears necrotic
explanation.pearls: The whirlpool sign on transvaginal ultrasound - a twisted vascular pedicle seen as a round hypoechoic structure with concentric internal echoes - is the most specific ultrasound finding for ovarian torsion, with specificity exceeding 95%.

sources.label: RCOG - Management of Ovarian Cysts in Pregnancy

options.rationale: Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency. Delayed surgery risks ovarian necrosis, peritonitis, and sepsis. The combination of sudden-onset colicky pain, enlarged ovary with absent venous flow on Doppler, and clinical features is highly suggestive of torsion. Conservative management is inappropriate when torsion is suspected. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

While appendicitis is an important differential for right iliac fossa pain in pregnancy, the ultrasound findings of an enlarged ovary with absent venous flow and a known ovarian cyst make ovarian torsion the most likely diagnosis. The upward displacement of the appendix during pregnancy also makes the location atypical for appendicitis at 14 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

Ovarian torsion in pregnancy requires urgent surgical intervention. Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian conservation is the standard approach regardless of the macroscopic appearance of the ovary, as ovarian recovery rates after detorsion exceed 90% even when the ovary appears dusky or black. Laparoscopy is safe in the first and second trimesters and is preferred over laparotomy. The cyst may be drained or excised if necessary, but the ovary should be preserved. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

Oophorectomy should be avoided as the ovary has high recovery potential even when Doppler flow is absent and the ovary appears macroscopically compromised. Studies show ovarian viability rates above 90% after detorsion. Laparotomy is also unnecessarily invasive when laparoscopy is feasible. Ovarian preservation is especially important in this young woman who conceived through IVF. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

When the clinical presentation and ultrasound findings are consistent with ovarian torsion, MRI should not delay surgical intervention. MRI has reasonable sensitivity for torsion but is not required when ultrasound shows absent venous flow in a symptomatic patient with a known risk factor. Time to surgery directly correlates with ovarian salvage rates. (Source: RANZCOG - Ovarian Masses in Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM) at 24-36 weeks is managed with expectant management to prolong the latency period and reduce prematurity-related morbidity. The key interventions are antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses 24 hours apart), prophylactic erythromycin for 10 days to prolong latency and reduce neonatal infection, and careful maternal and fetal surveillance. Amoxicillin-clavulanate should be avoided due to the association with neonatal necrotising enterocolitis in the ORACLE trial. Delivery is planned at 36-37 weeks unless complications develop earlier.
key_points: Antenatal corticosteroids are given between 24 and 34+6 weeks to promote fetal lung maturation
Erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days is the prophylactic antibiotic of choice in PPROM
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is avoided in PPROM due to increased neonatal NEC risk from the ORACLE trial
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is given when delivery before 30 weeks is imminent
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE trial showed erythromycin in PPROM reduced neonatal morbidity and prolonged latency by a median of 5 days, but amoxicillin-clavulanate was associated with a 4.6-fold increase in neonatal necrotising enterocolitis - this combination should never be used in PPROM.

options.rationale: At 29 weeks, the fetus is viable with good survival rates at tertiary centres. Immediate delivery would subject the neonate to significant prematurity-related morbidity. Expectant management with appropriate antibiotics and corticosteroids is the standard approach to gain time for fetal maturation while monitoring for complications. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

Erythromycin is appropriate prophylactic antibiotic therapy in PPROM (as per the ORACLE trial), but this answer omits the critical step of antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation. Without GBS status, GBS-specific intrapartum prophylaxis considerations are needed. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

This partially reflects the ORACLE protocol but is inaccurate. Australian practice follows erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days (or until delivery) as the prophylactic antibiotic. The amoxicillin-clavulanate combination was associated with increased necrotising enterocolitis risk in the ORACLE trial and should be avoided in PPROM. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

Management of PPROM at 29 weeks involves: (1) antenatal corticosteroids - betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart for fetal lung maturation, (2) prophylactic antibiotics - erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly for 10 days per the ORACLE trial protocol, to prolong latency and reduce neonatal infection, (3) expectant management with regular maternal observations, CTG monitoring, and ultrasound surveillance, and (4) planned delivery at 36-37 weeks if no complications, or earlier if chorioamnionitis, non-reassuring fetal status, or significant abruption develops. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM)

Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is indicated when preterm delivery before 30 weeks is anticipated within 24 hours. This patient has PPROM without active labour, so delivery is not imminent. Planning delivery within 48 hours at 29 weeks would be premature when expectant management could safely extend the pregnancy by several weeks. (Source: RANZCOG - Magnesium Sulfate for Neuroprotection)

explanation.summary: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome occurs in 10-15% of monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies due to unbalanced blood flow through placental vascular anastomoses. The donor twin develops oligohydramnios and a small or absent bladder, while the recipient develops polyhydramnios and a distended bladder. The Quintero staging system classifies severity from stage I (fluid discordance only) to stage V (fetal demise). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of placental anastomoses is the treatment of choice between 16 and 26 weeks, with survival of at least one twin in approximately 86% of cases. All monochorionic twins require 2-weekly ultrasound surveillance from 16 weeks.
key_points: TTTS diagnostic criteria - DVP below 2 cm in donor and above 8 cm in recipient in monochorionic twins
Fetoscopic laser ablation is superior to serial amnioreduction (Eurofetus trial)
Quintero staging guides prognosis - stages I-II have better outcomes than stages III-IV
All monochorionic twins require 2-weekly ultrasound from 16 weeks for early TTTS detection
explanation.pearls: In the Quintero staging system for TTTS, a non-visualised donor bladder marks stage II, absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery marks stage III, and hydrops in either twin marks stage IV - each progressive stage carries significantly worse prognosis without intervention.

options.rationale: This twin pair meets diagnostic criteria for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS): monochorionic pregnancy with oligohydramnios in the donor twin (DVP below 2 cm) and polyhydramnios in the recipient twin (DVP above 8 cm). TTTS is progressive and has high mortality without intervention. Waiting 2 weeks risks rapid deterioration. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

Amnioreduction was previously used as treatment for TTTS but only addresses the symptom (polyhydramnios), not the underlying pathology (unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses). The Eurofetus trial demonstrated superior outcomes with fetoscopic laser ablation compared with serial amnioreduction. Amnioreduction is reserved for cases where laser therapy is unavailable. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

Selective reduction is not appropriate when both twins are alive with normal growth and normal Dopplers. Fetoscopic laser ablation addresses the underlying vascular anastomoses and preserves both twins in the majority of cases (86% survival of at least one twin). Reduction is considered only when one twin has severe compromise. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

Delivery at 20 weeks results in the loss of both twins as the fetuses are previable. TTTS is treatable with fetoscopic laser ablation, which has survival rates of at least one twin in 86% and both twins in 60-70% of cases. The aim is to treat and prolong the pregnancy to a viable gestational age. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

This presentation meets Quintero stage II TTTS criteria (oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios sequence with non-visualised donor bladder). Fetoscopic laser photocoagulation of the placental vascular anastomoses is the treatment of choice for TTTS diagnosed between 16 and 26 weeks, as demonstrated by the Eurofetus trial. The procedure uses a fetoscope inserted into the polyhydramniotic sac to identify and ablate the inter-twin vascular anastomoses on the placental surface. (Source: RANZCOG - Twin Pregnancy Management)

explanation.summary: Vulval squamous cell carcinoma is the most common vulval malignancy, with two distinct pathways: HPV-related (via usual-type VIN in younger women) and HPV-independent (via differentiated VIN in older women, often associated with lichen sclerosus). Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of SCC. Any new, persistent, or changing vulval lesion in a patient with lichen sclerosus requires biopsy. Management of confirmed vulval SCC involves wide local excision with appropriate margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy depending on depth of invasion. Women with lichen sclerosus require lifelong vulval surveillance.
key_points: Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC via the dVIN pathway
Any new or changing vulval lesion in lichen sclerosus requires punch biopsy
dVIN is HPV-independent and does not respond to imiquimod, unlike usual-type VIN
Tissue diagnosis must precede definitive surgery to plan appropriate margins and lymph node assessment
explanation.pearls: Differentiated VIN (dVIN) associated with lichen sclerosus has a much higher malignant transformation rate (up to 30-50%) than HPV-related usual-type VIN (uVIN, approximately 5-10%), making vigilant long-term surveillance of lichen sclerosus essential.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: A new or changing vulval lesion in the context of long-standing lichen sclerosus requires urgent biopsy to exclude vulval squamous cell carcinoma. Lichen sclerosus carries a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC, mediated through differentiated vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (dVIN). A punch biopsy from the most suspicious area under local anaesthesia provides tissue diagnosis. Gynaecological oncology referral is essential for management planning. (Source: RANZCOG - Vulval Disease)

While lichen sclerosus can cause hyperkeratotic plaques, a new exophytic lesion with irregular borders and contact bleeding in long-standing lichen sclerosus must be biopsied to exclude malignancy before assuming a benign diagnosis. Treating empirically with potent topical steroids would delay diagnosis of a potentially invasive cancer. (Source: RANZCOG - Vulval Disease)

Proceeding directly to excision without a tissue diagnosis is inappropriate as the surgical margins and approach differ depending on histology (dVIN, microinvasive SCC, frankly invasive SCC). Punch biopsy first determines the diagnosis and depth of invasion, which guides definitive surgical planning including the need for sentinel lymph node biopsy or inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Imiquimod is used for usual-type VIN (uVIN), which is HPV-related and typically occurs in younger women. This elderly patient with lichen sclerosus is at risk of differentiated VIN (dVIN) or invasive SCC, which is not HPV-related and does not respond to imiquimod. A tissue diagnosis is mandatory before any treatment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

options.rationale: Imaging may be needed for staging if the biopsy confirms invasive cancer, but it should not delay tissue diagnosis. The appropriate sequence is biopsy first, then imaging and staging investigations based on the histological result. For small vulval lesions, clinical examination of inguinal nodes is the initial assessment. (Source: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia - Vulval Cancer Guidelines

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy occurs when intrauterine and ectopic pregnancies coexist. The incidence is approximately 1 in 30,000 in natural conception but rises to 1-3% with assisted reproduction, particularly with multiple embryo transfer. Management is exclusively surgical because methotrexate is contraindicated with a viable IUP. Laparoscopic salpingectomy is the standard approach when the patient is haemodynamically stable.
key_points: Heterotopic pregnancy incidence is 1-3% after IVF with multiple embryo transfer
Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated with a coexisting viable IUP
Laparoscopic salpingectomy is preferred over laparotomy when feasible
Free fluid and tachycardia suggest tubal rupture requiring urgent intervention
explanation.pearls: After surgical management of a heterotopic pregnancy, the intrauterine pregnancy continues successfully in approximately 65-70% of cases, with outcomes improving when intervention occurs before significant haemoperitoneum develops.

options.rationale: Expectant management is inappropriate here given haemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, borderline hypotension), free fluid suggesting rupture, and a sizeable adnexal mass. The ectopic component requires definitive surgical treatment. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

Heterotopic pregnancy with signs of tubal rupture requires urgent surgical management. Laparoscopic salpingectomy removes the ectopic while preserving the viable intrauterine pregnancy. Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated due to the coexisting viable IUP. The incidence of heterotopic pregnancy rises to 1-3% with ART. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines; RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of a viable intrauterine pregnancy as it is teratogenic and embryotoxic. Medical management of ectopic pregnancy is only appropriate when there is no coexisting IUP. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

Delaying intervention with a repeat scan is unsafe in a patient showing signs of haemoperitoneum with tachycardia and free fluid. The ultrasound findings already clearly demonstrate a heterotopic pregnancy with probable tubal rupture. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

Bilateral salpingectomy with termination is unnecessarily radical. The goal is to remove the ectopic component while preserving the viable IUP. Laparoscopy is preferred over laparotomy when the patient is haemodynamically stable enough. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guidelines)

explanation.summary: After single dose methotrexate the hCG usually rises to a peak around day 4, so that rise is expected and is not treatment failure. The decision point is the change between day 4 and day 7: a fall of at least 15 per cent means the treatment is working and weekly hCG continues until it is undetectable, while a smaller fall or a rise means a second dose, with day 4 and day 7 measured again from that injection. Surgery follows failure of the second dose or any clinical deterioration. In context, methotrexate is not a single visit treatment; a woman who cannot commit to the follow-up schedule is better served by laparoscopic surgery from the outset.
key_points: An hCG rise from day 0 to day 4 is expected and is not failure.
At least a 15 per cent fall from day 4 to day 7 means treatment is working.
A smaller fall or a rise means a second dose and a fresh day 4 and day 7 cycle.
Weekly hCG continues until undetectable; about one in seven needs a second dose.
explanation.pearls: Advise avoiding alcohol, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, folate supplements and sun exposure during treatment, and no conception until three months after the last dose.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: A fall of less than 15 per cent between day 4 and day 7 defines an inadequate response, and about one woman in seven needs a further dose with the monitoring cycle repeated from that day. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Weekly monitoring alone is what follows an adequate day 4 to day 7 fall, and it continues until the level is undetectable. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Emergency surgery is for haemodynamic compromise, significant free fluid with peritonism, or failure after a second dose; she is stable with mild pain. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.rationale: Intravenous methotrexate belongs to oncological and rheumatological regimens with folinic acid rescue, and has no place in tubal ectopic pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)
Mifepristone with misoprostol is the regimen for medical termination of an intrauterine pregnancy and does not treat trophoblast implanted in the tube. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion defined as heart failure with LVEF below 45% developing in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum. It can mimic pre-eclampsia with dyspnoea and oedema, but the absence of hypertension, proteinuria, and hepatic or haematological derangement distinguishes the two. Immediate management focuses on stabilising heart failure before delivery planning. Long-term prognosis depends on LVEF recovery, with approximately 50% of patients recovering normal function within 6 months.
key_points: PPCM is defined as LVEF < 45% in late pregnancy or early postpartum with no prior cardiac disease
Normal BP and absent proteinuria distinguish PPCM from pre-eclampsia with pulmonary oedema
IV furosemide and oxygen are first-line for acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema in pregnancy
Delivery timing requires joint cardiology-obstetric decision after haemodynamic stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine 2.5 mg twice daily for 2 weeks then 2.5 mg daily for 6 weeks has shown promise in improving LVEF recovery in peripartum cardiomyopathy by blocking the pro-apoptotic 16 kDa prolactin fragment, though it requires cessation of breastfeeding.

options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is indicated for seizure prophylaxis in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. This patient has no hypertension, no proteinuria, normal platelets, and normal LFTs, making pre-eclampsia unlikely. The echo findings of LVEF 28% point to a primary cardiac pathology. Magnesium could worsen cardiac output. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines; NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

Labetalol is appropriate for hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy, but this patient's blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and does not require antihypertensive therapy. Beta-blockers must also be used cautiously in acute decompensated heart failure as they can worsen cardiogenic shock. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

While delivery is ultimately beneficial in peripartum cardiomyopathy, this patient requires immediate cardiac stabilisation before any delivery planning. Oxytocin also has antidiuretic effects and can cause fluid retention, which could worsen pulmonary oedema in a patient with severely reduced LVEF. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

This patient has peripartum cardiomyopathy presenting with acute decompensated heart failure. The immediate priority is haemodynamic stabilisation with IV diuresis for pulmonary oedema, supplemental oxygen for hypoxia, and urgent joint cardiology-obstetric review. LVEF of 28% with elevated NT-proBNP, third heart sound, and bilateral crackles confirm cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Delivery timing is a joint decision after stabilisation. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines; ESC Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Position Statement)

While PE is on the differential for peripartum dyspnoea, the bedside echo showing LVEF 28% with global hypokinesis and a third heart sound already identifies the diagnosis. CTPA would delay treatment, expose mother and fetus to radiation unnecessarily, and the echo findings are not consistent with right heart strain from PE. (Source: NHFA Heart Failure Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is diagnosed when at least one clinical criterion (vascular thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity) and at least one laboratory criterion (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, or anti-beta2 glycoprotein I antibodies confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart) are met. In obstetric APS with recurrent pregnancy loss, aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH is the standard treatment, improving live birth rates substantially. Close antenatal surveillance including serial growth scans and uterine artery Doppler is recommended due to increased risk of pre-eclampsia and placental insufficiency.
key_points: Diagnosis requires clinical plus laboratory criteria with antibodies confirmed 12 weeks apart
Aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH is standard for obstetric APS without prior thrombosis
Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester and contraindicated
These pregnancies require surveillance for pre-eclampsia, FGR, and placental abruption
explanation.pearls: Triple-positive APS (positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2 glycoprotein I) carries the highest thrombotic risk and worst obstetric outcomes, with some experts advocating for higher-intensity anticoagulation in this subgroup despite limited trial evidence.

options.rationale: Aspirin alone is insufficient for obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome with recurrent pregnancy loss. The combination of aspirin plus heparin has been shown to significantly improve live birth rates compared with aspirin alone in APS-associated recurrent miscarriage. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation is indicated for APS with prior thrombotic events, not for purely obstetric APS without thrombotic history. Prophylactic-dose enoxaparin combined with aspirin is the standard for obstetric APS. Therapeutic dosing increases bleeding risk without proven additional benefit for pregnancy outcomes. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy)

The standard of care for obstetric APS with recurrent pregnancy loss is the combination of low-dose aspirin (commenced preconception or at positive pregnancy test) plus prophylactic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg daily) commenced once a viable intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed. This combination improves live birth rates from approximately 40% to 70-80%. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (causing warfarin embryopathy between 6 and 12 weeks) and is contraindicated in the first trimester and near term. It is replaced by LMWH in pregnancy. Warfarin may only be considered mid-trimester in women with mechanical heart valves. (Source: RANZCOG APS in Pregnancy)

Corticosteroids are not recommended for obstetric APS. Trials showed no benefit for pregnancy outcomes and increased maternal morbidity including gestational diabetes, hypertension, and preterm birth. The combination of aspirin plus heparin has superior evidence. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

explanation.summary: Inevitable miscarriage is characterised by an open cervical os with or without products of conception visible, often with heavy bleeding. Management options include surgical evacuation, medical management, or expectant management. Patient preference and clinical circumstances guide the choice. Rh-negative women require anti-D immunoglobulin after any pregnancy loss to prevent isoimmunisation in future pregnancies. The dose depends on gestational age: 250 IU before 12 weeks and 625 IU at or after 12 weeks in Australia.
key_points: Open os with products visible defines inevitable miscarriage
Surgical evacuation is preferred for heavy bleeding and patient preference for rapid resolution
Anti-D 250 IU is required for Rh-negative women losing a pregnancy before 12 weeks
All three management options are valid but clinical context guides selection
explanation.pearls: Anti-D immunoglobulin is not required for threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks unless bleeding is heavy, recurrent, or associated with abdominal pain, but it IS required for all complete, incomplete, and inevitable miscarriages regardless of gestational age in Rh-negative women.

sources.label: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage

options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is the medical management regimen for missed miscarriage when the cervix is closed. In inevitable miscarriage with an open os and products visible, surgical evacuation is more appropriate, particularly with heavy ongoing bleeding. Medical management risks prolonged bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

This patient has an inevitable miscarriage (open os, products visible, no cardiac activity) with heavy bleeding and a preference for rapid resolution. Surgical evacuation is the most appropriate active management. As she is Rh-negative and beyond 10 weeks by CRL sizing, anti-D immunoglobulin is required to prevent Rh isoimmunisation. At less than 12 weeks, the dose is 250 IU. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines; ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines)

While expectant management is an option for some miscarriages, this patient has heavy bleeding with products at the os and has expressed a preference for active management. Expectant management would prolong her symptoms and carries a risk of incomplete miscarriage and infection. (Source: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage)
source_refs: NICE NG126: Ectopic Pregnancy and Miscarriage

options.rationale: While misoprostol alone can be used for medical management of miscarriage, surgical evacuation is preferred when products are already at the os and bleeding is heavy. Medical management alone has a higher incomplete evacuation rate and would not address the patient's preference for rapid resolution. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

Tranexamic acid and oxytocin may reduce bleeding symptomatically but do not address the retained products of conception. Definitive management requires either surgical or medical evacuation. Temporising with uterotonics alone risks incomplete miscarriage and sepsis. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Menopausal hormone therapy route selection is critical in women with VTE risk factors. Transdermal oestradiol avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism and therefore does not increase clotting factor synthesis or VTE risk. This contrasts with oral oestrogen, which increases VTE risk 2-4 fold through hepatic effects. Micronised progesterone is preferred over synthetic progestogens for its more favourable safety profile. Women with a prior VTE are not absolutely contraindicated from MHT if the transdermal route is used, though shared decision-making with a haematologist may be advisable.
key_points: Transdermal oestradiol avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase VTE risk
Oral oestrogen increases VTE risk 2-4 fold via hepatic clotting factor synthesis
Micronised progesterone has the lowest VTE risk among progestogens
Prior provoked VTE is a relative, not absolute, contraindication to transdermal MHT
explanation.pearls: The ESTHER and E3N French cohort studies demonstrated that transdermal oestradiol combined with micronised progesterone carried no measurable increase in VTE risk (OR 0.9, 95% CI 0.5-1.6), even in women with BMI above 30 or thrombophilia.

options.rationale: Oral oestrogen undergoes first-pass hepatic metabolism, which increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and raises VTE risk 2-4 fold. In a woman with prior VTE and BMI over 35, oral oestrogen is relatively contraindicated due to compounding thrombotic risk factors. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Tibolone, while having fewer oestrogenic effects on coagulation than conjugated oestrogens, is still an oral agent with first-pass metabolism. Its VTE risk profile in women with prior thrombotic events is not sufficiently reassuring compared to transdermal oestradiol, which avoids hepatic first-pass entirely. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Non-hormonal options such as venlafaxine can reduce hot flush frequency by approximately 50-60%, but this patient is specifically requesting hormonal treatment and her symptoms are severe. A safer hormonal route exists that avoids the VTE risk of oral oestrogen. Non-hormonal therapy should be reserved for absolute contraindications. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Although micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen for metabolic safety, the oral oestradiol component still carries the first-pass hepatic VTE risk. In a woman with prior VTE and obesity, the oestrogen route must be transdermal rather than oral, regardless of which progestogen is chosen. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Transdermal oestradiol bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism and does not increase VTE risk, making it the preferred route in women with prior VTE or elevated thrombotic risk. Observational data consistently show no increased VTE risk with transdermal oestradiol at standard doses. Micronised progesterone is the preferred progestogen as it has the most favourable safety profile for VTE, breast, and cardiovascular outcomes. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT; Lancet 2019 meta-analysis)

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program recommends colposcopy for any HPV 16 or 18 detection regardless of cytology result. Colposcopy is safe during pregnancy and should be performed to exclude invasive disease. Routine biopsies are avoided due to bleeding risk from cervical hypervascularity, but directed biopsies are taken if high-grade or invasive disease is suspected. Treatment with excisional procedures is deferred until at least 3 months postpartum, with repeat colposcopy recommended at that time.
key_points: HPV 16 or 18 detection mandates colposcopy regardless of cytology grade
Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy; treatment is deferred postpartum
Biopsy only if high-grade or invasive disease is colposcopically suspected
LLETZ is contraindicated during pregnancy due to haemorrhage and cervical incompetence risk
explanation.pearls: HPV 16 is responsible for approximately 55-60% of all cervical cancers and has a 12% 10-year risk of CIN3+ even when the initial cytology is normal, which is why the NCSP mandates colposcopy for HPV 16 regardless of cytology.

options.rationale: HPV 16 positivity with any cytological abnormality requires colposcopy. Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy and should be performed to exclude high-grade disease. Biopsy is reserved for suspected high-grade or invasive lesions only, as routine biopsy risks bleeding from the hypervascular cervix. Treatment is deferred until postpartum. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; RANZCOG Cervical Screening in Pregnancy)

HPV 16 is the highest-risk HPV genotype and deferring all investigation until postpartum risks missing an underlying high-grade lesion or early invasive carcinoma. Colposcopy should be performed during pregnancy to exclude serious pathology, even though treatment is deferred. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

LLETZ is contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of haemorrhage from the hypervascular pregnant cervix, cervical incompetence, preterm rupture of membranes, and pregnancy loss. Excisional treatment is deferred to at least 3 months postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG Cervical Screening in Pregnancy)

HPV 16 with any cytological abnormality is not low risk. HPV 16 has the highest oncogenic potential of all HPV genotypes and requires direct colposcopic assessment regardless of the cytology grade. A 12-month repeat would be inappropriate for this high-risk genotype. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

Ultrasound-guided cervical biopsy is not a standard technique for cervical screening follow-up. Colposcopy is the standard assessment method. Biopsy during pregnancy is performed only under colposcopic guidance when a high-grade or invasive lesion is suspected. (Source: NCSP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Women who have undergone hysterectomy do not require a progestogen component in their MHT, as the sole purpose of progesterone is endometrial protection from unopposed oestrogen. Oestrogen-only therapy is preferred post-hysterectomy because it avoids the additional breast cancer risk associated with combined therapy. The WHI oestrogen-only arm demonstrated no increased breast cancer risk over 7 years of follow-up, in contrast to the combined arm.
key_points: Oestrogen-only MHT is appropriate after hysterectomy as no endometrial protection is needed
Adding progesterone post-hysterectomy increases breast cancer risk without benefit
The WHI oestrogen-only arm showed no increased breast cancer risk
Route selection depends on VTE risk factors and patient preference
explanation.pearls: The WHI oestrogen-only arm (conjugated equine oestrogen 0.625 mg daily) showed a non-significant 23% reduction in breast cancer incidence over 7 years (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.59-1.01), contrasting sharply with the 26% increase seen in the combined oestrogen-progestogen arm.

options.rationale: A progestogen is only required to protect the endometrium from unopposed oestrogen. This patient has had a total hysterectomy and therefore has no endometrium. Adding progesterone unnecessarily increases breast cancer risk and side effects without benefit. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Cyclical combined therapy produces a withdrawal bleed and is used in perimenopausal women with an intact uterus who prefer to menstruate regularly. This patient has no uterus, so cyclical progesterone is unnecessary and the withdrawal bleeds would be impossible. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

Tibolone is an option for postmenopausal symptom relief, but it is not first-line. In a woman post-hysterectomy, the combined oestrogenic-progestogenic properties of tibolone provide no advantage over oestrogen alone, and tibolone carries a small increased stroke risk in older women. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

After total hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy, oestrogen-only therapy is appropriate as there is no endometrium to protect. Oestrogen-only MHT provides effective symptom relief with a more favourable risk profile than combined therapy, including lower breast cancer risk. Either oral or transdermal route is acceptable in this patient without VTE risk factors. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT; WHI oestrogen-only arm)

Vaginal oestrogen is effective for urogenital atrophy symptoms but provides negligible systemic absorption and is insufficient for treating moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms. Systemic oestrogen therapy is required for hot flushes and night sweats. (Source: AMS Position Statement on MHT)

explanation.summary: PCOS is a metabolic as well as reproductive disorder. Women with PCOS have a 4-8 fold increased risk of type 2 diabetes compared to age-matched controls. The 2023 international evidence-based guideline emphasises lifestyle intervention as the cornerstone of PCOS management, particularly when metabolic features are present. A 5-10% weight reduction can restore ovulation in up to 60% of anovulatory women with PCOS and significantly improves insulin sensitivity, lipid profile, and cardiovascular risk markers.
key_points: Lifestyle intervention with 5-10% weight loss is first-line for all metabolic features of PCOS
OGTT 2-hour glucose of 9.4 mmol/L indicates impaired glucose tolerance (prediabetes)
Metabolic risk reduction takes priority over cosmetic symptoms like hirsutism
Metformin is second-line, added if lifestyle alone is insufficient after 3-6 months
explanation.pearls: Annual OGTT screening is recommended for all women with PCOS and BMI over 25 (or other risk factors), as HbA1c underestimates glycaemic impairment in PCOS due to the younger age demographic and may miss up to 50% of cases of impaired glucose tolerance.

options.rationale: The 2023 international evidence-based PCOS guideline identifies structured lifestyle intervention with 5-10% weight loss as the first-line treatment for all metabolic features of PCOS. A 5% weight loss can restore ovulation, improve insulin sensitivity, reduce testosterone, and improve the lipid profile. This patient has impaired glucose tolerance (2-hour glucose 7.8-11.0 mmol/L) and dyslipidaemia, both of which respond to weight management. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023; Jean Hailes for Women's Health)

The COCP addresses menstrual irregularity and hirsutism but does not address the metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, or impaired glucose tolerance which represent the greatest long-term health risks. With a BMI of 34 and metabolic syndrome features, lifestyle intervention takes priority. The COCP may also worsen insulin resistance and lipid profile. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

Metformin can improve insulin sensitivity and may modestly aid weight loss, but international guidelines position it as second-line to lifestyle intervention. Metformin alone without lifestyle change produces modest improvements in metabolic parameters. It may be added if lifestyle intervention alone is insufficient after 3-6 months. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

Spironolactone is effective for hirsutism and acne but does not address the metabolic complications which are this patient's greatest long-term health concern. It also requires reliable contraception due to teratogenicity. Cosmetic symptoms, while distressing, are secondary to metabolic risk reduction. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

Statin therapy may be considered for dyslipidaemia but is not the most important initial intervention in a 28-year-old with PCOS. Lifestyle intervention can substantially improve the lipid profile and address the underlying insulin resistance driving the dyslipidaemia. Statins also require reliable contraception. (Source: International PCOS Guideline 2023)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of reproductive-age women. First-line medical management is hormonal suppression using the combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously or a levonorgestrel intrauterine device. These suppress ovulation and decidualise endometrial implants, reducing pain in approximately 70-80% of patients. Second-line options include progestogen-only therapies and GnRH agonists. Surgical management is reserved for failed medical therapy, fertility planning, or diagnostic uncertainty.
key_points: COCP taken continuously is first-line medical therapy for endometriosis pain
LNG-IUD is an equivalent first-line alternative
GnRH agonists and danazol are second-line due to side effect profiles
Surgery is not first-line when hormonal suppression has not been tried
explanation.pearls: Continuous COCP use for endometriosis should genuinely suppress menstruation with no scheduled breaks; the traditional 21/7 cyclical regimen allows hormonal withdrawal that can reactivate endometrial implants and worsen pain during the pill-free interval.

options.rationale: GnRH agonists are second-line therapy for endometriosis, reserved for patients who fail first-line hormonal suppression. They cause significant hypo-oestrogenic side effects and require add-back therapy. They should not be used as initial treatment in a young woman who has not tried simpler hormonal options. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines; NICE NG73)

Surgery is not first-line for endometriosis management when the patient has not tried hormonal suppression. For a 25 mm endometrioma without fertility concerns, medical management should be attempted first. Surgery is appropriate for failed medical therapy, fertility planning, or diagnostic uncertainty. (Source: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline 2022)

Danazol is effective for endometriosis but is rarely used as first-line therapy due to androgenic side effects including acne, hirsutism, weight gain, and voice deepening. Modern first-line options have far better tolerability profiles. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guidelines)

Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is effective for endometriosis pain but carries significant concerns about bone mineral density loss with prolonged use, particularly in young women.
