Surgical evacuation is reserved for patient preference, failed medical/expectant management, or heavy bleeding.
key_points: Anembryonic pregnancy diagnosed when gestational sac >=25 mm without embryo
Misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally is first-line medical management
Success rate of medical management approximately 80-85%
All patients need safety-netting advice about heavy bleeding and infection signs
explanation.pearls: Adding mifepristone 200 mg 24-48 hours before misoprostol improves complete miscarriage rates from approximately 80% to 90% in missed miscarriage - though single-agent misoprostol remains the standard first-line protocol in many Australian centres.

sources.label: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early Pregnancy Loss

options.rationale: Medical management with misoprostol 800 mcg (vaginal or sublingual) is appropriate for confirmed first-trimester missed miscarriage when the patient prefers to avoid surgery. Success rates are approximately 80-85% within 7 days. She should receive written information about expected bleeding and when to present to emergency. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early Pregnancy Loss)
source_refs: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early Pregnancy Loss

options.rationale: Expectant management has lower success rates (approximately 50-60% at 2 weeks for anembryonic pregnancy) compared to medical management. While it is a valid option, it would not be the most appropriate initial approach given her preference to avoid surgery - medical management offers a better success rate while still avoiding surgical intervention. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guideline)

Surgical evacuation is effective and appropriate, but the patient has expressed a preference to avoid surgery. Medical management should be offered first as it aligns with her wishes and has good efficacy. Surgery remains available if medical management fails. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guideline)

Mifepristone alone without misoprostol is not the standard protocol. The combination of mifepristone 200 mg followed by misoprostol 800 mcg 24-48 hours later is used in some protocols and improves success rates, but mifepristone alone is insufficient. The standard single-agent approach is misoprostol. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guideline)

The diagnosis of anembryonic pregnancy is confirmed - a gestational sac of 28 mm with no fetal pole meets the diagnostic criteria (sac greater than or equal to 25 mm with no embryo). Repeating the ultrasound delays management without clinical benefit. (Source: RANZCOG Early Pregnancy Loss Guideline)

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of reproductive-age women and is the most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea. First-line hormonal treatment includes the COCP used continuously or a levonorgestrel IUD. GnRH agonists and high-dose progestogens are second-line. Surgery is considered when medical management fails or for fertility-related concerns. A tissue diagnosis via laparoscopy is no longer required before commencing empirical hormonal therapy when clinical and imaging findings are consistent.
key_points: COCP continuously is first-line hormonal therapy for endometriosis
Laparoscopy is not required before starting empirical hormonal treatment
GnRH agonists are second-line due to bone density effects
Continuous use of COCP is preferred over cyclical use
explanation.pearls: Continuous COCP use (no pill-free interval) reduces endometriosis pain more effectively than cyclical use - the 7-day hormone-free interval allows reactivation of endometrial implants and return of symptoms.

options.rationale: NSAIDs provide symptomatic relief but do not suppress the underlying endometriosis or prevent disease progression. This patient has already tried ibuprofen with limited benefit. Hormonal therapy aimed at suppressing oestrogen-dependent endometrial implant activity is the first-line approach. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

Laparoscopy is not required before commencing empirical hormonal therapy when the clinical and ultrasound findings are consistent with endometriosis. Surgery can be considered if hormonal therapy fails or if tissue diagnosis is needed for treatment planning. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline)

Continuous combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) is a first-line hormonal treatment for endometriosis in women not planning pregnancy. It suppresses ovulation and reduces menstrual flow, thereby reducing oestrogen-driven endometrial implant activity. Continuous use (skipping the pill-free interval) is preferred to cyclic use to eliminate withdrawal bleeds. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines)

GnRH agonists (leuprorelin) are effective but are second-line due to significant side effects including menopausal symptoms and bone density loss. They require add-back HRT if used beyond 6 months. Simpler first-line hormonal options should be tried initially. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; AMH)

High-dose progestogens are effective for endometriosis but carry more side effects (weight gain, mood changes, breakthrough bleeding) than the COCP. They are generally reserved for women who cannot take oestrogen-containing preparations or as second-line therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines; AMH)

explanation.summary: PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women and carries significant metabolic risks including insulin resistance, IGT, T2DM, and dyslipidaemia. The 2023 international evidence-based guideline recommends OGTT screening at diagnosis and periodically thereafter. Metformin is indicated when lifestyle modification is insufficient and IGT or metabolic features are present. It should be started at a low dose and titrated gradually to minimise gastrointestinal side effects.
key_points: OGTT screening recommended at PCOS diagnosis due to high IGT prevalence
Metformin indicated when IGT present despite lifestyle modification
IGT defined as 2-hour OGTT 7.8-11.0 mmol/L
Metformin also provides modest benefit for menstrual regularity and androgen levels
explanation.pearls: Women with PCOS and IGT have a 5-10 fold higher annual conversion rate to T2DM compared to women with IGT alone - metformin reduces this conversion rate by approximately 50% (Diabetes Prevention Program).

options.rationale: While her lipids are borderline elevated, her absolute cardiovascular risk is low given her age. Statin therapy is not first-line for a 26-year-old. Addressing insulin resistance is more important at this stage, as it drives both the metabolic and reproductive features of PCOS. (Source: RACGP Red Book; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Pioglitazone is an insulin sensitiser but is not recommended for PCOS management due to weight gain, fluid retention, and fracture risk. Metformin is the preferred insulin-sensitising agent in PCOS. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS; AMH)

Spironolactone addresses the hyperandrogenic symptoms (hirsutism, acne) but does not address the metabolic risk. Her impaired glucose tolerance makes metabolic risk management the priority. Spironolactone may be added for cosmetic symptoms separately. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS)

Orlistat may assist with weight loss but does not directly address insulin resistance. Given the impaired glucose tolerance (2-hour OGTT 8.8 mmol/L, above the 7.8 threshold), specific insulin-sensitising therapy with metformin is more appropriate. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS)

Metformin is indicated in PCOS when impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) is present (2-hour OGTT 7.8-11.0 mmol/L). Her result of 8.8 mmol/L confirms IGT. Metformin improves insulin sensitivity, may restore menstrual regularity, and reduces progression to T2DM. Starting at 500 mg and titrating reduces GI side effects. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS; ADIPS)

explanation.summary: Cervical screening is safe during pregnancy and should be performed when overdue, particularly when following up prior abnormal results. Under the Australian NCSP renewed pathway, non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with LSIL requires repeat testing at 12 months. If the repeat shows persistent oncogenic HPV, colposcopy is indicated. Colposcopy can be safely performed during pregnancy, but excisional treatment is deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum unless invasive cancer is suspected.
key_points: Cervical screening can be performed during pregnancy when overdue
Non-16/18 HPV with LSIL requires 12-month repeat, not immediate colposcopy
Colposcopy is safe in pregnancy but treatment is deferred postpartum
HPV 16/18 positive results trigger direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology
explanation.pearls: Under the NCSP renewed pathway, HPV 16/18 positivity triggers direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology result, while other oncogenic HPV types require reflex cytology to triage - this distinction drives the referral threshold.

options.rationale: Deferring entirely is not appropriate when a follow-up test was overdue. While cervical screening is generally deferred during pregnancy if the woman is up to date, this patient has an overdue follow-up for a prior abnormal result. Pregnancy does not preclude cervical screening. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia)

Cervical screening (HPV test with reflex cytology) can be safely performed during pregnancy and should not be deferred when a follow-up test is overdue. The prior result of non-16/18 HPV with LSIL required 12-month repeat, which is now overdue. The test is safe in pregnancy and the result will guide further management. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia)

Colposcopy referral without retesting is not indicated. The original result was non-16/18 HPV with LSIL, which required 12-month repeat testing, not immediate colposcopy. Colposcopy is indicated if the repeat test shows persistent HPV or higher-grade abnormality. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

Waiting until the second trimester unnecessarily delays follow-up. The overdue test can be performed at any gestation. Earlier testing allows timely colposcopy referral if needed, as colposcopy is safe in pregnancy but cervical treatment is deferred until postpartum. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

Urgent colposcopy is indicated for suspected invasive cancer or high-grade cytological abnormality, not for overdue follow-up of LSIL with non-16/18 HPV. The appropriate step is to repeat the screening test first to determine current HPV and cytology status. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: IUD insertion postpartum follows specific timing windows. Immediate post-placental insertion (within 10-48 minutes) is safe and increasingly promoted. Between 48 hours and 4 weeks, expulsion rates are highest, so insertion is generally deferred. From 4-6 weeks onwards, insertion is safe with expulsion rates comparable to interval insertion. The copper IUD is compatible with breastfeeding and offers effective non-hormonal long-acting contraception.
key_points: Post-placental insertion (within 48 minutes) is safe and effective
48 hours to 4 weeks postpartum carries highest expulsion risk - avoid insertion
Standard postpartum insertion is at 4-6 weeks
Both copper and hormonal IUDs are compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: The 48-hour to 4-week postpartum window has IUD expulsion rates of 15-25%, compared to 3-5% for post-placental insertion and 2-5% for insertion at 6 weeks or later - making early postpartum counselling for immediate insertion critical.

options.rationale: While immediate post-placental IUD insertion (within 10-48 minutes of placental delivery) is safe and effective, insertion at 3 days postpartum falls in the higher-expulsion-risk window (48 hours to 4 weeks). The optimal approach at this point is to delay until 4-6 weeks postpartum. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception Guideline; FSRH UK MEC)

IUD insertion at 4-6 weeks postpartum is the standard recommended timing if immediate post-placental insertion was not performed. By this time, uterine involution is well advanced, the risk of perforation is lower, and the expulsion rate is comparable to interval insertion. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception Guideline; FSRH Contraception Guideline)

Waiting until 12 weeks is unnecessarily long and exposes the patient to unintended pregnancy risk. Uterine involution is adequately complete by 4-6 weeks for safe IUD insertion. The patient should be counselled about interim contraception if waiting. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception Guideline)

Insertion between 48 hours and 4 weeks postpartum carries the highest risk of IUD expulsion and is generally avoided. The uterus is involuting and the cervix remains dilated, contributing to higher expulsion rates of up to 15-25%. (Source: FSRH Contraception Guideline; WHO MEC)

IUDs are safe and effective postpartum - both copper and hormonal types. Breastfeeding is not a contraindication. The key consideration is timing of insertion. The copper IUD is an excellent choice for a patient wanting non-hormonal long-acting contraception. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception Guideline)

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM) includes vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, and recurrent UTIs due to oestrogen deficiency in the urogenital tissues. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen is the gold-standard treatment, with minimal systemic absorption at recommended doses. In breast cancer survivors, it may be considered after discussion with the oncology team. Systemic HRT is contraindicated. Non-hormonal options include vaginal moisturisers and lubricants.
key_points: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen is first-line for GSM after non-hormonal measures fail
Systemic HRT is contraindicated in breast cancer survivors
Vaginal oestrogen at recommended doses produces minimal systemic absorption
Oncology team involvement is important when prescribing vaginal oestrogen to breast cancer survivors
explanation.pearls: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen (25 mcg oestradiol pessary or 0.5 g oestriol cream twice weekly) maintains serum oestradiol within the postmenopausal range (<20 pmol/L) - this minimal systemic absorption underpins its considered use in breast cancer survivors.

options.rationale: Systemic HRT is generally contraindicated in women with a history of oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. Even if ER status is unknown, systemic HRT poses an unacceptable risk of recurrence. Her symptoms are genitourinary, not vasomotor, so systemic therapy is also not the most targeted approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines; AMS Position Statement)

Systemic oestrogen (even transdermal) is contraindicated in women with breast cancer history. Her symptoms are limited to the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which responds well to local therapy without systemic oestrogen exposure. (Source: AMS Position Statement; AMH)

Switching to an aromatase inhibitor would worsen genitourinary symptoms as AIs further reduce circulating oestrogen. This does not address the GSM and may exacerbate vaginal atrophy. The oncology team manages tamoxifen/AI decisions based on cancer factors. (Source: AMS Position Statement)

Low-dose vaginal oestrogen (cream, pessary, or ring) is the most appropriate treatment for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Minimal systemic absorption occurs at recommended doses. It can be used in breast cancer survivors after discussion with the treating oncologist, as serum oestradiol levels remain within the postmenopausal range. (Source: AMS Position Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines)

Ospemifene is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator approved for dyspareunia due to vulvovaginal atrophy, but its use in breast cancer survivors is not established as safe due to its oestrogenic effects on some tissues. Low-dose vaginal oestrogen has a better evidence base in this population. (Source: AMS Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum with prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine (vitamin B1) stores within 2-3 weeks. Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia) is a rare but devastating complication. Thiamine must be given BEFORE any dextrose-containing IV fluids, as glucose metabolism depletes remaining thiamine. Standard management includes IV normal saline, electrolyte correction, antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide), and thromboprophylaxis if immobile.
key_points: Thiamine 100 mg IV must precede any dextrose-containing fluids
Body thiamine stores deplete within 2-3 weeks of reduced intake
Wernicke encephalopathy is preventable but irreversible if established
Potassium and other electrolyte replacement is also important but secondary
explanation.pearls: Body thiamine stores last only 18-21 days - any patient with vomiting beyond 3 weeks should receive empirical IV thiamine before dextrose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, which has a 20% mortality if untreated.

options.rationale: Thiamine (vitamin B1) must be administered before any dextrose-containing fluids in hyperemesis gravidarum. Prolonged vomiting depletes thiamine stores, and dextrose metabolism consumes remaining thiamine, potentially precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. IV thiamine 100 mg should be given empirically. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Hyperemesis; Queensland Clinical Guideline: Hyperemesis)

Folic acid supplementation is important in pregnancy but is not the priority intervention in acute hyperemesis with dehydration and ketonuria. She likely cannot tolerate oral supplements currently. Thiamine deficiency prevention is more urgent due to the risk of Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Hyperemesis)

Potassium replacement is important given her K of 3.1 mmol/L, but this is a standard electrolyte correction, not the most critical supplementation. Thiamine deficiency carries the risk of irreversible neurological damage (Wernicke encephalopathy) and must be prioritised, especially before any glucose administration. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Hyperemesis)

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is a first-line antiemetic for mild nausea in pregnancy but is inadequate for severe hyperemesis gravidarum requiring hospital admission. Oral intake is not tolerated in this patient. Thiamine supplementation takes priority. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Hyperemesis)

Vitamin B12 deficiency is not an acute concern in hyperemesis gravidarum of 3 weeks duration. B12 stores last months to years. Thiamine (B1) is the vitamin of concern in prolonged vomiting due to its small body stores (only 2-3 weeks) and the risk of Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: Hyperemesis)

explanation.summary: Rh D-negative women should receive anti-D immunoglobulin after any potentially sensitising event to prevent isoimmunisation. Sensitising events include vaginal bleeding, abdominal trauma, invasive procedures, miscarriage, and ectopic pregnancy. Before 20 weeks, the standard dose of 250 IU is given without Kleihauer testing. After 20 weeks, 625 IU is the standard dose with Kleihauer performed to determine if additional doses are needed for large fetomaternal haemorrhage.
key_points: Anti-D given after any sensitising event in unsensitised Rh D-negative women
Before 20 weeks: 250 IU without Kleihauer
After 20 weeks: 625 IU with Kleihauer to quantify FMH
Anti-D should be given within 72 hours of the event
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is also standard
explanation.pearls: The dose of anti-D in Australia changes at the 20-week threshold: 250 IU before 20 weeks (without Kleihauer) versus 625 IU from 20 weeks onwards (with Kleihauer to detect FMH >6 mL requiring additional doses).

options.rationale: Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event regardless of whether vaginal bleeding is present. Fetomaternal haemorrhage can occur from placental disruption without external bleeding. Anti-D should be administered to all unsensitised Rh D-negative women after abdominal trauma. (Source: ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines; RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

At 14 weeks gestation, the standard prophylactic dose of anti-D (250 IU in Australia) is given, but a Kleihauer-Betke test is not required before 20 weeks as the fetal blood volume is too small for significant fetomaternal haemorrhage quantification. However, the dose is correct for first-trimester/early-second-trimester events. The option is incomplete - anti-D should be given as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours. (Source: ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines)

Before 20 weeks gestation, the Kleihauer-Betke test is not routinely performed as the fetal red cell volume is insufficient for reliable quantification. Anti-D is given empirically at the standard dose without waiting for Kleihauer results. After 20 weeks, Kleihauer is performed to quantify FMH and determine if additional anti-D is needed. (Source: ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines; RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

Repeating the indirect Coombs test does not replace the need for anti-D prophylaxis. The Coombs test detects existing antibodies, but anti-D is given to PREVENT sensitisation after the potentially sensitising event. A negative Coombs confirms she is not yet sensitised, which is the indication for prophylaxis. (Source: ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines)

Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU IM should be given as soon as possible after a potentially sensitising event in an unsensitised Rh D-negative woman, ideally within 72 hours. At less than 20 weeks gestation, the standard dose of 250 IU is sufficient without Kleihauer testing. Abdominal trauma is a recognised sensitising event. (Source: ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines; RANZCOG Anti-D Guideline)

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is stratified by bile acid levels: mild (19-39 micromol/L, delivery at 39-40 weeks), moderate (40-99 micromol/L, delivery at 37 weeks), and severe (100+ micromol/L, consider immediate delivery or at 34-36 weeks with corticosteroids). UDCA is the mainstay of symptom treatment. Weekly bile acid and LFT monitoring is important as levels can fluctuate. Vitamin K supplementation may be needed if coagulation is affected.
key_points: Bile acids 40-99 micromol/L: moderate ICP, plan delivery at 37 weeks
Bile acids >100 micromol/L: severe ICP with highest stillbirth risk
UDCA is first-line pharmacological treatment for symptom relief
Weekly bile acid and LFT monitoring is recommended
explanation.pearls: Stillbirth risk in ICP rises sharply at bile acids above 100 micromol/L (prevalence 3.4%) compared to 40-99 micromol/L (0.3%) - this threshold drives the decision between 37-week delivery and earlier intervention.

options.rationale: Bile acids of 42 micromol/L represent moderate intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP). While UDCA is appropriate for symptom relief, a delivery plan at 39 weeks is only suitable for mild ICP (bile acids 19-39 micromol/L). At 40 micromol/L or above, earlier delivery is recommended due to increased stillbirth risk. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: ICP; Queensland Clinical Guideline: ICP)

Bile acids of 42 micromol/L confirm the diagnosis of ICP and require active management. Delaying treatment and monitoring risks ongoing fetal exposure to elevated bile acids, which are associated with adverse fetal outcomes including preterm birth, meconium-stained liquor, and stillbirth. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: ICP)

With bile acids of 42 micromol/L (40-99 range), ursodeoxycholic acid should be commenced for symptom relief, and planned delivery at 37 weeks gestation is recommended. The stillbirth risk increases significantly when bile acids exceed 40 micromol/L, particularly above 100 micromol/L. Weekly bile acid and LFT monitoring is also indicated. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: ICP; Queensland Clinical Guideline: ICP)

Immediate delivery at 35 weeks for bile acids of 42 micromol/L exposes the neonate to unnecessary prematurity risks. Delivery at 37 weeks balances fetal maturity with stillbirth risk. Immediate delivery is reserved for bile acids above 100 micromol/L or if fetal compromise is demonstrated. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: ICP)

Colestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant that is poorly tolerated and less effective than UDCA for ICP symptoms. It also interferes with fat-soluble vitamin absorption, including vitamin K, which could worsen coagulopathy risk. UDCA is the preferred pharmacological treatment. (Source: AMH; RCOG Green-top Guideline: ICP)

explanation.summary: Levothyroxine requirements increase by 30-50% during pregnancy, primarily due to increased thyroxine-binding globulin, expanded plasma volume, and placental deiodination. The TSH target in pregnancy is below 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester. Dose adjustments should be made promptly when TSH rises above target, with TSH rechecked every 4-6 weeks. A practical strategy is to increase the weekly dose by 2 extra tablets immediately upon pregnancy confirmation in women on established replacement.
key_points: TSH target <2.5 mIU/L in first trimester of pregnancy
Levothyroxine requirements increase 30-50% in pregnancy
Dose adjustment should be prompt when TSH is above target
Recheck TSH every 4-6 weeks during pregnancy until stable
explanation.pearls: A practical approach to thyroid replacement in early pregnancy is the '2 extra tablets per week' rule - women on stable levothyroxine should take 2 additional tablets per week (approximately 29% increase) upon pregnancy confirmation while awaiting formal TSH testing.

options.rationale: In pregnancy, the target TSH is below 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester (and below 3.0 in later trimesters per some guidelines). Her TSH of 4.8 exceeds this target. Levothyroxine requirements typically increase by 30-50% in pregnancy. An empirical increase of 25-30% (100 to 125 mcg) is appropriate with recheck in 4-6 weeks. (Source: ATA Thyroid in Pregnancy Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Maintaining the current dose is inappropriate as TSH of 4.8 mIU/L in early pregnancy is above the recommended threshold. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism in the first trimester is associated with impaired fetal neurodevelopment. Prompt dose adjustment is needed. (Source: ATA Thyroid in Pregnancy Guidelines)

Doubling the dose from 100 to 200 mcg is excessive and risks iatrogenic hyperthyroidism. A dose increase of 25-50% is recommended. The TSH of 4.8 requires correction but not a dramatic dose change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH)

Combination T4/T3 therapy is not recommended in pregnancy. Liothyronine does not cross the placenta as effectively as T4, and the evidence base supports levothyroxine monotherapy for maternal hypothyroidism in pregnancy. (Source: ATA Thyroid in Pregnancy Guidelines)

Desiccated thyroid extract contains variable T3/T4 ratios and is not recommended in pregnancy due to inconsistent dosing. Levothyroxine monotherapy is the standard of care. The correct approach is to increase the levothyroxine dose. (Source: ATA Thyroid in Pregnancy Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy requires prompt correction as it increases risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, and peripartum transfusion. IV iron is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated, has failed, or when rapid correction is needed in the third trimester. Ferric carboxymaltose allows a single infusion of up to 1000 mg and can be given from the second trimester onwards. Hb response is expected within 2-3 weeks. Transfusion is reserved for severe anaemia (Hb <70) or haemodynamic instability.
key_points: IV iron indicated when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, or rapid correction needed
Ferric carboxymaltose up to 1000 mg can be given as a single infusion
IV iron is safe from the second trimester onwards
Hb response expected within 2-3 weeks of IV iron
explanation.pearls: Ferric carboxymaltose raises haemoglobin by approximately 20 g/L within 2-3 weeks of a single 1000 mg infusion - making it the preferred parenteral iron preparation in late pregnancy when time to delivery is limited.

options.rationale: While alternate-day dosing and switching formulations may improve tolerance, this patient's Hb has dropped from 102 to 88 g/L despite 4 weeks of oral iron. At 32 weeks with depleted ferritin (6 microg/L) and worsening anaemia, there is insufficient time for oral iron to replenish stores before delivery. IV iron is indicated. (Source: ANZSBT Iron Deficiency Anaemia Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines)

Increasing the dose will likely worsen her GI side effects, which are already limiting adherence. The declining Hb despite oral supplementation and severely depleted ferritin at 32 weeks indicates that oral iron alone is unlikely to correct the anaemia before delivery. (Source: ANZSBT Iron Deficiency Anaemia Guidelines)

Blood transfusion is reserved for Hb below 70 g/L in stable patients or when there is haemodynamic compromise. This patient's Hb of 88 g/L with stable vital signs does not meet transfusion criteria. IV iron is the appropriate intervention. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

Delaying further investigation and treatment when there is progressive iron deficiency anaemia at 32 weeks is inappropriate. The diagnosis is clear (ferritin 6 microg/L, microcytic anaemia failing oral therapy), and delivery may be only 5-8 weeks away. IV iron should be commenced promptly. (Source: ANZSBT Iron Deficiency Anaemia Guidelines)

IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose or iron polymaltose) is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated, fails to correct anaemia, or when rapid correction is needed in the third trimester. This patient meets all three criteria: intolerance, declining Hb, and limited time before delivery. A single dose of ferric carboxymaltose (up to 1000 mg) can be given after the first trimester. (Source: ANZSBT Iron Deficiency Anaemia Guidelines; RANZCOG; AMH)

explanation.summary: VTE risk in pregnancy is 5-10 times higher than in non-pregnant women. Risk stratification guides prophylaxis timing. Women with a single prior provoked VTE and no thrombophilia typically commence LMWH from 28 weeks until 6 weeks postpartum. Higher-risk women (unprovoked VTE, thrombophilia, recurrent events) start from the first trimester. DOACs and warfarin are avoided in pregnancy. LMWH is safe as it does not cross the placenta.
key_points: Single provoked VTE with no thrombophilia: LMWH from 28 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum
Unprovoked VTE or thrombophilia: LMWH from first trimester
DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy
LMWH does not cross the placenta and is safe for the fetus
explanation.pearls: The thrombotic risk stratification in pregnancy hinges on whether a prior VTE was provoked versus unprovoked: provoked events with negative thrombophilia screen carry approximately 2-3% recurrence risk in pregnancy, while unprovoked events carry 6-10% recurrence risk.

options.rationale: A previous VTE, even if provoked, confers increased risk during pregnancy. The hypercoagulable state of pregnancy represents a significant prothrombotic challenge. Pharmacological prophylaxis is warranted. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a: VTE in Pregnancy; RANZCOG VTE Guideline)

For a single previous provoked VTE with no thrombophilia and no other major risk factors, RCOG and RANZCOG recommend antenatal LMWH prophylaxis from 28 weeks gestation continuing for 6 weeks postpartum. Earlier commencement (from first trimester) is reserved for higher-risk women such as those with unprovoked VTE, thrombophilia, or multiple VTEs. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a; RANZCOG VTE Guideline)

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) including rivaroxaban are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity and placental transfer. Low molecular weight heparin is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy as it does not cross the placenta. (Source: AMH; RANZCOG VTE Guideline)

First-trimester LMWH prophylaxis is indicated for higher-risk women: unprovoked VTE, known thrombophilia with previous VTE, recurrent VTE, or antiphospholipid syndrome. This woman had a single provoked event with negative thrombophilia screen, placing her in the intermediate-risk category suitable for prophylaxis from 28 weeks. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a)

Postnatal-only prophylaxis is used for women with risk factors but no personal history of VTE. A prior DVT, even if provoked, warrants antenatal prophylaxis in the third trimester in addition to postnatal prophylaxis. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 37a; RANZCOG VTE Guideline)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia occurs when the fetal shoulders fail to deliver after the head, typically due to impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the symphysis pubis. The HELPERR mnemonic guides management: Help, Evaluate for episiotomy, Legs (McRoberts), suprapubic Pressure, Enter (internal rotation/posterior arm), Roll (all-fours), Replace (Zavanelli). McRoberts with suprapubic pressure resolves 40-60% of cases and should always be performed first. Fundal pressure is absolutely contraindicated.
key_points: McRoberts positioning with suprapubic pressure is the first-line manoeuvre
Fundal pressure is contraindicated and worsens impaction
Internal rotation and posterior arm delivery are second-line
Document the time from head to body delivery and all manoeuvres used
explanation.pearls: Suprapubic pressure should be applied in a downward and lateral direction (CPR-style, not rocking) above the symphysis pubis to push the anterior shoulder away from the midline - this is distinct from fundal pressure which is never applied in shoulder dystocia.

options.rationale: Fundal pressure is contraindicated in shoulder dystocia. It pushes the anterior shoulder further into the symphysis pubis, worsening impaction and increasing the risk of brachial plexus injury. It should never be applied. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline; ALSO Course Manual)

The Zavanelli manoeuvre (cephalic replacement followed by caesarean) is a last-resort intervention used only when all other manoeuvres have failed. It should not be attempted as a first-line response. First-line manoeuvres (McRoberts, suprapubic pressure) resolve the majority of shoulder dystocias. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)

Episiotomy alone does not relieve bony shoulder impaction, as shoulder dystocia is a bony obstruction at the pelvic inlet. However, episiotomy may facilitate internal manoeuvres if needed subsequently. It is not the immediate first-line action. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline)

McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflexion of the maternal hips onto the abdomen) combined with suprapubic pressure (applied by an assistant above the symphysis to dislodge the anterior shoulder) is the first-line intervention for shoulder dystocia. It resolves 40-60% of cases by straightening the lumbosacral angle and rotating the pelvis. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline; ALSO Course Manual)

Delivery of the posterior arm (Barnum manoeuvre) or rotational manoeuvres (Rubin II, Wood's screw) are effective but are second-line interventions used when McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail. The HELPERR mnemonic dictates the sequence, with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure first. (Source: RANZCOG Shoulder Dystocia Guideline; ALSO Course Manual)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate action to prevent fetal hypoxia and death. The key interventions are: digital elevation of the presenting part to relieve cord compression, maternal repositioning (knee-chest or left lateral with head down), keeping the cord warm and moist, and emergency category 1 caesarean section. Bladder filling with 500-700 mL normal saline via a Foley catheter can also elevate the presenting part while transferring to theatre. Tocolysis may reduce uterine contractions as an adjunct.
key_points: Digital elevation of the presenting part is the critical immediate action
Do not attempt to replace the cord above the cervix
Emergency category 1 caesarean section is the definitive management
Bladder filling can be used as an adjunct to elevate the presenting part
explanation.pearls: Rapid bladder filling with 500-700 mL normal saline via Foley catheter provides sustained elevation of the presenting part off the prolapsed cord - this 'hands-free' technique frees the operator during transfer to theatre and is taught in the ALSO and PROMPT courses.

options.rationale: Clamping the prolapsed cord would completely occlude blood flow to the fetus and cause rapid fetal demise. The cord must be kept warm and moist, and compression must be relieved. The cervix is only 5 cm dilated, so vaginal delivery is not imminent. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: Cord Prolapse)

Augmenting labour with oxytocin is inappropriate. At 5 cm dilatation with a prolapsed cord, vaginal delivery cannot be achieved rapidly enough. Category 1 emergency caesarean section is the appropriate mode of delivery. Oxytocin would increase uterine contractions, worsening cord compression. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Guideline)

The most critical immediate action is continuous digital elevation of the presenting part off the prolapsed cord to relieve compression. This should be maintained until emergency caesarean section is performed. The patient should be placed in the left lateral or knee-chest position to reduce cord compression, and the cord kept warm with moist gauze. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: Cord Prolapse)

Tocolysis may be considered as an adjunct to reduce uterine contractions and cord compression, but it is not the most important immediate action. Digital elevation of the presenting part is the priority to relieve cord compression. Tocolysis may be given concurrently but should not delay manual decompression. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Cord Prolapse)

Attempting to replace the cord (funic reduction) is associated with cord spasm and further compression. It is not recommended as standard practice. Digital elevation of the presenting part is the proven emergency manoeuvre while arranging caesarean delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Guideline)

explanation.summary: GDM management follows a stepwise approach: lifestyle modification first, then pharmacological therapy if targets are not met within 1-2 weeks. The ADIPS targets are fasting less than 5.0 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial less than 6.7 mmol/L. Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia is best addressed with evening/bedtime intermediate-acting insulin (NPH), which controls overnight hepatic glucose output. Metformin is more useful for postprandial hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance.
key_points: ADIPS fasting BSL target is <5.0 mmol/L in GDM
Persistent fasting hyperglycaemia indicates need for bedtime NPH insulin
Metformin is preferred when postprandial readings are the main issue
Lifestyle modification should be trialled for 1-2 weeks before pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: The choice between metformin and insulin in GDM depends on the glycaemic pattern: fasting hyperglycaemia responds better to bedtime NPH insulin (targeting overnight hepatic glucose output), while isolated postprandial hyperglycaemia may respond to metformin alone.

options.rationale: Her fasting BSL consistently exceeds the ADIPS target of less than 5.0 mmol/L, despite 4 weeks of dietary modification. Continuing the same approach when targets are not being met delays necessary pharmacological intervention and risks macrosomia and other GDM complications. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

Metformin is a reasonable first-line pharmacological agent for GDM, particularly for postprandial hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance. However, when fasting hyperglycaemia is the primary problem (as here, with fasting readings 5.3-5.6 consistently above target), insulin is more effective at controlling overnight hepatic glucose output. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines; AMH)

Initiation of insulin for GDM is within the scope of obstetric and diabetes-in-pregnancy teams and does not require endocrinology referral. Delaying treatment for a specialist referral when targets are clearly not being met is inappropriate at 30 weeks. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines)

Glibenclamide (glibenclamide) crosses the placenta and is associated with neonatal hypoglycaemia. It is not recommended as first-line in Australian GDM guidelines. When fasting BSL is persistently elevated, insulin provides more predictable and titratable control. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines; AMH)

Intermediate-acting insulin (NPH or isophane) given at bedtime is the most appropriate treatment for persistent fasting hyperglycaemia in GDM that has not responded to lifestyle modification. It controls overnight hepatic glucose production. The ADIPS fasting target is less than 5.0 mmol/L. Starting dose is typically 4-8 units, titrated based on fasting BSL readings. (Source: ADIPS GDM Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a severe variant of pre-eclampsia characterised by haemolysis (elevated LDH, schistocytes, falling Hb), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. The definitive treatment is delivery. At preterm gestations, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation are given while preparing for delivery. HELLP can progress rapidly to hepatic rupture, DIC, or maternal death. Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and antihypertensives for BP control are critical concurrent treatments. Differentiation from TTP and HUS is important.
key_points: HELLP = Haemolysis + Elevated Liver enzymes + Low Platelets
Delivery is the definitive treatment regardless of gestation for severe HELLP
Betamethasone given for fetal lung maturity, not as treatment for HELLP
Differentiate from TTP (ADAMTS13 low), HUS (renal predominant), and AFLP
explanation.pearls: ADAMTS13 activity below 10% distinguishes TTP from HELLP syndrome - both cause microangiopathic haemolysis and thrombocytopaenia, but TTP requires plasma exchange while HELLP requires delivery.

options.rationale: While corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation are appropriate, delaying delivery for a full 48 hours until 34 weeks is not safe in this clinical situation. HELLP syndrome with thrombocytopaenia below 100, significantly elevated transaminases, and haemolysis is an indication for delivery once initial maternal stabilisation is achieved, regardless of gestation. (Source: ISSHP Classification 2018; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

Plasma exchange is the treatment for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), not HELLP syndrome. While both cause microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopaenia, HELLP is characterised by elevated transaminases (typically mild in TTP) and resolves with delivery. ADAMTS13 activity testing can differentiate if clinical doubt exists. (Source: ISSHP Classification 2018)

HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) in this presentation requires delivery as definitive treatment. Betamethasone should be administered for fetal lung maturation, and delivery planned within 24-48 hours to allow maximum steroid benefit while limiting maternal risk. The timing reflects the severity - platelets below 100 with active haemolysis and markedly elevated transaminases do not permit prolonged expectant management. (Source: ISSHP Classification 2018; SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy; RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline)

Expectant management to 37 weeks is not appropriate with HELLP syndrome. The condition carries risks of hepatic rupture, DIC, placental abruption, and maternal death. HELLP with platelets below 100 and markedly elevated transaminases mandates delivery. Expectant management is only considered in mild pre-eclampsia without end-organ damage before 37 weeks. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy)

High-dose dexamethasone was previously used to attempt to improve platelet count and liver function in HELLP. However, systematic reviews have shown no benefit in maternal or fetal outcomes. Corticosteroids in this setting are given for fetal lung maturity (betamethasone), not as a treatment for HELLP itself. (Source: Cochrane Review: Corticosteroids for HELLP; ISSHP)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption is the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall. Severity ranges from mild (small retroplacental clot, reassuring CTG) to severe (large abruption, fetal compromise, DIC). Management depends on fetal and maternal status. Non-reassuring fetal status mandates immediate delivery. Fibrinogen below 2.0 g/L indicates DIC risk. Tocolysis is contraindicated. Risk factors include smoking, hypertension, cocaine use, and previous abruption.
key_points: Non-reassuring CTG with abruption mandates emergency caesarean
Fibrinogen <2.0 g/L indicates developing DIC requiring cryoprecipitate
Tocolysis is contraindicated in placental abruption
Betamethasone should be given but must not delay delivery when fetus is compromised
explanation.pearls: Fibrinogen is the earliest coagulation marker to fall in abruption-related DIC - a level below 2.0 g/L has an 80% positive predictive value for severe PPH, and cryoprecipitate should be administered to maintain fibrinogen above 2.0 g/L.

options.rationale: Expectant management is inappropriate here. The CTG shows non-reassuring fetal status (reduced variability with late decelerations), and the clinical picture is consistent with a significant abruption. The falling fibrinogen (2.1 g/L, threshold of concern is below 2.0) suggests developing consumptive coagulopathy. Urgent delivery is required. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: APH; Queensland Clinical Guideline: APH)

Emergency caesarean section is indicated for significant placental abruption with non-reassuring fetal status. The CTG pattern (reduced variability, late decelerations) indicates fetal compromise requiring immediate delivery. The falling fibrinogen suggests incipient DIC. Cross-matched blood and coagulation products should be available. At 29 weeks, betamethasone should be given but must not delay delivery. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: APH; Queensland Clinical Guideline: APH; RANZCOG APH Statement)

Delaying delivery for 48 hours to complete a steroid course is not safe when the fetus is showing signs of compromise on CTG and there is active abruption with coagulopathy risk. The benefit of steroids does not outweigh the immediate fetal risk. Betamethasone should be given but delivery should not be delayed. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: APH)

Tocolysis is absolutely contraindicated in placental abruption. It may mask clinical deterioration and delay necessary intervention. The non-reassuring CTG mandates urgent delivery, not prolongation of the pregnancy. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline: APH; RANZCOG APH Statement)

Vaginal delivery may be considered in mild abruption with reassuring fetal status and a favourable cervix. However, with non-reassuring CTG, the delivery must be expedited - emergency caesarean is faster and safer than attempting induction at 29 weeks with an unfavourable cervix. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: APH)

explanation.summary: Failed induction of labour is diagnosed when adequate uterine contractions with ruptured membranes and maximal oxytocin fail to produce cervical change over an adequate duration (typically 6-8 hours at maximum dose). This differs from failed cervical ripening (inability to achieve a favourable cervix for amniotomy). In a primigravida with no cervical change after 8 hours of adequate contractions, caesarean section is the appropriate recommendation. The decision requires clear documentation and informed consent.
key_points: Failed IOL requires adequate contractions + ruptured membranes + no cervical change
Minimum 6-8 hours of adequate oxytocin before diagnosing failure
Prostaglandins must not be given concurrently with oxytocin
Primigravida with failed IOL has very low chance of vaginal delivery with further intervention
explanation.pearls: Failed induction is a distinct entity from labour dystocia - the former reflects failure to establish active labour despite adequate stimulation, while the latter occurs after active labour is established but progress ceases. The management is the same (caesarean), but the distinction matters for documentation and future pregnancy counselling.

options.rationale: Failed induction is defined as failure to achieve cervical change despite adequate uterine contractions (3 in 10 minutes) with ruptured membranes and oxytocin at maximum dose for an adequate duration. After 8 hours of maximum oxytocin with no cervical change, ongoing induction is unlikely to succeed. A primigravida at 41+2 who has had maximal cervical ripening and adequate oxytocin without progress should be offered caesarean section. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: IOL; NICE Induction of Labour)

While resting and restarting oxytocin is sometimes considered, after 8 hours at maximum dose with ruptured membranes and no cervical change in a primigravida, the likelihood of vaginal delivery is very low. Prolonged induction increases risks of chorioamnionitis, maternal exhaustion, and fetal compromise. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: IOL)

The cervical ripening phase is complete - two prostaglandin doses and a Foley catheter have been used, and the cervix responded to 3 cm. The problem is failure to progress during the active oxytocin phase, not inadequate ripening. Additional mechanical ripening is not indicated. (Source: Queensland Clinical Guideline: IOL)

Adding prostaglandins while on oxytocin infusion is contraindicated due to the risk of uterine hyperstimulation. The cervix has already been ripened with prostaglandins. The issue is failed progression with adequate contractions, not inadequate cervical ripening. (Source: AMH; Queensland Clinical Guideline: IOL)

Prolonging oxytocin for another 8 hours (total 16 hours at maximum dose) without any cervical change is unlikely to succeed and increases maternal and fetal risks. After adequate contractions and ruptured membranes for 8 hours with no progress, continuing is not evidence-based practice. (Source: NICE Induction of Labour)

explanation.summary: External cephalic version is recommended for breech presentation from 36-37 weeks. Multiparous women have higher success rates (approximately 60-70%) compared to nulliparous women (40-50%). ECV is a potentially sensitising event requiring anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh D-negative women. Tocolysis (terbutaline) may be used to facilitate the procedure. Complications are rare but include transient fetal bradycardia, abruption, and premature rupture of membranes. Continuous CTG monitoring is required before, during, and after the procedure.
key_points: ECV offered from 36-37 weeks for breech presentation
Anterior placenta is not a contraindication
Anti-D required for Rh D-negative women after ECV
Success rate higher in multiparous women (60-70%)
explanation.pearls: ECV success is predicted by multiparity (strongest predictor), posterior placenta, normal amniotic fluid, and non-engaged breech - a multiparous woman with these features has an ECV success rate exceeding 70%.

options.rationale: An anterior placenta is not a contraindication to ECV. While it may make the procedure technically more difficult, it is not listed among absolute or relative contraindications. Absolute contraindications include placenta praevia, abnormal CTG, ruptured membranes, multiple pregnancy, and recent APH. (Source: RANZCOG ECV Statement; RCOG Green-top Guideline: ECV)

ECV is recommended from 36-37 weeks in nulliparous women and from 37 weeks in multiparous women (or 36+ weeks per some guidelines). Deferring to 38 weeks risks spontaneous labour or rupture of membranes before the procedure. At 36+2 weeks with frank breech, ECV should be offered now. (Source: RANZCOG ECV Statement)

While elective caesarean is the alternative if ECV fails or is declined, the patient is keen to attempt vaginal birth. ECV should be offered first as it converts breech to cephalic in approximately 50-60% of cases (higher in multiparous women). (Source: RANZCOG ECV Statement; RCOG Green-top Guideline: ECV)

ECV is a potentially sensitising event, so anti-D immunoglobulin must be administered to Rh D-negative women after the procedure. The ECV itself is appropriately timed at 36+ weeks for this multiparous woman. Anti-D 625 IU (standard dose after 20 weeks) should be given post-procedure. A Kleihauer test should also be performed. She should also receive her overdue routine prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG ECV Statement; ANZSBT Anti-D Guidelines)

While vaginal breech delivery may be offered in selected cases (frank breech, EFW 2.5-3.5 kg, experienced accoucheur), ECV should be attempted first as it is safer and converts breech to cephalic in the majority of multiparous women. Vaginal breech delivery is the fallback if ECV fails and the patient declines caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG ECV Statement)

explanation.summary: The PPH management escalation follows a systematic approach: uterotonics, then tamponade, then surgical intervention, then hysterectomy as the final step. Intrauterine balloon tamponade bridges the gap between medical and surgical management and is effective in 80-90% of refractory uterine atony. If tamponade fails, surgical options include B-Lynch compression sutures, uterine artery ligation, and internal iliac artery ligation before hysterectomy. Concurrent resuscitation with blood products should follow massive transfusion protocol principles.
key_points: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is the next step after medical management fails
Bakri balloon or condom catheter can be placed rapidly
The tamponade test determines if surgical intervention is needed
Hysterectomy is the last resort after tamponade and surgical techniques fail
explanation.pearls: The Bakri balloon is filled with warm saline (typically 300-500 mL for vaginal delivery, 500 mL for post-caesarean) - the cessation of bleeding after inflation ('positive tamponade test') predicts that surgical intervention can be avoided in over 85% of cases.

options.rationale: Bimanual compression has already been performed for 10 minutes without success, and all medical uterotonics have been exhausted. Continuing the same intervention is unlikely to achieve haemostasis. Escalation to mechanical or surgical intervention is required. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: PPH)

A second dose of TXA can be given after 30 minutes if bleeding continues, but this is an adjunct and does not address the primary problem of uterine atony refractory to all uterotonics. Definitive mechanical or surgical intervention is the priority. (Source: WOMAN Trial; Queensland Clinical Guideline: PPH)

Intrauterine balloon tamponade (Bakri balloon or condom catheter) is the next step when pharmacological uterotonics fail. It provides direct tamponade of the uterine cavity, can be placed rapidly, and is effective in 80-90% of cases. It buys time while preparing for surgical intervention if needed. It also serves as a 'tamponade test' - if bleeding stops, surgery is avoided. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: PPH; FIGO PPH Guideline)

Hysterectomy is the definitive surgical treatment but should be reserved for when all conservative measures, including balloon tamponade and uterine compression sutures, have failed. Proceeding directly to hysterectomy without attempting balloon tamponade skips a step that is effective in the majority of cases. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

Uterine artery embolisation requires interventional radiology facilities and a haemodynamically stable patient who can be transferred safely. This patient is hypotensive and tachycardic. Balloon tamponade or surgical measures are more appropriate for an unstable patient in the delivery suite. (Source: RANZCOG PPH Guideline)

explanation.summary: Ectopic pregnancy management requires weighing beta-hCG level, mass size, presence of cardiac activity, haemodynamic stability, fertility wishes, and patient reliability for follow-up. Methotrexate success rates decline as beta-hCG rises above 3000-5000 IU/L. Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingotomy when the contralateral tube is normal and fertility is not desired, as it avoids the 5-8% risk of persistent trophoblast requiring further treatment. The decision between medical and surgical management should be individualised.
key_points: Methotrexate success rate drops significantly above beta-hCG 5000 IU/L
Salpingectomy preferred when contralateral tube normal and fertility not desired
Salpingotomy preferred when contralateral tube absent/damaged
Mass >35 mm is a relative contraindication to methotrexate
explanation.pearls: Persistent trophoblast occurs in 5-8% of salpingotomies (requiring methotrexate rescue) versus 0% after salpingectomy - this is the key trade-off when choosing between tube-preserving and tube-removing surgery for ectopic pregnancy.

options.rationale: While methotrexate criteria include haemodynamic stability and no cardiac activity, the beta-hCG of 4200-4500 IU/L exceeds the threshold where methotrexate has reliable efficacy (success rate drops to approximately 60% above 3000-5000 IU/L). The mass size of 30 mm also approaches the upper limit. Combined with the patient having completed her family (fertility preservation is not a concern), surgical management is more appropriate and definitive. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline; RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

Multi-dose methotrexate has higher success rates than single-dose but still carries significant failure risk at this beta-hCG level. The mass is 30 mm, which is near the 35 mm cutoff some guidelines use. Given completed family (no fertility concern) and borderline parameters, surgery is more appropriate as a definitive single intervention. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

The diagnosis is already established (tubal ectopic on ultrasound with rising beta-hCG). Further observation delays definitive treatment. The suboptimal rise (7% in 48 hours) is consistent with an ectopic pregnancy but does not change the management decision. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline)

Laparoscopic salpingectomy is the most appropriate management for several reasons: beta-hCG above the optimal threshold for methotrexate (4200 IU/L), mass approaching 35 mm, and importantly, the patient has completed her family so tube preservation is not a priority. Salpingectomy provides definitive treatment with a single intervention and no need for prolonged beta-hCG monitoring. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Guideline; RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

Salpingotomy (tube-preserving surgery) is preferred when future fertility is desired and the contralateral tube is absent or damaged. This patient has completed her family and has a normal contralateral tube, making salpingectomy the preferred option. Salpingotomy also requires ongoing beta-hCG monitoring for persistent trophoblast. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 21)

explanation.summary: Recurrent miscarriage (3 or more consecutive losses) affects 1-2% of couples. The recommended workup includes antiphospholipid antibody testing, parental karyotyping, pelvic ultrasound for uterine anomalies, and thyroid function. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important treatable cause, with aspirin plus LMWH improving live birth rates from approximately 40% to 70-80%. APS diagnosis requires positive antibodies on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart plus clinical criteria.
key_points: Antiphospholipid antibody testing is the most important investigation in recurrent miscarriage
Positive result must be confirmed at least 12 weeks later
Treatment with aspirin + LMWH improves live birth rate to 70-80%
Inherited thrombophilia screening is not routinely recommended for recurrent early loss
explanation.pearls: Aspirin 100 mg plus prophylactic LMWH from positive pregnancy test until 36 weeks improves the live birth rate from approximately 40% to 70-80% in antiphospholipid syndrome - making it the most effective treatment for any identified cause of recurrent miscarriage.

options.rationale: Parental karyotyping identifies balanced translocations in approximately 3-5% of couples with recurrent miscarriage. While important, the partner's karyotype is already normal. Maternal karyotyping may be warranted but is lower yield than antiphospholipid antibody testing, which is the most treatable cause. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Investigation; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

Inherited thrombophilias (Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin gene mutation, Protein C/S) have weak and inconsistent associations with recurrent first-trimester miscarriage. RANZCOG and RCOG do not recommend routine thrombophilia screening for recurrent early miscarriage. Antiphospholipid antibodies are the exception as they are treatable. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 17; RANZCOG)

Luteal phase progesterone testing is not recommended in the workup for recurrent miscarriage. Evidence for luteal phase deficiency as a cause of recurrent loss is weak, and progesterone supplementation has not been shown to benefit women with recurrent miscarriage in the absence of early bleeding (PRISM trial). (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

Chronic endometritis is an emerging area of research in recurrent miscarriage and implantation failure, but it is not yet part of the standard recommended workup. Antiphospholipid antibody testing is the priority investigation given its established diagnostic and therapeutic implications. (Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline 17)

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is the most important treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage, found in 5-15% of women with recurrent pregnancy loss. Testing includes lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies (IgG and IgM), and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies. Positive results must be confirmed on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart. Treatment with aspirin and LMWH significantly improves live birth rates. (Source: RANZCOG Recurrent Miscarriage Investigation; RCOG Green-top Guideline 17; Revised Sydney Criteria)

explanation.summary: Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) involves penetration of endometrial implants more than 5 mm into the peritoneal surface, often affecting the rectovaginal septum, uterosacral ligaments, bladder, and bowel. Management requires a multidisciplinary approach at a specialist centre. MRI is the imaging modality for surgical planning. Surgery aims for complete excision but carries risks of bowel injury, ureteric damage, and impact on ovarian reserve. Fertility preservation must be discussed preoperatively.
key_points: Deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement requires specialist MDT assessment
MRI pelvis is the key imaging for surgical planning
Colonoscopy has poor sensitivity for endometriosis
Complete excision at a specialist centre improves outcomes vs piecemeal surgery
explanation.pearls: Endometriosis invades the bowel from the serosal surface inward - colonoscopic biopsies are typically negative because the mucosa is the last layer involved, making MRI pelvis the investigation of choice for staging deep infiltrating disease.

options.rationale: Deep infiltrating endometriosis involving the rectovaginal septum with bowel wall involvement requires management at a specialist endometriosis centre with a multidisciplinary team including gynaecologist, colorectal surgeon, and radiologist. Surgery for bowel endometriosis carries significant risks and should only be performed by surgeons with appropriate expertise. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline)

GnRH agonists may suppress symptoms temporarily but do not treat deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement. The patient has already failed first-line hormonal therapy (COCP). With bowel wall invasion and rectal bleeding, surgical assessment is needed to determine if excision is required. (Source: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline)

Simply excising the endometrioma without addressing the deep rectovaginal disease would provide incomplete treatment. The bowel nodule requires preoperative assessment (MRI), MDT discussion, and potentially involvement of a colorectal surgeon. A piecemeal approach risks incomplete surgery and complications. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

While a LNG-IUD is effective for endometriosis-related pain and is second-line therapy, this patient has deep infiltrating endometriosis with bowel involvement and rectal bleeding despite hormonal therapy. The clinical picture warrants surgical assessment at a specialist centre rather than a further trial of hormonal suppression alone. (Source: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline)

Colonoscopy has poor sensitivity for endometriosis as the disease infiltrates from the serosal surface. Mucosal involvement is rare. MRI pelvis is the preferred imaging modality for staging deep endometriosis and planning surgery. Colonoscopy may be performed if there is diagnostic uncertainty about the cause of rectal bleeding. (Source: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: The 2023 international evidence-based guideline for PCOS recommends letrozole as first-line ovulation induction based on the PPCOS II trial showing superior live birth rates compared to clomifene. Letrozole works by inhibiting aromatase, reducing oestrogen, and stimulating FSH release. Advantages over clomifene include a thinner anti-oestrogenic endometrial effect, lower multiple pregnancy rates, and shorter half-life. Lifestyle modification remains an important adjunct.
key_points: Letrozole is first-line for PCOS ovulation induction (2023 guideline)
PPCOS II trial: letrozole live birth rate 27.5% vs clomifene 19.1%
Letrozole has lower multiple pregnancy rates than clomifene
Gonadotrophins and ovarian drilling are second-line options
explanation.pearls: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) avoids the anti-oestrogenic endometrial effects of clomifene and has a half-life of only 48 hours versus 5-7 days for clomifene - this shorter duration means the endometrium is exposed to rising endogenous oestrogen during the follicular phase, supporting implantation.

options.rationale: Clomifene citrate was historically first-line for PCOS ovulation induction. However, the 2023 international evidence-based guideline for PCOS now recommends letrozole as first-line based on higher ovulation and live birth rates. Clomifene has higher multiple pregnancy rates and anti-oestrogenic effects on the endometrium. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS; RANZCOG)

Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) is the recommended first-line ovulation induction agent for PCOS per the 2023 international guideline. The landmark PPCOS II trial demonstrated higher live birth rates with letrozole (27.5%) compared to clomifene (19.1%), lower multiple pregnancy rates, and better endometrial thickness. Letrozole is used off-label for this indication. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS; PPCOS II Trial)

Gonadotrophins (FSH injections) are second-line for PCOS ovulation induction, reserved for when oral agents fail. They require intensive ultrasound monitoring due to the high risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in PCOS, are more expensive, and carry higher multiple pregnancy rates. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS)

Metformin alone has lower ovulation and live birth rates compared to letrozole or clomifene. While it may be used as an adjunct, particularly in women with BMI over 30, it is not recommended as a primary ovulation induction agent. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS)

Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is a second-line option for PCOS anovulation, considered when oral ovulation induction agents fail. It is not first-line treatment and carries surgical risks including adhesion formation and potential reduction in ovarian reserve. (Source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS; RANZCOG)

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP renewed pathway treats HPV 16 and 18 differently from other oncogenic HPV types due to their significantly higher risk of progression to cervical cancer. HPV 16/18 detection triggers direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology, while other oncogenic types with normal cytology are managed with 12-month repeat. During pregnancy, colposcopy and directed biopsy are safe, but treatment is deferred until postpartum unless invasive cancer is suspected.
key_points: HPV 16/18 triggers direct colposcopy regardless of cytology result
Non-16/18 oncogenic HPV with negative cytology: repeat at 12 months
Colposcopy is safe during pregnancy, but treatment deferred postpartum
LLETZ/LEEP contraindicated during pregnancy
explanation.pearls: HPV 16 carries a 10-year cumulative risk of CIN 3+ of approximately 17% even when initial cytology is negative - this is why the NCSP pathway mandates direct colposcopy referral for HPV 16/18 regardless of cytology result.

options.rationale: A 12-month repeat is the pathway for non-16/18 oncogenic HPV types with negative or LSIL cytology. HPV 16 and 18 carry the highest risk of high-grade disease and cervical cancer, so they trigger direct colposcopy referral regardless of cytology result under the NCSP renewed pathway. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia)

Under the NCSP renewed pathway, HPV 16 or 18 detection triggers direct referral for colposcopy regardless of the cytology result. Colposcopy is safe during pregnancy and should not be deferred. If high-grade disease is found, biopsy may be taken but excisional treatment is deferred until at least 6 weeks postpartum unless invasive cancer is suspected. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia)

Deferring colposcopy for HPV 16 with potential high-grade disease is not appropriate. While treatment is deferred to the postpartum period, colposcopic assessment and biopsy if needed should be performed during pregnancy to exclude invasive cancer. The risk of progression during pregnancy is low but assessment is still indicated. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

Normal 5-yearly screening applies only when HPV is negative. HPV 16 positivity with negative cytology still carries a significant cumulative risk of CIN 2+ (approximately 10% at 5 years). Colposcopy referral is mandatory under the NCSP pathway. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

Excisional procedures (LLETZ/LEEP) are contraindicated during pregnancy due to risks of haemorrhage, preterm rupture of membranes, and preterm labour. Treatment is deferred to 6 weeks postpartum. During pregnancy, colposcopy and biopsy only are performed. (Source: NCSP Clinical Guidelines)

explanation.summary: DMPA causes reversible bone mineral density loss of 2-4% over 2 years due to oestrogen suppression. This is particularly relevant in adolescents who are accruing peak bone mass. BMD typically recovers within 1-2 years of stopping DMPA. Guidelines recommend reviewing risk-benefit after 2 years, especially in young women and those with osteoporosis risk factors. DMPA is not absolutely contraindicated in adolescents but should be considered alongside alternatives such as the LNG-IUD or implant, which do not affect BMD.
key_points: DMPA reduces BMD by 2-4% over 2 years
BMD typically recovers within 1-2 years of cessation
Particularly relevant in adolescents accruing peak bone mass
No absolute time limit but review risk-benefit after 2 years
explanation.pearls: The etonogestrel implant (Implanon NXT) does not suppress oestrogen to the same degree as DMPA and has no clinically significant effect on bone mineral density - making it the preferred long-acting injectable/implant option in adolescents concerned about bone health.

options.rationale: DMPA suppresses oestrogen and reduces bone mineral density by 2-4% over 2 years. In adolescents, this is particularly relevant as peak bone mass is being accrued (until approximately age 25). However, BMD typically recovers within 1-2 years of cessation. FSRH and RANZCOG advise that DMPA can be used in adolescents after careful risk-benefit discussion, including family history of osteoporosis. It should not be first-line in young women unless other methods are unsuitable. (Source: FSRH DMPA Guideline; RANZCOG Contraception Guideline)

DMPA does not require liver function monitoring. It is metabolised by the liver but does not have significant hepatotoxic effects. No routine blood monitoring is required during DMPA use. (Source: AMH; FSRH DMPA Guideline)

DMPA actually reduces the risk of endometrial cancer through progestogenic suppression of the endometrium. It also reduces the risk of ovarian cancer. There is a small possible increase in breast cancer risk with current use, which diminishes after cessation. (Source: FSRH DMPA Guideline)

Intellectual disability is not a contraindication to DMPA. If the patient has capacity to consent (or valid substitute decision-making is in place), DMPA can be offered. The method may be particularly practical for patients who find daily pill-taking or device insertion challenging. (Source: RANZCOG Contraception Guideline)

There is no absolute time limit for DMPA use. Guidelines advise reviewing the risk-benefit balance after 2 years of use, particularly in women under 18 and those with additional osteoporosis risk factors. Continuation beyond 2 years is acceptable if the benefits outweigh the risks and alternatives have been discussed. (Source: FSRH DMPA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Premature ovarian insufficiency is defined as ovarian failure before age 40, confirmed by FSH above 25-40 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart. HRT is essential and should continue until the average age of natural menopause (50-52). Unlike HRT in naturally menopausal women, HRT in POI replaces a physiological deficit and does not carry the same risks. Women should be counselled about reduced but not absent fertility and the possibility of spontaneous pregnancy. Oocyte donation remains the most effective fertility option.
key_points: POI diagnosed by FSH >25-40 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart
HRT should continue until at least age 50-52
Physiological HRT (17-beta oestradiol + progestogen) preferred over COCP
Spontaneous pregnancy possible in 5-10% but oocyte donation is most reliable fertility option
explanation.pearls: HRT in premature ovarian insufficiency is replacement therapy, not additive therapy - the cardiovascular risk data from the WHI study does not apply to women under 40 who are replacing a physiological oestrogen deficit.

options.rationale: Tibolone is not first-line for young women with POI. It provides less physiological oestrogen replacement than combined oestrogen-progestogen and has limited data on cardiovascular and bone protection in women under 40. Physiological HRT that mimics normal premenopausal hormone levels is preferred. (Source: AMS Position Statement on POI; ESHRE POI Guideline)

Bisphosphonates are not appropriate first-line treatment in a 28-year-old. HRT is the primary intervention for bone protection in POI, as it replaces the missing oestrogen. Bisphosphonates are reserved for postmenopausal women at high fracture risk. Bisphosphonates are teratogenic and must be avoided in women who may conceive. (Source: ESHRE POI Guideline)

While the COCP provides oestrogen and progestogen, it delivers supraphysiological doses of synthetic oestrogen and has a 7-day hormone-free interval. Physiological HRT (17-beta oestradiol with a progestogen) is preferred in POI as it provides more consistent, physiological hormone levels and better bone protection. The COCP also provides contraception, which is rarely needed in POI. (Source: ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS Position Statement on POI)

While spontaneous ovarian activity can occur in 5-10% of women with POI, this is unpredictable and should not delay HRT. Untreated oestrogen deficiency in a young woman leads to accelerated bone loss, increased cardiovascular risk, urogenital atrophy, and impaired quality of life. HRT should be commenced promptly. (Source: ESHRE POI Guideline)

Physiological combined HRT (17-beta oestradiol plus a progestogen for endometrial protection) is the standard of care for POI. It should be continued at least until the average age of natural menopause (50-52 years) to maintain bone density, cardiovascular health, and quality of life. This is not the same risk profile as HRT in naturally menopausal women - it replaces a physiological deficit. (Source: ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS Position Statement on POI)

explanation.summary: Gestational trophoblastic disease surveillance after complete hydatidiform mole evacuation requires serial hCG monitoring to detect the 15-20% that develop gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. The protocol is weekly hCG until normal, then monthly for 6 months (complete mole) or 6 months (partial mole varies by centre). Contraception is essential during surveillance to avoid confounding hCG interpretation. Criteria for GTN referral include rising hCG, plateau (less than 10% fall over 3 weeks), or hCG still elevated at 6 months.
key_points: Weekly hCG until normal, then monthly for 6 months for complete mole
15-20% of complete moles develop GTN requiring chemotherapy
Contraception (not IUD) required during surveillance period
GTN referral if hCG rises, plateaus, or remains elevated at 6 months
explanation.pearls: The GTN referral criteria include hCG plateau (less than 10% fall over 3 consecutive weekly values), hCG rise over 2 consecutive weekly values, or histological evidence of choriocarcinoma - these trigger chemotherapy referral rather than repeat evacuation.

options.rationale: A single undetectable hCG does not complete the surveillance requirement. Complete hydatidiform mole requires ongoing surveillance after hCG normalisation to detect late persistent/malignant gestational trophoblastic disease, which can present months after apparent normalisation. (Source: FIGO GTD Guidelines; RANZCOG GTD Statement)

Prophylactic chemotherapy is not standard practice for complete molar pregnancy. Approximately 15-20% of complete moles develop gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, but the majority resolve with evacuation alone. Chemotherapy is reserved for those who develop GTN (rising or plateauing hCG). (Source: FIGO GTD Guidelines)

Repeat evacuation is not routinely performed when hCG is falling as expected. It increases the risk of uterine perforation and Asherman syndrome. Repeat evacuation may be considered if hCG plateaus or there is ultrasound evidence of significant retained molar tissue. (Source: FIGO GTD Guidelines)

The standard surveillance protocol for complete hydatidiform mole in Australia is weekly serum hCG until normal (less than 5 IU/L), then monthly hCG for 6 months from the date of first normal result. Reliable contraception (not IUD) should be used during surveillance. If hCG rises, plateaus (less than 10% decline over 3 weeks), or remains elevated at 6 months, referral for GTN assessment is indicated. (Source: FIGO GTD Guidelines; RANZCOG GTD Statement)

Monthly monitoring alone from the outset is insufficient. Weekly monitoring is needed while hCG is elevated to detect early GTN (rising or plateauing hCG). Monthly monitoring begins only after hCG has normalised. The surveillance duration for complete mole is 6 months after normalisation, not 12 months from evacuation. (Source: FIGO GTD Guidelines)
