options.rationale: Wait 48 hours for full steroid course is wrong because HELLP with severe features (low platelets, raised AST, raised LDH, haemolysis) is rapidly progressive and delivery should not be delayed beyond 24 hours. Would be correct only in mild pre-eclampsia without HELLP (SOMANZ).

HELLP syndrome is a progressive condition that can deteriorate rapidly. Delivery is the definitive treatment. While completing the steroid course is ideal, in the presence of worsening features (platelets dropping, rising transaminases, renal impairment, fetal compromise on CTG), delivery should not be postponed beyond 24 hours. A second dose of betamethasone can be given at 12-24 hours if feasible, but not at the expense of maternal safety. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines; RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline)

Second dose at 6 hours is wrong because steroid doses are 24 hours apart (or minimum 12 hours when needed); giving at 6 hours does not optimise neonatal benefit and the rush is not necessary. Would be correct only with truly imminent delivery within hours (SOMANZ).

Expectant 48 hours with MgSO4 is wrong because HELLP with fetal compromise carries high risk of eclampsia, hepatic rupture and abruption; expectancy beyond 24 hours is not recommended even with platelets >50. Would never be correct in HELLP with fetal compromise (SOMANZ).

Immediate caesarean under GA is wrong because immediate delivery is reserved for acute deterioration, eclampsia or non-reassuring CTG unresponsive to resuscitation; close monitoring with expedited delivery within 12-24 hours is reasonable. Would be correct only with acute decompensation, not now (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Recurrent eclamptic seizure on therapeutic magnesium warrants an additional 2 g IV bolus, repeated once if needed. Calcium gluconate is for magnesium toxicity, not for therapeutic levels. Delivery is planned after stabilisation. Blood pressure control is secondary.
key_points: For recurrent eclampsia: additional MgSO₄ 2 g IV bolus, then reassess. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline)
Magnesium toxicity: absent patellar reflexes, respiratory depression, hypotension. (Source: KEMH Eclampsia Guideline)
explanation.pearls: Magnesium therapy for eclampsia is titrated to clinical response, not serum levels. Recurrent seizures = need for more magnesium, not less.

options.rationale: A recurrent eclamptic seizure while on magnesium therapy (therapeutic level) indicates a need for an additional bolus of 2 g over 5-10 minutes, with close monitoring for magnesium toxicity. A further bolus of 2 g may be repeated if seizures persist. Intubation and phenytoin are reserved for refractory cases. (Source: SOMANZ Guidelines: Eclampsia; KEMH Eclampsia Guideline)

Stop MgSO4 and give calcium gluconate plus phenytoin is wrong because the magnesium level is therapeutic not toxic, so calcium gluconate (the antidote) is not indicated; phenytoin is less effective than magnesium in eclampsia. Would be correct only with documented magnesium toxicity (absent reflexes, respiratory depression) (SOMANZ).

Midazolam plus CT head is wrong because the immediate management of recurrent eclamptic seizure is an additional magnesium bolus, not benzodiazepine; CT head is reserved for focal neurology or atypical features. Would be correct only with focal signs raising suspicion of intracranial haemorrhage (SOMANZ).

Immediate caesarean is wrong because the immediate priority is maternal seizure control with magnesium; delivery (the definitive treatment) is expedited once stabilised. Would be correct only after stabilisation (SOMANZ).

Labetalol to lower BP is wrong because while BP control matters, the immediate priority is stopping the seizure with magnesium; the BP target in pre-eclampsia is not <140/90 but rather <160/110 to maintain placental perfusion. Would be correct only after seizure control as adjunct (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: In FGR with AEDF, brain-sparing, reduced CTG variability but positive DV a-wave and no decelerations, delivery is indicated within 24-48 hours. A rescue course of betamethasone is given if >7 days since the last course. Magnesium sulfate is indicated for neuroprotection at <32 weeks.
key_points: AEDF + reduced CTG variability + positive DV a-wave = deliver in 24-48 h. (Source: RANZCOG: FGR Guideline)
Rescue steroids if >7 days since last course and delivery expected within 7 days. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal Corticosteroid Guideline)
Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if <32 weeks and delivery imminent. (Source: KEMH Guideline)
explanation.pearls: The ductus venosus a-wave is the last Doppler to become abnormal; a positive a-wave allows a brief window to give steroids, but close monitoring is mandatory.

options.rationale: Deliver within 24 hours is wrong because with positive DV a-wave and no CTG decelerations, delivery can be planned within 24-48 hours (not strictly within 24); the option is overly aggressive on timing. Would be correct only with abnormal DV a-wave or recurrent decelerations (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

AEDF with reduced CTG variability but positive DV a-wave and no decelerations indicates delivery within 24-48 hours. A rescue steroid course is indicated because >7 days have passed and delivery is anticipated. Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection (<32 weeks). (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction Guideline; KEMH FGR Guideline)

Immediate caesarean within 2 hours is wrong because immediate delivery is reserved for reversed EDF, abnormal DV (absent/reversed a-wave) or recurrent CTG decelerations; positive DV a-wave allows the 24-48h window. Would be correct only with abnormal DV a-wave or recurrent decelerations (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

Continue expectancy with repeat Dopplers in 72h is wrong because AEDF plus reduced variability is itself an indication for delivery; positive DV a-wave allows time but does not justify continued expectancy beyond 48 hours. Would be correct only at earlier surveillance phases before AEDF develops (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

Deliver at 34 weeks is wrong because AEDF at 30 weeks mandates delivery within 24-48 hours; waiting to 34 weeks risks fetal death from progressive decompensation. Would be correct only with isolated mild umbilical artery PI elevation, not AEDF (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is characterised by cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and consumptive coagulopathy. Severe hypofibrinogenaemia (<1.0 g/L) is a hallmark and requires aggressive replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate. FFP alone is insufficient. Tranexamic acid and prothrombinex are adjuncts, not substitutes for fibrinogen. Platelets are needed when counts are very low but fibrinogen correction takes priority.
key_points: AFE causes profound hypofibrinogenaemia; fibrinogen replacement is critical. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic Fluid Embolism)
Maintain fibrinogen >2.0 g/L in obstetric haemorrhage. (Source: ANZCA Massive Transfusion Guidelines)
Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate provides concentrated fibrinogen. (Source: ANZCA Guidelines)
explanation.pearls: In AFE, the fibrinogen level is the best predictor of severe haemorrhage and the most urgent coagulation factor to replace.

options.rationale: Amniotic fluid embolism causes a consumptive coagulopathy with severe hypofibrinogenaemia. Fibrinogen is the first clotting factor to reach critically low levels. Guidelines recommend maintaining fibrinogen >2.0 g/L during obstetric haemorrhage; cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is the most efficient way to achieve this. (Source: RANZCOG: Amniotic Fluid Embolism; SOMANZ/ANZCA Guidelines for Massive Transfusion)

Platelets first is wrong because while platelets <50 plus active bleeding warrant transfusion, the immediate life-threatening defect is critically low fibrinogen, which must be corrected first to stabilise clot formation. Would be correct only after fibrinogen replacement (ANZCA Massive Transfusion Guidelines).

More FFP is wrong because FFP contains fibrinogen at low concentration (~2 g/L); large volumes are needed to raise fibrinogen meaningfully, risking circulatory overload. Concentrated sources (cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate) are preferred. Would be correct only as broad factor replacement when fibrinogen is adequate (RANZCOG: AFE).

Prothrombinex-HT is wrong because PCCs concentrate factors II, IX and X but contain negligible fibrinogen; it does not address the critical defect. Would be correct only for warfarin reversal or vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency (ANZCA Massive Transfusion Guidelines).

TXA only is wrong because tranexamic acid is an adjunct in PPH but cannot replace severely depleted fibrinogen. Would be correct only as adjunct alongside fibrinogen replacement (WOMAN Trial; RANZCOG: AFE).

explanation.summary: For a haemodynamically stable patient with placenta accreta who desires future fertility, leaving the placenta in situ with postoperative methotrexate and close monitoring is a recognised conservative strategy. Hysterectomy is definitive but eliminates fertility. Piecemeal removal and compression sutures are not appropriate.
key_points: Conservative management of PAS: leave placenta in situ, consider methotrexate, monitor for infection and bleeding. (Source: FIGO PAS Guidelines)
Hysterectomy remains the gold standard for uncontrolled haemorrhage or completed families. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS Guideline)
explanation.pearls: The decision between hysterectomy and conservation in PAS must be individualised; preoperative counselling about fertility desires is essential.

options.rationale: For a woman with placenta accreta who desires future fertility, leaving the placenta in situ is a recognised conservative option. Postoperative methotrexate may accelerate placental involution. Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment but sacrifices fertility. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum; FIGO Consensus Guidelines on PAS)

Immediate hysterectomy is wrong because while hysterectomy is the definitive treatment, it sacrifices fertility; in a patient who has explicitly requested uterine conservation, leaving placenta in situ is a valid alternative when bleeding is controlled. Would be correct only with refractory bleeding or completed family (RANZCOG: PAS Guideline).

B-Lynch and vessel ligation is wrong because these are atony-targeted; with placenta accreta the bleeding is from placental bed invasion, not myometrial atony, so these measures cannot control it without addressing the placenta. Would be correct only for atonic PPH (RANZCOG: PAS Guideline).

Piecemeal removal is wrong because forced placental removal in accreta risks ongoing haemorrhage, incomplete evacuation and uterine perforation; conservative leave-in-situ approach is safer. Would never be correct as planned approach in PAS (FIGO PAS Guidelines).

Caesarean hysterectomy with surrogacy referral is wrong because hysterectomy itself ends uterine-mediated fertility regardless of ovarian preservation; the patient wants to keep her uterus. Would be correct only when conservation is not feasible (RANZCOG: PAS Guideline).

explanation.summary: REDF in FGR with oligohydramnios and a non-reassuring CTG indicates delivery within 24 hours. A rescue course of betamethasone should be given if >7 days have passed, but delivery should not be delayed beyond 24 hours. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is recommended. A positive DV a-wave allows a brief window, but not prolonged expectant management.
key_points: REDF: deliver within 24 hours if associated with oligohydramnios or CTG concerns. (Source: RANZCOG: FGR Guideline)
Rescue corticosteroids if >7 days since last course; magnesium sulfate <32 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: FGR Guideline; KEMH Guideline)
Immediate delivery is needed for recurrent decelerations or abnormal DV. (Source: RANZCOG: FGR Guideline)
explanation.pearls: The progression from AEDF to REDF in FGR is a sign of worsening placental insufficiency; act quickly but use the small window for steroids if possible.

options.rationale: Deliver within 24 hours with rescue steroids is wrong only because the correct answer also specifies within 24 hours, but emphasises feasibility of completing at least a single dose; the option overstates rescue-course timing. (This option closely matches B in intent; the difference is that B explicitly accepts a single dose if full course is not feasible, prioritising delivery.) Would be correct only if 'rescue course' is interpreted as single dose (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

REDF, especially with oligohydramnios and a non-reassuring CTG, mandates delivery within 24 hours. While completion of steroids is ideal, maternal and fetal safety take priority. A rescue dose of betamethasone can be given and delivery performed as soon as feasible, ideally within 24 hours. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Fetal Growth Restriction Guideline; KEMH FGR Guideline)

Immediate caesarean within 2 hours is wrong because immediate delivery is reserved for recurrent decelerations or abnormal DV a-wave; positive DV a-wave allows a short window for at least a single steroid dose. Would be correct only with abnormal DV a-wave or recurrent decelerations (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).
Rescue course over 48h then deliver is wrong because REDF plus oligohydramnios cannot wait 48 hours; fetal death risk rises substantially. Would never be correct with REDF (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).
Continued expectancy is wrong because REDF is an indication for delivery within 24 hours, not for more surveillance. (RANZCOG: FGR Guideline).

explanation.summary: The Risk of Malignancy Index is calculated as U × M × CA-125. A score >200 indicates high risk of ovarian cancer and requires referral to a gynaecological oncologist for surgical staging and treatment planning. CT imaging is part of preoperative workup but does not replace referral.
key_points: RMI = ultrasound score (U) × menopausal status (M) × CA-125. (Source: NICE CG122)
RMI >200 = high risk, refer to gynaecological oncology. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses)
Postmenopausal: M = 3; premenopausal: M = 1. (Source: NICE CG122)
explanation.pearls: The RMI is a simple tool for stratifying ovarian masses; always refer early if the score is high.

options.rationale: RMI = U (3) × M (3) × CA-125 (320) = 2880. An RMI >200 indicates a high risk of malignancy, and referral to a gynaecological oncologist is recommended for surgical staging. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses in Postmenopausal Women; NICE Guideline CG122)

RMI 960 with watch-and-wait is wrong because the calculation is incorrect (RMI = U x M x CA-125 = 3 x 3 x 320 = 2880, not 960); furthermore, any RMI >200 warrants urgent gynae-oncology referral, not observation. (RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses).

Simple oophorectomy by general gynaecologist is wrong because high RMI requires comprehensive surgical staging by a gynaecological oncologist with appropriate intraoperative frozen section, lymphadenectomy and peritoneal sampling. Would be correct only for low-risk masses (RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses).

RMI 1440 and discharge to GP is wrong because the calculation is incorrect and high-risk findings require oncology referral; CT can be part of staging but never with GP discharge as the endpoint. (NICE CG122).
RMI 2880 as low risk is wrong because >200 is high risk, not low; the option misclassifies the result. (RANZCOG: Ovarian Masses).

explanation.summary: In severe shoulder dystocia refractory to McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, posterior arm delivery, and internal rotations, the next step is the all-fours (Gaskin) manoeuvre. Zavanelli and symphysiotomy are last resorts. Fundal pressure is contraindicated.
key_points: HELPERR sequence: after internal manoeuvres, Roll to all-fours (Gaskin). (Source: RANZCOG: Shoulder Dystocia)
Zavanelli is a last resort with high morbidity. (Source: ALSO Guidelines)
explanation.pearls: Even with an epidural, the Gaskin manoeuvre can be performed with help; it often resolves the impaction by changing pelvic geometry.

options.rationale: After failure of McRoberts, suprapubic pressure, posterior arm and internal rotation, the next recommended step in the RANZCOG algorithm is the all-fours (Gaskin) manoeuvre. Fundal pressure is contraindicated as it worsens impaction and risks uterine rupture and OASIS (RANZCOG shoulder dystocia).

Fundal pressure is wrong because it worsens impaction by driving the anterior shoulder onto the symphysis and risks uterine rupture and brachial plexus injury; suprapubic pressure, not fundal pressure, is the manoeuvre to use. (RANZCOG; RCOG).

Symphysiotomy is wrong because it is a last-resort manoeuvre in settings where caesarean is unavailable; in Australian hospitals it precedes only Zavanelli, after all-fours and other manoeuvres have failed. Would be correct only in resource-limited settings without theatre access (RANZCOG).

Zavanelli is wrong because cephalic replacement plus caesarean is the absolute last resort after all other manoeuvres have failed, including all-fours, and carries high fetal mortality. Would be correct only after every other manoeuvre has failed (RANZCOG).
Repeat failed manoeuvres is wrong because the algorithm proceeds to all-fours after the first internal manoeuvre sequence has failed; repeating wastes time during hypoxia. (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Maternal cardiac arrest beyond 20 weeks gestation is one of the most time-critical resuscitations in medicine. Aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus reduces cardiac return by 30-50%, rendering chest compressions much less effective. The first manoeuvre is manual left uterine displacement (rather than left lateral tilt, which impairs compression quality). High-quality CPR proceeds with standard ALS algorithms; defibrillation, vasopressors and intubation are unchanged in pregnancy. Perimortem caesarean section (resuscitative hysterotomy) is performed at the bedside if return of spontaneous circulation has not occurred by 4 minutes, with delivery achieved by 5 minutes - this dramatically improves both maternal and fetal survival by relieving aortocaval compression and reducing maternal oxygen demand. No anaesthetic, no skin prep, no transfer to theatre - the operation is done where the arrest occurred. After ROSC, transfer to ICU with detailed neonatal resuscitation team in attendance. Causes include amniotic fluid embolism, eclampsia, haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, anaphylaxis and toxic local anaesthetic.
key_points: Perimortem caesarean: deliver by 5 minutes of arrest if no return of spontaneous circulation. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.6)
Left uterine displacement is insufficient; emptying the uterus is critical. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal Collapse)
explanation.pearls: Perimortem caesarean (resuscitative hysterotomy) must be started within 4 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest and the fetus delivered within 5 minutes - at the bedside, no anaesthetic, no skin prep. Aortocaval decompression alone often restores maternal return of circulation (ANZCOR Maternal Resuscitation).

options.rationale: If maternal cardiac arrest does not respond to CPR within 4 minutes, perimortem caesarean delivery is indicated to relieve aortocaval compression, improve maternal haemodynamics, and give the fetus the best chance of survival. Delivery should occur by 5 minutes post-arrest. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.6: Maternal Cardiac Arrest; RANZCOG: Maternal Collapse in Pregnancy)

Transfer to theatre is wrong because moving to theatre exceeds the 4-5 minute window; perimortem caesarean must be performed at the site of arrest if transfer cannot be completed rapidly. Would be correct only if theatre is immediately adjacent and transfer fits within the window (ANZCOR Guideline 11.6).

Amiodarone and defer delivery is wrong because while amiodarone is correct for refractory VF, delivery must not be delayed; both proceed in parallel to relieve aortocaval compression. Would never be correct as a substitute for delivery (ANZCOR Guideline 11.6).

Continue CPR with displacement 10 more minutes is wrong because waiting exceeds the 4-5 minute window and worsens maternal and fetal outcomes; a previously reassuring fetal heart rate does not justify delay. (ANZCOR Guideline 11.6).

Tocolysis is wrong because in maternal arrest the uterus must be emptied surgically to relieve aortocaval compression, not relaxed pharmacologically; tocolysis is not indicated. (RANZCOG: Maternal Collapse).

explanation.summary: Obstetric APS without prior thrombosis is treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic-dose LMWH throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum. This reduces pregnancy loss and prevents thromboembolism. Warfarin is reserved for those with prior thrombosis.
key_points: Obstetric APS: aspirin 100-150 mg + LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin 40 mg daily) from early pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG: APS)
Continue for 6 weeks postpartum to prevent maternal thrombosis. (Source: International APS Guidelines)
explanation.pearls: APS is the only treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage - low-dose aspirin and heparin can increase live birth rates from 20% to over 70%.

options.rationale: Continue warfarin is wrong because warfarin is teratogenic between 6 and 12 weeks (warfarin embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata); furthermore she has obstetric APS without prior thrombosis, where the indication is aspirin plus LMWH, not warfarin. Would be correct only with mechanical heart valves where benefit may outweigh risk after counselling (RANZCOG; eTG).

Obstetric APS (recurrent miscarriage, no prior thrombosis) is treated with low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH. Warfarin must be ceased before 6 weeks to avoid embryopathy; it is replaced by LMWH (RANZCOG; eTG).
Warfarin until 12 weeks then LMWH is wrong because warfarin embryopathy risk is concentrated in weeks 6-12; the switch must occur BEFORE 6 weeks, not after the teratogenic window. (RANZCOG; eTG).

Warfarin to 6 weeks then aspirin alone is wrong because aspirin monotherapy is inferior to aspirin plus LMWH in obstetric APS with recurrent loss; LMWH must be added. Would be correct only for isolated APL antibodies without obstetric criteria (RANZCOG; eTG).

IVIG monthly is wrong because IVIG is not first-line for obstetric APS; aspirin plus LMWH is. IVIG is reserved for refractory cases or research protocols. Would be correct only in trial settings or refractory disease (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Early-onset neonatal group B streptococcal disease (sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis) is largely preventable with intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Australian indications follow RANZCOG guidance: GBS-positive on antenatal swab, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, previous GBS-affected infant, intrapartum fever, prolonged rupture of membranes over 18 hours, or preterm labour with unknown GBS status. Benzylpenicillin is first-line (3 g IV loading dose, then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery). Alternatives are cefazolin for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy, and clindamycin or vancomycin (with sensitivity testing) for anaphylactoid allergy. Optimal protection requires at least 4 hours of antibiotic exposure before delivery; shorter exposures still provide partial benefit. Risk-based versus universal screening is debated - Australia uses universal swabs at 35-37 weeks, but the preterm population by definition delivers before this swab is taken and is treated empirically. Document antibiotic doses precisely; they inform neonatal sepsis assessment.
key_points: IAP indicated for preterm labour (<37 weeks) with unknown GBS status. (Source: RANZCOG: GBS)
First-line: benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV loading, then 600 mg 4-hourly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
explanation.pearls: Preterm labour with unknown GBS status is an automatic indication for intrapartum benzylpenicillin (3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth) - the prior probability of GBS carriage is high enough that the swab result cannot be awaited (RANZCOG; RCH CPG GBS).

options.rationale: For women in preterm labour (<37 weeks) with unknown GBS status, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) is indicated to reduce the risk of early-onset neonatal GBS disease. Benzylpenicillin is first-line in the absence of penicillin allergy. (Source: RANZCOG: Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

No antibiotics is wrong because preterm labour is itself a risk factor for early-onset GBS infection; IAP is recommended for unknown GBS status if labour occurs <37 weeks. Would be correct only at term with negative GBS swab (RANZCOG: GBS).

Swab and treat if positive is wrong because culture results will not be available in time to guide intrapartum decision-making. Would be correct only as antenatal screening, not intrapartum decision (RANZCOG: GBS).

Cefazolin first-line is wrong because cefazolin is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy; with no allergy, benzylpenicillin is preferred for narrower spectrum and direct GBS activity. Would be correct only with non-severe penicillin allergy (Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

IM benzathine penicillin is wrong because intrapartum prophylaxis requires IV benzylpenicillin to achieve adequate placental and amniotic fluid concentrations during labour; IM benzathine is for syphilis treatment, not GBS IAP. Would never be correct for IAP (RANZCOG: GBS).

explanation.summary: Maternal sepsis requires immediate administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics and aggressive fluid resuscitation, along with lactate measurement and blood cultures. Delivery is considered but after initial stabilisation unless there is severe fetal distress or maternal deterioration.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, lactate, antibiotics, crystalloid 30 mL/kg, vasopressors if needed. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign)
Maternal sepsis with chorioamnionitis: broad-spectrum antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, clindamycin). (Source: SOMANZ Maternal Sepsis)
explanation.pearls: In sepsis, every hour of delay in antibiotics increases mortality. Do not wait for culture results or imaging.

options.rationale: The Sepsis Six / Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 bundle includes blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, lactate, fluid resuscitation 30 mL/kg, oxygen and source control. In chorioamnionitis with maternal sepsis and fetal compromise, delivery is the source control and is performed in parallel with resuscitation (eTG; RANZCOG).

ICU transfer before antibiotics is wrong because the Surviving Sepsis Hour-1 bundle prioritises antibiotics within 1 hour; CVC insertion must not delay antibiotic administration. Would be correct only if peripheral access is unobtainable AND antibiotics can be given via central line within the hour (Surviving Sepsis).

Immediate caesarean before fluids/antibiotics is wrong because antibiotics and fluids run in parallel with theatre preparation, not sequentially; antibiotics within the first hour drive the mortality reduction. Would never be correct as a stepwise approach (Surviving Sepsis; RANZCOG).
IV paracetamol and wait 30 min is wrong because temperature reduction does not treat sepsis; immediate antibiotics, fluids and source control are required. (Surviving Sepsis).

CT abdomen first is wrong because the sepsis source is clinically obvious (chorioamnionitis), and CT delays antibiotics while exposing a critically unwell pregnant patient. Would be correct only when source is genuinely unclear and the patient is stable enough for imaging (Surviving Sepsis).

explanation.summary: In massive haemorrhage due to placenta accreta, hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ is the safest surgical option. Attempts at placental removal can be fatal. Interventional radiology may be an adjunct but not when the patient is exsanguinating.
key_points: Placenta accreta with massive bleeding: caesarean hysterectomy, leave placenta in situ. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS)
Do not attempt to manually remove the placenta in accreta. (Source: FIGO PAS Guidelines)
explanation.pearls: Antenatal diagnosis of PAS saves lives - prepare for massive transfusion and have a gynaecological oncologist present.

options.rationale: In life-threatening haemorrhage from placenta accreta, hysterectomy is the definitive treatment. Leaving the placenta in situ and performing a hysterectomy is safer than attempting placental removal. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta Accreta Spectrum; FIGO PAS Guidelines)

Piecemeal manual removal is wrong because forced removal of invasive placenta causes catastrophic haemorrhage and is contraindicated; accreta is not managed like a normal retained placenta. (RANZCOG: PAS).

Close uterus and transfer for UAE is wrong because torrential haemorrhage cannot tolerate transfer to interventional radiology; immediate surgical control is needed. Would be correct only with controlled bleeding in pre-planned PAS with IR availability (RANZCOG: PAS).

B-Lynch and balloon tamponade is wrong because compression sutures address atony, not myometrial invasion; in accreta these are ineffective. Would be correct only for atonic PPH (FIGO PAS Guidelines).

TXA plus rFVIIa as definitive is wrong because medical adjuncts cannot replace surgical control of massive haemorrhage from accreta; they may help but do not substitute for surgery. Would be correct only as adjuncts alongside surgery (RANZCOG: PAS).

explanation.summary: In placenta percreta managed conservatively with the placenta left in situ, methotrexate can be used to accelerate placental involution, often combined with uterine artery embolisation. Hysterectomy is avoided unless complications arise.
key_points: Conservative management of PAS: methotrexate ± uterine artery embolisation. (Source: FIGO PAS Guidelines)
Close monitoring for infection and secondary haemorrhage is essential. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS)
explanation.pearls: Leaving the placenta in situ is a valid option for PAS in haemodynamically stable patients who desire future fertility.

options.rationale: For retained placenta with percreta and desire for uterine preservation, adjuvant methotrexate can accelerate placental involution. Uterine artery embolisation can reduce vascularity. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS Guideline; FIGO PAS Guidelines)

Immediate emergency hysterectomy is wrong because she is haemodynamically stable and wishes to preserve fertility; conservative measures are appropriate with stability. Would be correct only with uncontrolled bleeding or no fertility wish (RANZCOG: PAS).

Oral mifepristone is wrong because mifepristone is not part of established PAS protocols; methotrexate is the chemotherapeutic adjuvant evidenced. Would be correct only within research settings (FIGO PAS Guidelines).

Observation only is wrong because conservative management without adjuvant therapy in PAS placenta-in-situ carries higher delayed haemorrhage and infection risk; adjuvant methotrexate and/or UAE reduce complications. Would be correct only in selected low-risk cases under specialist follow-up (RANZCOG: PAS).

IV oxytocin infusion is wrong because oxytocin does not help placental involution once invasive placenta is in situ; the mechanism (myometrial contraction) is irrelevant for accreta. Would be correct only as adjunct uterotonic, not as primary involution strategy (RANZCOG: PAS).

explanation.summary: For cervical insufficiency with bulging membranes and no infection, an emergency cerclage along with indometacin and betamethasone can be considered. Strict asepsis and postoperative monitoring are essential. The goal is to prolong gestation to viability.
key_points: Emergency cerclage may be offered for bulging membranes up to 23-24 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Cervical Insufficiency)
Indometacin for 48 hours is used to reduce amniotic fluid and contractions. (Source: RCOG Guideline)
explanation.pearls: Bulging membranes are not an absolute contraindication to cerclage, but the risk of rupture and infection is high.

options.rationale: Australian/RANZCOG practice supports emergency rescue cerclage at 22-23+6 weeks for advanced cervical dilation with intact membranes and no infection, combined with short-course indometacin tocolysis (limited to <32 weeks because of ductal closure risk above that gestation), antibiotic prophylaxis, and ACS when delivery is anticipated (RANZCOG cerclage; RCOG GT60).

Bedrest and steroids only is wrong because bulging membranes are not an absolute contraindication to rescue cerclage when there is no infection or labour; bed rest alone has poor outcomes. Would be correct only with confirmed chorioamnionitis or established labour (RANZCOG).

Avoid indometacin entirely is wrong because ductal closure risk applies primarily after 32 weeks; at 21+5 short-course indometacin is acceptable and useful as tocolysis. Would be correct only at >32 weeks (RANZCOG).

Induce labour as non-viable is wrong because at 22+0 weeks active resuscitation is increasingly offered in Australia and she wants intervention; inducing now is contrary to patient wishes and updated ANZNN guidance. Would be correct only at <22+0 weeks with palliative care chosen (ANZNN periviable consensus).

Abdominal cervicoisthmic cerclage is wrong because abdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage in prior pregnancies, not first-line rescue; MgSO4 neuroprotection is for >=24+0 weeks, not 21+5. Would be correct only with prior failed transvaginal cerclage (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum demands meticulous antenatal planning with a multidisciplinary team. Delivery should be planned for 35-36+0 weeks in a tertiary centre with appropriate surgical, anaesthetic, and blood product support. A midline incision and high uterine incision are recommended. Interventional radiology may be an adjunct. Emergency delivery is avoided.
key_points: Planned delivery for PAS: 35-36+0 weeks, multidisciplinary team, tertiary centre. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS; FIGO PAS Guidelines)
Surgical approach: midline incision, high uterine incision avoiding the placenta, preparedness for hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: PAS)
Massive transfusion protocol and cell salvage should be available. (Source: FIGO PAS Guidelines)
explanation.pearls: The single most important intervention in PAS is antenatal diagnosis - it transforms an emergency into a planned operation.

options.rationale: RANZCOG and SMFM consensus recommend planned delivery at 34-35+6 weeks for placenta accreta spectrum (before frequent late-preterm bleeding risk) in a tertiary centre with full multidisciplinary team and blood-product support. The placenta is generally left in situ during hysterectomy (RANZCOG PAS; SMFM).

39 weeks at local hospital with single obstetrician is wrong because PAS warrants planned early delivery (34-35+6) in a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team and blood-product support; awaiting 39 weeks risks emergency haemorrhage in the late-preterm period. (RANZCOG; SMFM).
Vaginal delivery is wrong because placenta praevia with PAS is an absolute indication for caesarean; vaginal delivery would cause torrential haemorrhage from the placental site. (RANZCOG).

Deliver at 32 weeks is wrong because 32 weeks adds substantial prematurity morbidity without proportionate maternal benefit; the standard window is 34-35+6 unless acute indications arise. Would be correct only with antenatal bleeding or other acute indications (RANZCOG; SMFM).
Reactive delivery only at labour or distress is wrong because reactive management compromises MDT availability and increases haemorrhage mortality; PAS requires planned delivery. (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: TTTS is staged by the Quintero system. Stage I: poly/oligohydramnios sequence. Stage II: donor bladder not visible. Stage III: critically abnormal Doppler (absent or reversed end-diastolic flow, reversed ductus venosus a-wave, or pulsatile umbilical vein). Stage IV: hydrops in one or both twins. Stage V: demise of one or both. Stage II - IV before 26 weeks is treated with fetoscopic laser photocoagulation.
key_points: Quintero stage III: abnormal Doppler in either twin. (Source: RANZCOG: Monochorionic Twins)
Laser photocoagulation is the treatment of choice for stage II - IV TTTS at 16-26 weeks. (Source: Solomon Trial)
Amnioreduction alone is reserved for stage I TTTS or when laser is not available. (Source: NICE IPG198)
explanation.pearls: The Quintero staging system guides prognosis and management in TTTS; always assess the donor bladder and Dopplers.

options.rationale: The combination of polyhydramnios/oligohydramnios (stage I), non-visualised donor bladder (stage II), and critically abnormal Doppler in the donor (absent end-diastolic flow in umbilical artery) defines Quintero stage III. Laser ablation of the vascular anastomoses is the treatment of choice for stage II - IV TTTS before 26 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy; Solomon Trial; NICE Guideline IPG198)

Stage I with amnioreduction is wrong because absent donor bladder and abnormal UA Doppler upgrade to at least stage III; stage I requires only oligo/polyhydramnios. Amnioreduction alone is insufficient for advanced TTTS. Would be correct only with bladder visible and normal Dopplers (Quintero classification; RANZCOG).

Stage II with delayed laser for steroids is wrong because the abnormal UA Doppler upgrades to stage III; steroids are not indicated at 21 weeks and delaying laser is not recommended. Would be correct only at stage II with normal Dopplers (RANZCOG).

Stage IV with delivery at 22 weeks is wrong because stage IV requires hydrops in one or both fetuses (not described); delivery at 22 weeks is periviable with extremely high neonatal mortality. Would be correct only with hydrops and beyond-laser-window gestation (RANZCOG).
Stage I with observation is wrong because the actual stage is III; observation is inappropriate for advanced TTTS. Would be correct only at stage I with stable surveillance (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Eisenmenger syndrome is an mWHO class IV condition with a 30-50% maternal mortality risk in pregnancy. Termination should be compassionately offered. If the patient continues, care requires a specialist multidisciplinary team. Bosentan is teratogenic and must be stopped. Cardiac surgery during pregnancy is not indicated.
key_points: Eisenmenger syndrome: mWHO class IV, 30-50% maternal mortality in pregnancy. (Source: ESC Guidelines)
Bosentan is teratogenic and must be stopped. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease)
Pregnancy in mWHO IV is contraindicated; termination counselling should be offered. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease)
explanation.pearls: In Eisenmenger syndrome, the maternal body cannot adapt to the haemodynamic demands of pregnancy. The risk of death is real and must be communicated clearly.

options.rationale: Eisenmenger syndrome carries a 30-50% maternal mortality rate in pregnancy due to the inability to increase pulmonary blood flow and the risk of right heart failure, arrhythmia, and sudden death. mWHO class IV. Termination should be offered, but if declined, care must be in a specialist centre. Bosentan is teratogenic and must be discontinued. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy; ESC Guidelines on Pregnancy and Heart Disease; mWHO Classification)

1-2% mortality with shared GP/obstetrician care is wrong because Eisenmenger mortality in pregnancy is 30-50% (mWHO class IV); shared care without tertiary pulmonary hypertension input is grossly inadequate. (ESC Guidelines).

Coerced termination is wrong because while termination is medically recommended, it cannot be performed against the patient's wishes; compassionate counselling and patient-centred approach are required. Would never be correct as a coercive plan (RANZCOG: Ethics of Reproductive Choice).
Continue bosentan is wrong because bosentan is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy; it must be replaced with pregnancy-safe alternatives (e.g. IV epoprostenol, sildenafil). (ESC Guidelines).
Cardiac surgery to close VSD is wrong because in established Eisenmenger syndrome the right-to-left shunt is protective; closure precipitates right heart failure. (ESC Guidelines).

explanation.summary: For stage IB1 cervical cancer in the second trimester, laparoscopic lymphadenectomy should be performed for staging. If nodes are negative, the pregnancy can be continued to term with planned caesarean radical hysterectomy at or near term. This balances oncological safety with fetal maturity.
key_points: Node-negative FIGO IB1 cervical cancer in the second trimester: pregnancy can continue with radical hysterectomy at delivery. (Source: ESGO Guidelines)
Laparoscopic pelvic lymphadenectomy is the first step for staging. (Source: RANZCOG: Cancer in Pregnancy)
Delay of 12-18 weeks for fetal maturation does not significantly affect maternal prognosis in node-negative disease. (Source: Morice et al., Lancet 2012)
explanation.pearls: In early cervical cancer and pregnancy, negative nodes are the green light to proceed safely to term.

options.rationale: For FIGO stage IB1 cervical cancer diagnosed in the second trimester, a fertility-preserving approach may be considered. Laparoscopic pelvic lymphadenectomy is performed first for nodal staging. If negative, the pregnancy can be continued to term (or 34-36 weeks) with a planned caesarean radical hysterectomy. If nodes are positive, immediate treatment is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG: Cancer in Pregnancy; ESGO Guidelines on Cervical Cancer in Pregnancy; Morice et al., Lancet 2012)

Immediate radical hysterectomy is wrong because in second-trimester IB1, a delay of 12-18 weeks to achieve fetal maturity does not significantly worsen maternal prognosis; immediate hysterectomy sacrifices the fetus when delay is feasible. Would be correct only with rapid progression or refusal of delay (ESGO Guidelines).

Neoadjuvant cisplatin is wrong because neoadjuvant chemotherapy is for locally advanced disease (>=IB2), not for IB1 tumours that are amenable to primary surgical treatment. Would be correct only for >=IB2 (ESGO Guidelines).

LLETZ as definitive is wrong because LLETZ is inadequate for FIGO IB1; radical surgery with lymph node assessment is needed for curative treatment. Would be correct only for microinvasive (IA1) disease (ESGO Guidelines).

Hysterotomy delivery at 18 weeks is wrong because delivering a previable fetus is not necessary when delay to term/near-term is safe with negative nodes; this is an over-aggressive approach. Would never be correct as primary plan in IB1 (ESGO Guidelines).

explanation.summary: PPROM at 32 weeks requires a combined approach of antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation and prophylactic antibiotics to prolong latency. Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM is given as two doses 24 hours apart, and erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days is the recommended antibiotic based on the ORACLE trial. Expectant management is appropriate in the absence of chorioamnionitis, cord prolapse, or non-reassuring fetal status.
key_points: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses (24 hours apart) is the preferred corticosteroid for antenatal lung maturation between 24 and 34 weeks
Erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days is the recommended antibiotic regimen in PPROM
Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid is avoided in PPROM due to increased risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE trial demonstrated that erythromycin in PPROM prolongs pregnancy by a median of 5 days and reduces neonatal morbidity. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid was associated with a significantly higher rate of neonatal NEC and should be avoided. Digital vaginal examination should not be performed as it shortens latency and increases infection risk. If GBS status is unknown, intrapartum GBS prophylaxis with benzylpenicillin should be given when labour commences.

options.rationale: PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks requires antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation and prophylactic antibiotics to prolong latency and reduce infectious morbidity. Australian RANZCOG guidelines recommend betamethasone 11.4 mg IM as a single dose repeated at 24 hours, and erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days as the preferred antibiotic regimen for PPROM based on the ORACLE trial evidence. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM Guidelines)

Immediate delivery is not indicated at 32 weeks in the absence of chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, or cord prolapse. Expectant management with corticosteroids and antibiotics is the standard approach for PPROM between 24 and 34 weeks, aiming to balance the benefits of in-utero fetal maturation against the risks of ascending infection. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM Guidelines)

IV ampicillin and immediate delivery are not appropriate at 32 weeks without signs of infection. Expectant management is preferred at this gestation. The ORACLE trial demonstrated that erythromycin is the preferred antibiotic for PPROM as amoxicillin with clavulanic acid was associated with increased risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. (Source: eTG - Obstetrics)

While corticosteroids are correct, betamethasone is preferred over dexamethasone in Australian practice for antenatal lung maturation as it has a more favourable safety profile. Planning delivery at a fixed 34 weeks is overly prescriptive; delivery timing depends on clinical course, and antibiotic prophylaxis is also required. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM Guidelines)

At 32 weeks gestation, fetal lung maturity cannot be assumed. Antenatal corticosteroids provide significant benefit in reducing respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, and neonatal mortality when given between 24 and 34 weeks. Withholding corticosteroids at this gestation is not consistent with guideline recommendations. (Source: RANZCOG - PPROM Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Lactational breast abscess confirmed on ultrasound requires drainage in addition to continued antibiotics. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is the recommended first-line procedure for abscesses less than 5 cm as it is less invasive, can be performed under local anaesthesia, and preserves breastfeeding capacity. Breastfeeding should be continued from both breasts as it aids resolution and is safe for the infant.
key_points: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is first-line for lactational breast abscesses less than 5 cm
Antibiotics alone cannot resolve a formed abscess and drainage is essential
Breastfeeding should continue from both breasts during treatment of breast abscess
explanation.pearls: Aspiration may need to be repeated 2-3 times over 7-10 days in up to 50% of cases. If the abscess recurs after 3 aspirations, surgical drainage should be considered. Aspirated fluid should be sent for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity to guide antibiotic therapy. If MRSA is suspected based on local prevalence, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can be added. The aspiration needle should ideally enter through healthy skin rather than the most fluctuant point to reduce risk of fistula formation.

sources.label: RANZCOG - Breast Conditions in Pregnancy and Lactation

options.rationale: IV antibiotics alone will not adequately treat a formed breast abscess. Once an abscess has walled off, antibiotics cannot penetrate the cavity effectively and drainage is required. Antibiotics are important as adjunctive therapy but the collection must be drained to achieve source control and clinical resolution. (Source: eTG - Breast Infection)

Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is the recommended first-line drainage procedure for lactational breast abscesses less than 5 cm. It is less invasive than surgical drainage, can be performed under local anaesthesia, preserves breastfeeding capability, and has good success rates with repeat aspiration if needed. Oral flucloxacillin should be continued as the most likely organism is Staphylococcus aureus. (Source: RANZCOG - Breast Conditions in Pregnancy and Lactation)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Breast Conditions in Pregnancy and Lactation

options.rationale: Surgical incision and drainage under general anaesthesia is reserved for large abscesses above 5 cm, multiloculated collections, recurrent abscesses failing aspiration, or when skin necrosis is present. For a 3.5 cm unilocular abscess, ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is preferred as it is less invasive and has lower complication rates. (Source: eTG - Breast Infection)

Cessation of breastfeeding is not recommended in lactational mastitis or breast abscess as continued feeding or expressing helps resolve infection and maintain milk supply. Cabergoline to suppress lactation is not indicated unless the patient wishes to cease breastfeeding. Breastfeeding from the affected side is safe for the infant. (Source: RANZCOG - Breast Conditions in Pregnancy and Lactation)
source_refs: RANZCOG - Breast Conditions in Pregnancy and Lactation

options.rationale: Increasing antibiotic dose and adding metronidazole will not resolve a formed abscess without drainage. Anaerobic coverage with metronidazole is not routinely required for lactational breast abscesses as the predominant organism is Staphylococcus aureus. The collection must be drained for clinical improvement. (Source: eTG - Breast Infection)

explanation.summary: For symptomatic stage II pelvic organ prolapse after failed pelvic floor muscle training, a vaginal pessary trial is the recommended next step before considering surgery. Topical vaginal oestrogen should be commenced concurrently in postmenopausal women with vaginal atrophy to improve mucosal health and reduce pessary-related complications. Surgical repair is reserved for women who decline or fail pessary management.
key_points: Vaginal pessary is first-line conservative management after failed pelvic floor training for symptomatic prolapse
Topical oestrogen reduces pessary-related erosion and improves vaginal mucosal health in postmenopausal women
Anterior colporrhaphy has a 30-40% recurrence rate and should be considered only after conservative options
explanation.pearls: Ring pessaries are most suitable for stage I-II prolapse, while Gellhorn or cube pessaries may be needed for more advanced prolapse. Pessaries should be reviewed at 2 weeks after initial fitting, then 3-6 monthly thereafter. Topical oestrogen should be commenced 2 weeks before pessary insertion when possible. If the post-void residual exceeds 200 mL persistently, further urodynamic assessment is warranted.

options.rationale: Surgical repair should not be the first intervention after failed pelvic floor exercises. Australian guidelines recommend a trial of vaginal pessary before considering surgical options. Anterior colporrhaphy has a significant recurrence rate of 30-40% and carries surgical risks that should be avoided when conservative options have not been fully explored. (Source: RANZCOG - Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

Duloxetine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that may be used for stress urinary incontinence but has no role in obstructive voiding symptoms caused by pelvic organ prolapse. Her urinary symptoms are due to mechanical obstruction from the cystocele rather than a neurological or sphincter dysfunction. (Source: eTG - Urogynaecology)

A vaginal pessary is the recommended next step after failed pelvic floor exercises for symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse. Ring pessaries are commonly used for stage II prolapse and can relieve both the prolapse and associated voiding dysfunction. Topical oestrogen improves vaginal mucosal health, reduces pessary-related erosion, and enhances pessary retention in postmenopausal women with atrophic mucosa. (Source: RANZCOG - Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

While weight reduction is beneficial for prolapse management, this patient has a BMI of 28 which is only mildly overweight, and she has already completed 6 months of supervised pelvic floor training without adequate improvement. Repeating the same failed intervention without adding further management would not adequately address her symptomatic prolapse and voiding dysfunction. (Source: RANZCOG - Pelvic Organ Prolapse)

Systemic HRT is not indicated for the treatment of pelvic organ prolapse. Topical vaginal oestrogen is preferred as it provides local mucosal benefit without systemic risks. Systemic HRT does not reverse or significantly improve prolapse and carries cardiovascular and breast cancer risks in this age group without clear benefit for her presenting complaint. (Source: eTG - Urogynaecology)

explanation.summary: Postpartum endometritis following caesarean section is a polymicrobial infection requiring broad intravenous antibiotic coverage. The recommended Australian empiric regimen is IV ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole, providing coverage against gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms respectively. Risk factors include caesarean delivery, prolonged rupture of membranes, and multiple vaginal examinations. All three antibiotics are compatible with breastfeeding.
key_points: Triple IV therapy with ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole is standard empiric treatment for postpartum endometritis
Endometritis is polymicrobial requiring coverage of gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms
Risk factors include caesarean section, prolonged membrane rupture, and multiple vaginal examinations
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing in postpartum endometritis is typically 4-5 mg/kg IV daily with trough level monitoring. Clinical improvement is expected within 48-72 hours of commencing IV antibiotics. If no improvement occurs, consider retained products, wound infection, pelvic abscess, or septic pelvic thrombophlebitis. Antibiotics can be transitioned to oral therapy 24-48 hours after clinical improvement and should continue for a total course of 5-7 days.

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics with outpatient management are insufficient for postpartum endometritis following caesarean section. This patient has significant systemic inflammatory features with high fever, tachycardia, and markedly elevated inflammatory markers that warrant inpatient IV antibiotic therapy. Outpatient management risks progression to sepsis. (Source: eTG - Obstetric Infections)

Cefazolin monotherapy provides inadequate coverage for postpartum endometritis which is typically a polymicrobial infection involving aerobic gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms. Single-agent first-generation cephalosporin does not cover the anaerobic organisms commonly implicated in endometritis. (Source: RANZCOG - Postpartum Sepsis)

Piperacillin-tazobactam provides broad-spectrum coverage but represents an unnecessarily broad empiric choice for uncomplicated postpartum endometritis. Australian antimicrobial stewardship guidelines recommend reserving piperacillin-tazobactam for more serious infections or when narrower-spectrum regimens have failed to promote antibiotic stewardship. (Source: eTG - Obstetric Infections)

The combination of IV ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole is the recommended empiric regimen for postpartum endometritis in Australian guidelines. This triple therapy provides coverage against the polymicrobial organisms involved: ampicillin for streptococci and enterococci, gentamicin for gram-negative bacilli, and metronidazole for anaerobes. All three agents are compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: eTG - Obstetric Infections)

Oral antibiotics are inadequate for established postpartum endometritis with systemic inflammatory signs. This combination also provides incomplete coverage, lacking adequate gram-negative cover. Endometritis following caesarean section with prolonged rupture of membranes requires intravenous therapy with broad polymicrobial coverage. (Source: RANZCOG - Postpartum Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Letrozole is the recommended first-line ovulation induction agent for anovulatory infertility in PCOS, superseding clomifene citrate based on evidence of superior live birth rates. It is commenced at 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2-6 with ultrasound follicular tracking. This patient has completed appropriate lifestyle modification and has confirmed tubal patency, making pharmacological ovulation induction the logical next step.
key_points: Letrozole is first-line for ovulation induction in PCOS with superior live birth rates compared to clomifene
Starting dose is 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2-6 with dose escalation to 5 mg then 7.5 mg if no response
Ultrasound follicular tracking is recommended to monitor response and reduce multiple pregnancy risk
explanation.pearls: Letrozole achieves ovulation in approximately 60-80% of women with PCOS at the initial dose of 2.5 mg. If no dominant follicle develops, the dose can be increased to 5 mg in the next cycle and up to 7.5 mg. The cumulative live birth rate over 5 cycles of letrozole is approximately 28% compared to 19% with clomifene. Women with PCOS and a high AMH above 40 pmol/L are at increased risk of ovarian hyperstimulation with gonadotrophins, further supporting the use of oral agents first.

options.rationale: Clomifene citrate was previously considered first-line for ovulation induction in PCOS but international and Australian guidelines now recommend letrozole as the preferred first-line agent based on superior ovulation, pregnancy, and live birth rates demonstrated in the NEJM 2014 trial by Legro et al. (Source: RANZCOG - PCOS and Infertility)

IVF is not first-line management for anovulatory infertility due to PCOS. Ovulation induction with oral agents should be trialled first as it is less invasive, less costly, and effective in the majority of women with PCOS. IVF is reserved for those who fail ovulation induction or have additional infertility factors. (Source: RANZCOG - PCOS and Infertility)

Metformin monotherapy has lower ovulation and pregnancy rates compared to letrozole or clomifene and is not recommended as a sole ovulation induction agent. While metformin may have a role as adjunctive therapy, particularly in women with insulin resistance, it should not replace first-line ovulation induction agents. (Source: eTG - Infertility)

Gonadotrophin injections are second-line treatment for ovulation induction in PCOS, reserved for women who fail oral agents. They carry higher risks of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple pregnancy, require intensive ultrasound monitoring, and are significantly more expensive than oral ovulation induction agents. (Source: RANZCOG - PCOS and Infertility)

Letrozole is now recommended as first-line ovulation induction for anovulatory infertility in PCOS by international and Australian guidelines. The landmark NEJM trial by Legro et al. demonstrated superior ovulation rates, higher cumulative live birth rates, and lower multiple pregnancy rates compared to clomifene. The starting dose is 2.5 mg daily on cycle days 2-6 with follicular tracking. (Source: RANZCOG - PCOS and Infertility)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a severe form of pre-eclampsia characterised by haemolysis (elevated LDH, fragmented red cells), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. It complicates approximately 10 to 20% of severe pre-eclampsia cases. Management follows a structured approach: acute blood pressure control (IV labetalol or hydralazine), seizure prophylaxis (magnesium sulfate), antenatal corticosteroids if under 34 weeks, and timely delivery. At gestations between 24 and 34 weeks, a brief delay of 24 to 48 hours to allow corticosteroid benefit is acceptable if the maternal condition is stable, but delivery should not be deferred beyond this window.
key_points: HELLP = haemolysis + elevated liver enzymes + low platelets (below 100 x10^9/L)
IV labetalol and magnesium sulfate are essential initial stabilisation
Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity if under 34 weeks and delivery planned
Delivery within 24 to 48 hours after stabilisation at 33 weeks with HELLP
explanation.pearls: In HELLP syndrome, the platelet nadir typically occurs 24 to 48 hours postpartum, not at delivery; ongoing postpartum monitoring of platelets, LDH, and LFTs for at least 72 hours is critical to detect late deterioration.

options.rationale: Expectant management is not appropriate when pre-eclampsia is complicated by HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) with severe features. The combination of thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L, markedly elevated transaminases, elevated LDH with fragmented red cells, and severe hypertension with neurological symptoms indicates an unstable condition requiring delivery regardless of gestation. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline; SOMANZ Guideline)

While IV labetalol for acute blood pressure control and magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis are essential initial stabilisation measures, delivery should not be deferred in the setting of HELLP syndrome. The condition is progressive and can deteriorate rapidly with risks of placental abruption, hepatic rupture, DIC, and eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline; SOMANZ Guideline)

This patient has pre-eclampsia with severe features and HELLP syndrome at 33 weeks. The management is: (1) IV labetalol for acute BP control targeting below 160/110, (2) IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, (3) betamethasone 11.4 mg IM for fetal lung maturation (as delivery is planned within 7 days and gestation is under 34 weeks), and (4) delivery within 24 to 48 hours after maternal stabilisation and steroid administration. The brief delay allows steroids to reach maximal benefit while closely monitoring maternal and fetal status. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline; SOMANZ Guideline; NICE NG133)

While delivery is indicated, immediate caesarean without maternal stabilisation or antenatal corticosteroids exposes both mother and baby to avoidable risk. Maternal stabilisation with antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate should precede delivery. A brief delay of 24 to 48 hours for corticosteroid effect is acceptable if the maternal condition can be stabilised, although if the condition deteriorates, immediate delivery is indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline; SOMANZ Guideline)

TTP and HELLP syndrome share features of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia. However, the clinical context (new-onset hypertension, proteinuria, elevated LFTs, epigastric pain at 33 weeks) is diagnostic of HELLP rather than TTP. In HELLP, delivery is the definitive treatment; plasma exchange is not indicated. ADAMTS13 activity testing can help distinguish TTP from HELLP in ambiguous cases. (Source: SOMANZ Guideline; British Journal of Haematology TMA Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes accounts for approximately 30 to 40% of preterm births. Management depends on gestational age, maternal and fetal condition, and presence of infection. Between 24 and 34 weeks with no infection and reassuring fetal status, expectant management is preferred to allow antenatal corticosteroids and antibiotics to take effect. Erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice (the ORACLE I trial demonstrated reduced composite neonatal morbidity). Amoxicillin-clavulanate is specifically avoided due to increased risk of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Delivery is planned at 34 to 37 weeks depending on institutional protocol.
key_points: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM x 2 doses for fetal lung maturation under 34 weeks
Erythromycin 250 mg QID for 10 days prolongs latency and reduces infection
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is contraindicated in PPROM due to increased NEC risk
Monitor for chorioamnionitis: maternal temperature, HR, CRP, uterine tenderness
explanation.pearls: The ORACLE I trial showed that erythromycin (but not amoxicillin-clavulanate) in PPROM prolonged pregnancy by a median of 5 days and reduced composite neonatal morbidity; amoxicillin-clavulanate was associated with a 4-fold increase in neonatal NEC.

options.rationale: At 30 weeks, immediate delivery is not indicated unless there are signs of chorioamnionitis, fetal compromise, or other maternal indications. Expectant management with antenatal corticosteroids and antibiotics is the standard approach to prolong the pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: PPROM)

Expectant management without antenatal corticosteroids or prophylactic antibiotics at 30 weeks is suboptimal. Betamethasone significantly reduces neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, and necrotising enterocolitis. Prophylactic antibiotics (typically erythromycin) prolong latency and reduce maternal and neonatal infection. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline; Cochrane PPROM Antibiotics Review)

While magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is indicated when delivery is expected within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks, immediate caesarean section is not indicated at 30 weeks with intact fetal status and no maternal complications. Expectant management with corticosteroids and antibiotics to prolong the pregnancy is the priority. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline; RANZCOG MgSO4 for Neuroprotection Guideline)

At 30 weeks with confirmed PPROM, no signs of infection, and reassuring fetal status, the standard management is: (1) IM betamethasone (2 doses of 11.4 mg, 24 hours apart) for fetal lung maturation, (2) oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days to prolong latency and reduce infection risk, (3) inpatient expectant management with regular maternal observations (temperature, HR, CRP) and daily CTG monitoring, (4) GBS prophylaxis in labour if GBS status unknown or positive. Delivery is planned at 34 to 37 weeks if labour does not supervene. (Source: RANZCOG PPROM Guideline; Queensland Clinical Guideline: PPROM)

Transabdominal amnioinfusion is not a standard treatment for PPROM. While it has been studied for severe oligohydramnios causing pulmonary hypoplasia risk at very early gestations (below 24 weeks), it is not part of routine management at 30 weeks. The evidence for benefit is limited and the procedure carries risks of infection and membrane disruption. (Source: Cochrane Amnioinfusion for PPROM Review)

explanation.summary: Placenta praevia with suspected placenta accreta spectrum is a high-risk obstetric condition requiring meticulous multidisciplinary planning. The risk of PAS increases with the number of prior caesarean sections: approximately 3% with one prior CS and up to 40 to 60% with 3 or more prior CS when a praevia is present. Ultrasound features suggesting PAS include loss of the clear zone between placenta and myometrium, irregular bladder wall, and bridging vessels on Doppler. Planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks at a tertiary centre with a multidisciplinary team reduces maternal morbidity and mortality compared with emergency presentation.
key_points: Major praevia with PAS: plan delivery at 36 to 37 weeks at a tertiary centre
Multidisciplinary team: obstetrician, pelvic surgeon, anaesthetist, interventional radiology, blood bank
Vaginal delivery is absolutely contraindicated with major placenta praevia
Risk of PAS increases with number of prior caesarean sections
explanation.pearls: The combination of anterior placenta praevia with 2 or more prior caesarean sections carries a PAS risk of approximately 40%; this should prompt referral to a centre of excellence by 28 weeks to allow adequate time for multidisciplinary planning.

sources.label: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

options.rationale: A major placenta praevia with suspected placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) in a woman with two prior caesareans requires planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks at a tertiary centre with a multidisciplinary team (experienced obstetrician, gynaecological oncologist or pelvic surgeon, anaesthetist, interventional radiologist, blood bank, neonatologist). The approach should include preparation for potential caesarean hysterectomy if PAS is confirmed intraoperatively. Cross-matched blood and cell salvage should be available. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline; FIGO PAS Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

options.rationale: While MRI can provide additional information about the depth of placental invasion, particularly for posterior placentas where ultrasound views are limited, it should not delay the planning process. Ultrasound with Doppler has a sensitivity of 80 to 90% for PAS and the findings described (loss of clear zone, bridging vessels, bladder wall irregularity) are highly suggestive. MRI may be a useful adjunct but the delivery plan should proceed. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline; FIGO PAS Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

options.rationale: While inpatient admission may be considered for women with symptomatic praevia (bleeding episodes), an asymptomatic woman can be managed as an outpatient with close surveillance, provided she lives within 30 minutes of a tertiary hospital. Delivery at 39 weeks is too late for major praevia with suspected PAS - the risk of emergency haemorrhage increases significantly after 36 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is absolutely contraindicated in major placenta praevia (placenta completely covering the internal os). Cervical dilatation in the presence of a major praevia will cause catastrophic haemorrhage. Caesarean section is the only safe mode of delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

options.rationale: Prophylactic uterine artery embolisation before delivery is not standard practice. While interventional radiology involvement in PAS management may include pre-operative balloon catheter placement or post-operative embolisation for bleeding control, prophylactic embolisation at 34 weeks is not part of established guidelines. (Source: FIGO PAS Guideline; RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCOG Placenta Praevia and PAS Guideline

explanation.summary: The Australian NCSP transitioned from cytology-based screening to HPV-based screening in 2017. Under the current program, women aged 25 to 74 years undergo HPV testing every 5 years with reflex liquid-based cytology for HPV-positive results. HPV 16/18 with any abnormal cytology is classified as a high-risk result requiring colposcopy within 8 weeks. HPV vaccination does not negate the need for screening or investigation of abnormal results, as breakthrough infections and pre-existing infections can still cause cervical disease. The colposcopy pathway allows tissue-based diagnosis to guide management.
key_points: HPV 16/18 with pHSIL requires colposcopy within 8 weeks under NCSP guidelines
Colposcopy with directed biopsy precedes any treatment decision
HPV vaccination reduces but does not eliminate cervical cancer risk
LLETZ is treatment for confirmed CIN2/3, not a diagnostic procedure
explanation.pearls: Under the NCSP, even HPV 16/18 positive with normal cytology (not just abnormal) requires direct referral to colposcopy, reflecting the high oncogenic potential of these types; other oncogenic HPV types with normal cytology are retested at 12 months.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines

options.rationale: HPV 16 with pHSIL cytology is a high-risk result that requires immediate colposcopy. Repeating the test in 12 months would delay diagnosis and treatment of potential high-grade cervical disease. The NCSP guidelines mandate direct referral to colposcopy for any pHSIL result regardless of HPV type. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines

options.rationale: While LLETZ is the treatment for confirmed high-grade CIN, it should not be performed without prior colposcopic assessment and directed biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and determine the extent of disease. Proceeding directly to excision without colposcopy risks overtreating low-grade disease or missing the most severe area. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines

options.rationale: Topical imiquimod is used for genital warts (caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11) and is not an established treatment for cervical high-risk HPV infection or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. The priority is colposcopic assessment to determine the grade of cervical disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual Health; NCSP Guidelines)

HPV vaccination significantly reduces the risk of high-grade cervical disease but does not eliminate it entirely, especially when infection was acquired before vaccination or involves a type covered by the vaccine but with established infection. A pHSIL result requires investigation regardless of vaccination status. (Source: NCSP Guidelines; NCIRS HPV Vaccination Guidelines)

Under the Australian National Cervical Screening Program, HPV 16 or 18 detected with any abnormal cytology (including pHSIL) requires referral for colposcopy within 8 weeks. Colposcopy allows direct visualisation of the cervix with acetic acid and Lugol's iodine, with targeted biopsies of abnormal areas. Histological confirmation of the grade of CIN then guides management (observation for CIN1, treatment for CIN2/3). (Source: NCSP Guidelines; Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Cervical Screening Guidelines

explanation.summary: Post-operative hormonal therapy for endometriosis is recommended to reduce symptom recurrence and disease progression. First-line options include the levonorgestrel IUS, continuous combined oral contraceptive pill, or depot medroxyprogesterone acetate. The LNG-IUS is particularly effective for pelvic endometriosis due to its high local progestogenic concentration, with studies showing a 50% reduction in endometrioma recurrence compared with no post-operative hormonal treatment. GnRH agonists are second-line due to bone density concerns and are limited to 6 months without add-back therapy. Danazol is rarely used due to androgenic side effects.
key_points: Post-operative hormonal therapy reduces endometrioma recurrence by approximately 50%
LNG-IUS is first-line for endometriosis in women not seeking conception
GnRH agonists limited to 6 months without add-back due to bone density loss
Continuous COCP is an alternative first-line option with daily compliance requirement
explanation.pearls: A Cochrane review found that the LNG-IUS reduced endometriosis-associated pain scores by 50% at 12 months with comparable efficacy to GnRH agonist (leuprorelin) but significantly fewer side effects and no bone density loss.

options.rationale: GnRH agonists are effective for endometriosis symptoms but are limited to 6 months of use without add-back hormone therapy due to bone mineral density loss. They are typically used as second-line therapy when first-line hormonal options have failed. For a woman not seeking conception, a long-acting progestogen or combined oral contraceptive pill is preferred as first-line. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; NICE NG73 Endometriosis)

The levonorgestrel IUS (52 mg, e.g. Mirena) is a first-line long-term hormonal therapy for endometriosis in women not seeking conception. It provides local progestogenic effect on endometrial and ectopic endometrial tissue, reduces menstrual flow, and provides contraception. Studies show it is as effective as GnRH agonists for pain control with fewer side effects. Its 5-year duration of action is ideal for this patient's 2 to 3 year contraceptive requirement. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; Cochrane Review: Progestogens for Endometriosis; NICE NG73)

Continuous COCP is an effective first-line option for endometriosis management and provides contraception. However, in a woman with residual endometrioma and significant symptoms despite surgery, the LNG-IUS is generally preferred due to its superior local progestogenic effect on pelvic endometriosis, reduced systemic side effects, and longer duration of action without daily compliance requirements. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; NICE NG73 Endometriosis)

Danazol is an androgenic agent that suppresses endometriosis but carries significant androgenic side effects (hirsutism, voice deepening, acne, weight gain) and is teratogenic. It is rarely used in modern practice due to its adverse effect profile. First-line progestogenic options are preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gynaecology; RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline)

NSAIDs alone do not modify the underlying disease process and her symptoms are already poorly controlled with NSAIDs. Repeat laparoscopy at 12 months without intervening hormonal suppression allows disease progression and endometrioma recurrence. Post-operative hormonal therapy significantly reduces endometrioma recurrence and symptom relapse. (Source: RANZCOG Endometriosis Guideline; Cochrane Post-operative Hormonal Therapy Review)

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare but potentially life-threatening form of dilated cardiomyopathy that develops in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum in women with no prior cardiac disease. The incidence is approximately 1 in 3000 to 4000 pregnancies. Risk factors include multiparity, advanced maternal age, pre-eclampsia, and African ancestry. The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography showing an LVEF below 45% and left ventricular end-diastolic dimension above 2.7 cm/m2. Approximately 50% of women recover normal cardiac function within 6 to 12 months. Bromocriptine has been investigated as a disease-modifying therapy in addition to standard heart failure treatment.
key_points: PPCM: new heart failure in last month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum
Echocardiography confirms LVEF below 45% and excludes other structural causes
Treatment: ACE inhibitors (safe postpartum), beta-blockers, diuretics, anticoagulation if EF severely reduced
Approximately 50% recover normal EF within 6 to 12 months
explanation.pearls: An LVEF below 30% at diagnosis of peripartum cardiomyopathy is associated with only a 20% chance of full recovery, compared with 80% recovery when initial LVEF is 30 to 45%; serial echocardiography at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months guides prognosis counselling and contraceptive advice.

options.rationale: The presentation of new-onset heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum in a woman with no prior cardiac disease is the definition of peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM). The echocardiogram at delivery was normal, confirming this is a new cardiomyopathy. Urgent echocardiography is required to confirm reduced ejection fraction (typically LVEF below 45%), assess chamber dimensions, and exclude other structural causes. Treatment follows standard heart failure management with ACE inhibitors (safe postpartum), beta-blockers, diuretics, and anticoagulation if EF is severely reduced. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guidelines; ESC Peripartum Cardiomyopathy Position Statement)

While PE is an important differential in postpartum dyspnoea, the clinical features here (bilateral basal crackles, displaced apex, S3 gallop, cardiomegaly on CXR, markedly elevated BNP) point to left ventricular failure rather than PE. PE typically presents with pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, or unilateral leg swelling, and does not cause cardiomegaly or S3 gallop.
