Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line pharmacological treatment, started at 250 mg twice daily and titrated up to a maximum of 2 g/day based on response. Weekly monitoring of bile acids and liver function tests is recommended. RANZCOG guidelines recommend planned delivery at 37 weeks gestation when bile acids are between 40 and 99 micromol/L to reduce the risk of stillbirth while balancing neonatal morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

While ursodeoxycholic acid is the correct first-line treatment, the timing of delivery at 38 weeks is not aligned with current RANZCOG recommendations for bile acid levels in the 40-99 micromol/L range. The recommended delivery timing is 37 weeks gestation for this category of ICP severity, as the risk of stillbirth increases after this point. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

Rifampicin is a second-line agent used for ICP pruritus refractory to ursodeoxycholic acid. It should not be used as first-line therapy due to potential hepatotoxicity and the need for careful liver function monitoring. First-line treatment remains ursodeoxycholic acid. Rifampicin may be considered if symptoms persist despite maximum dose ursodeoxycholic acid. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

explanation.summary: Severe ICP with bile acids above 100 micromol/L carries a stillbirth risk of approximately 3.4%, which is significantly higher than the risk at lower bile acid levels. The relationship between bile acid concentration and stillbirth risk is dose-dependent, with a steep increase above 100 micromol/L. Delivery between 34 and 36 weeks is recommended in this severe category. Coagulopathy from fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (vitamins A, D, E, K) may develop and should be corrected with oral vitamin K before delivery. It is important to differentiate ICP from HELLP syndrome, which presents with hypertension, low platelets, haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated LDH), and elevated transaminases.
key_points: Bile acids above 100 micromol/L define severe ICP with significantly increased stillbirth risk warranting delivery at 34-36 weeks
Raised INR in ICP indicates fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption and should be corrected with oral vitamin K before delivery
Normal platelets, normal LDH, and absence of schistocytes help differentiate severe ICP from HELLP syndrome
explanation.pearls: Oral vitamin K 10 mg should be administered to correct the coagulopathy in severe ICP (INR above 1.1), and delivery should occur between 34 and 36 weeks when bile acids exceed 100 micromol/L.

sources.label: Ovadia C et al. Lancet 2019 - PITCHES trial and bile acid thresholds
RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 43: Obstetric Cholestasis

options.rationale: With bile acids now above 100 micromol/L, delivery should not be deferred to 37 weeks. The PITCHES trial and RANZCOG guidelines indicate that bile acid levels above 100 micromol/L carry a significantly increased risk of stillbirth (up to 3.4%), and delivery between 34 and 36 weeks is recommended. Increasing ursodeoxycholic acid and adding colestyramine while waiting until 37 weeks exposes the fetuses to unacceptable risk. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

While vitamin K supplementation is appropriate given the raised INR suggesting fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, the plan to deliver at 36 weeks does not reflect the urgency warranted by bile acids above 100 micromol/L in a twin pregnancy. Current guidelines recommend delivery between 34 and 36 weeks for severe ICP, and at 34 weeks in a twin pregnancy this is already achievable. The management should prioritise early delivery rather than continued monitoring to 36 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

Dexamethasone is not an effective treatment for reducing bile acids in ICP. While antenatal corticosteroids may be appropriate for fetal lung maturation before preterm delivery, they are not used to treat maternal cholestasis. Ursodeoxycholic acid should be continued even if bile acids are rising, as it may still provide partial benefit for pruritus and hepatoprotection. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

This is severe ICP with bile acids above 100 micromol/L, placing both fetuses at significantly increased risk of stillbirth. The raised INR of 1.3 indicates fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption from cholestasis, requiring oral vitamin K supplementation. RANZCOG guidelines recommend delivery between 34 and 36 weeks for bile acids above 100 micromol/L. At 34 weeks with a twin pregnancy and bile acids of 112 micromol/L, delivery within 48 hours after confirming fetal wellbeing and correcting coagulopathy is appropriate. Ursodeoxycholic acid should be continued until delivery. The normal platelet count, normal LDH, and absence of schistocytes help exclude HELLP syndrome. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

While admission and cardiotocography are reasonable, awaiting bile acid levels to trend down is inappropriate at this severity. Bile acids of 112 micromol/L represent severe ICP with a high stillbirth risk that warrants expedited delivery rather than expectant management. Oral vitamin K is preferred over intravenous in this setting as there is no active bleeding or urgent surgical need. The coagulopathy can be corrected orally while planning delivery. (Source: RANZCOG ICP guideline)

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is common in postmenopausal multiparous women. The POP-Q staging system classifies prolapse by the position of the leading edge relative to the hymen. Stage II prolapse reaches within 1 cm of the hymen. First-line management is conservative: supervised pelvic floor muscle training (minimum 3 months), vaginal pessary trial, lifestyle modifications (weight management, avoiding heavy lifting, managing constipation), and topical vaginal oestrogen for postmenopausal women. Surgical options are considered when conservative measures fail or are declined by the patient.
key_points: First-line management of symptomatic prolapse is conservative: pelvic floor muscle training, vaginal pessary, and topical vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training by a specialist physiotherapist has Level 1 evidence for symptom improvement in Stage I-II prolapse
Surgery is reserved for patients who fail or decline conservative management after an adequate trial period of three to six months
explanation.pearls: Topical vaginal oestrogen (e.g., oestriol 0.5 mg pessary or cream nightly for 2 weeks then twice weekly) improves pessary tolerance and local tissue quality in postmenopausal women with prolapse.

sources.label: NICE NG123: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women

options.rationale: Surgical management is not the initial approach for a patient who has not yet tried conservative measures. Guidelines recommend a trial of conservative management before surgery. Surgery carries risks including mesh complications, recurrence, and anaesthetic risks, particularly in older patients. First-line treatment should include pelvic floor muscle training and a vaginal pessary trial. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

Sacrocolpopexy is a major abdominal procedure typically reserved for vault prolapse or recurrent prolapse, not as first-line management. While topical vaginal oestrogen is appropriate to improve tissue quality, surgery should not be the initial step when the patient has not attempted conservative management including pelvic floor muscle training and pessary use. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

While weight management is a reasonable general recommendation, weight loss alone is unlikely to resolve Stage II prolapse. Oral HRT is not the preferred route for treating prolapse - topical vaginal oestrogen is preferred as it directly improves local tissue quality. This plan also omits the two key conservative interventions: supervised pelvic floor muscle training and vaginal pessary trial. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

While topical vaginal oestrogen and managing constipation are appropriate components of care, this plan omits the two key conservative interventions: supervised pelvic floor muscle training and a vaginal pessary trial. Pelvic floor muscle training has Level 1 evidence for improving prolapse symptoms, and a pessary can provide immediate symptom relief. These should be offered before considering surgery. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

First-line management of symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse is conservative, consisting of supervised pelvic floor muscle training, vaginal pessary trial, and topical vaginal oestrogen in postmenopausal women. Pelvic floor muscle training has strong evidence for improving prolapse symptoms and should be supervised by a pelvic floor physiotherapist. A vaginal pessary (ring or Gellhorn) can provide immediate mechanical support and symptom relief. Topical vaginal oestrogen improves local tissue quality and pessary tolerance. Surgery is reserved for women who fail or decline conservative management. (Source: RANZCOG prolapse guideline)

explanation.summary: Stress urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine with increased intra-abdominal pressure (coughing, sneezing, lifting, exercise) in the absence of detrusor contraction. It is common postpartum, particularly in multiparous women. First-line treatment is supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a specialist continence physiotherapist for at least 3 months. Urodynamic studies are not required for initial management when the clinical picture is clear. Surgery (mid-urethral sling) is reserved for women who fail conservative treatment.
key_points: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for a minimum of 3 months is first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence with Level 1 evidence
Antimuscarinic medications such as oxybutynin are for urge incontinence, not stress incontinence
Urodynamic studies are indicated before surgical intervention or when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain, not before initiating conservative treatment
explanation.pearls: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months with a continence physiotherapist improves stress urinary incontinence in up to 70% of women and should be trialled before any surgical intervention.

options.rationale: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) is the first-line treatment for stress urinary incontinence. Level 1 evidence demonstrates that a supervised program of at least 3 months duration is superior to unsupervised exercises. The program should include both strength and endurance training of the pelvic floor muscles. The Continence Foundation of Australia and eTG both recommend this as initial management before considering further investigation or surgical options. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic medication used for overactive bladder and urge urinary incontinence, not stress urinary incontinence. This patient has classic stress incontinence symptoms (leaking with coughing, sneezing, lifting) without urgency, frequency, or nocturia. Anticholinergic medications are ineffective for stress incontinence and would cause unnecessary side effects including dry mouth, constipation, and cognitive impairment. (Source: eTG)

Urodynamic studies are not required before initiating first-line conservative treatment for clinically obvious stress urinary incontinence. The history (leaking with raised intra-abdominal pressure, no urgency symptoms) and positive cough stress test provide sufficient clinical evidence. Urodynamics are indicated before surgical intervention, when the diagnosis is uncertain, or when initial conservative treatment has failed. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

Mid-urethral sling surgery is effective for stress incontinence but is not first-line management. Conservative treatment with supervised pelvic floor muscle training should be trialled for at least 3 months before considering surgery. Up to 70% of women with stress incontinence improve with PFMT, potentially avoiding the risks of surgery including mesh complications, voiding dysfunction, and de novo urgency. (Source: RANZCOG)

While general lifestyle advice including caffeine reduction is reasonable, general core strengthening exercises such as Pilates and yoga are not equivalent to targeted supervised pelvic floor muscle training. Evidence supports specific pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist as the effective intervention, not general fitness exercises. Some exercises like high-impact activities may worsen symptoms. A six-month wait-and-see approach without specific PFMT delays effective treatment. (Source: Continence Foundation Australia)

explanation.summary: The PALM-COEIN classification system (FIGO 2011) provides a structured approach to evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding. PALM refers to structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) that can be identified on imaging or histology. COEIN refers to non-structural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified). Initial investigations should include full blood count and ferritin to assess the impact of bleeding, and pelvic ultrasound to identify structural causes. Further investigations are directed by clinical findings and initial results.
key_points: First-line investigations for heavy menstrual bleeding are full blood count, serum ferritin, and pelvic ultrasound
The PALM-COEIN classification system guides systematic evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding
Endometrial biopsy is indicated in women aged 45 or older, or those with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia such as obesity, anovulation, or tamoxifen use
explanation.pearls: For heavy menstrual bleeding with regular cycles, the initial investigation triad is FBC, serum ferritin, and pelvic ultrasound - coagulation studies and endometrial biopsy are reserved for specific clinical indications.

options.rationale: Hysteroscopy is not a first-line investigation for heavy menstrual bleeding. While it may be needed later to evaluate intracavitary pathology, the initial workup should include less invasive investigations. Full blood count and ferritin to assess for iron deficiency anaemia, and pelvic ultrasound to evaluate structural causes, are the appropriate first steps. Coagulation studies are considered if there is a personal or family history suggestive of a bleeding disorder. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

The RANZCOG and NICE guidelines recommend that initial investigations for heavy menstrual bleeding include a full blood count and serum ferritin to assess for iron deficiency anaemia, and pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for structural causes classified under the PALM component of PALM-COEIN (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia). This patient has symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, exertional dyspnoea) and a bulky uterus suggesting possible fibroids or adenomyosis. These investigations are minimally invasive, widely available, and provide the essential information needed to guide further management. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

While beta-hCG should be considered in any woman of reproductive age with abnormal bleeding to exclude pregnancy, thyroid function tests and prolactin are not first-line investigations for heavy menstrual bleeding with regular cycles. Thyroid dysfunction and hyperprolactinaemia more commonly cause irregular or absent periods rather than regular heavy menstrual bleeding. The priority is to assess for anaemia (FBC, ferritin) and structural pathology (pelvic ultrasound). (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

Pelvic MRI is not a first-line investigation for heavy menstrual bleeding. While MRI provides excellent soft tissue characterisation, it is expensive and reserved for cases where ultrasound findings are indeterminate or where surgical planning requires detailed fibroid mapping. Pelvic ultrasound is the appropriate first-line imaging modality. Von Willebrand testing is indicated when clinical history suggests a bleeding disorder, not routinely. Endometrial biopsy is indicated for women over 45 or with risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

This panel is overly extensive for initial investigation. Coagulation studies and von Willebrand screening are indicated when there is a personal or family history of bleeding disorders, heavy bleeding since menarche, or easy bruising - none of which are present here. Thyroid function tests are not first-line for regular heavy periods. Saline infusion sonohysterography is a second-line investigation when intracavitary pathology is suspected. The initial workup should be targeted: FBC, ferritin, and pelvic ultrasound. (Source: NICE NG88)

explanation.summary: The management stepladder for heavy menstrual bleeding progresses from non-hormonal medical treatment (tranexamic acid, NSAIDs) to hormonal treatment (LNG-IUS as first-line hormonal, then COCP or progestogens), and then surgical options (endometrial ablation, hysterectomy) if medical treatment fails. The LNG-IUS reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90% and is the most effective non-surgical treatment. It can be used in the presence of fibroids up to 3 cm that do not distort the cavity. Iron deficiency should be corrected concurrently with oral iron supplementation.
key_points: The LNG-IUS (52 mg) reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90% and is the first-line hormonal treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding
Small intramural fibroids (less than 3 cm) not distorting the endometrial cavity do not prevent LNG-IUS insertion and are unlikely to be the primary cause of HMB
Iron deficiency (ferritin below 30 microg/L) should be treated with oral iron supplementation alongside treatment of the bleeding cause
explanation.pearls: The 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (Mirena) reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90% at 12 months and is effective even with intramural fibroids up to 3 cm not distorting the cavity.

options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for HMB but is not the next step after failure of first-line non-hormonal agents. The management stepladder requires a trial of hormonal treatment before proceeding to surgery. The LNG-IUS is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding and should be offered before surgical options. Bilateral oophorectomy in a 42-year-old is not indicated for HMB alone. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

While the combined oral contraceptive pill can reduce menstrual blood loss by up to 50%, it is less effective than the LNG-IUS which reduces loss by over 90%. Adding the COCP to existing non-hormonal agents rather than switching to the most effective hormonal option is not the optimal next step. The LNG-IUS is recommended as the preferred treatment when non-hormonal agents are insufficient. At 42, combined hormonal contraception also carries higher cardiovascular risk. (Source: NICE NG88)

A 2 cm intramural fibroid that does not distort the endometrial cavity is unlikely to be the primary cause of her heavy menstrual bleeding. Uterine artery embolisation is typically reserved for symptomatic fibroids that are larger or distort the uterine cavity. The next step should be a trial of the most effective medical treatment (LNG-IUS), which is also effective in the presence of small non-cavity-distorting fibroids. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

A 2 cm intramural fibroid that does not distort the cavity is not amenable to hysteroscopic resection, which is used for submucosal fibroids (FIGO type 0, 1, or 2). Endometrial ablation is an option but should not be offered before a trial of the LNG-IUS, which is the most effective non-surgical treatment. Ablation also has limitations including a significant re-treatment rate and the requirement for reliable contraception afterwards. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

The LNG-IUS (Mirena, 52 mg levonorgestrel) is the most effective medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, reducing menstrual blood loss by over 90% at 12 months. RANZCOG and NICE guidelines recommend it as first-line hormonal treatment when non-hormonal agents have been insufficient. It is effective in the presence of small fibroids that do not distort the cavity. Oral iron supplementation is needed to correct her iron deficiency (ferritin 12 microg/L) and anaemia (haemoglobin 108 g/L). Review at 3-6 months allows assessment of bleeding pattern and haemoglobin response, noting that irregular bleeding is common in the first 3 months after insertion. (Source: RANZCOG HMB guideline)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is a potentially life-threatening iatrogenic complication of controlled ovarian stimulation. It is mediated by VEGF-driven increased capillary permeability, leading to third-space fluid shift with intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration despite total body fluid excess. Risk factors include young age, low BMI, high antral follicle count, high oestradiol levels, large number of oocytes retrieved (more than 15), and hCG trigger. Severity is classified by clinical and laboratory parameters. Management is primarily supportive: intravenous fluid resuscitation, VTE prophylaxis, electrolyte monitoring, and albumin infusion for refractory cases. Diuretics are contraindicated initially as they worsen intravascular depletion.
key_points: OHSS causes intravascular depletion due to third-space fluid shift - diuretics are contraindicated as they worsen haemoconcentration
VTE prophylaxis with LMWH is essential for all hospitalised patients with moderate-severe OHSS due to the significant hypercoagulable state
Intravenous albumin (25%) is considered when oliguria persists despite adequate crystalloid resuscitation, to restore intravascular oncotic pressure
explanation.pearls: In severe OHSS, enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily should be commenced on admission and continued until resolution of symptoms and mobilisation - OHSS-related VTE can occur weeks after the acute presentation.

options.rationale: Diuretics are contraindicated in the initial management of OHSS. The abdominal distension is caused by third-space fluid shift due to increased capillary permeability, not fluid overload. Diuretics will worsen intravascular depletion and haemoconcentration, potentially precipitating thromboembolic events and renal failure. The haemoconcentration (haematocrit 0.48) confirms intravascular volume depletion despite total body fluid excess. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS guideline)

This patient has severe OHSS with haemoconcentration, oliguria, raised creatinine, and hypoalbuminaemia requiring more aggressive management than oral fluids and observation alone. Intravenous fluid resuscitation is required given the tachycardia, hypotension, and haemoconcentration. VTE prophylaxis with LMWH is recommended for all hospitalised patients with moderate-severe OHSS regardless of whether thrombosis has occurred, as OHSS is a significant hypercoagulable state. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS guideline)

This patient has severe OHSS characterised by haemoconcentration (haematocrit 0.48), oliguria, raised creatinine, hypoalbuminaemia, tachycardia, and hypotension. Management priorities include: (1) intravenous crystalloid resuscitation to restore intravascular volume, targeting urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour; (2) VTE prophylaxis with LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg daily) as OHSS is a high-risk hypercoagulable state; (3) intravenous human albumin solution (25%) if the patient remains oliguric or hypotensive despite crystalloid resuscitation, as the low serum albumin (22 g/L) impairs intravascular oncotic pressure. Diuretics should be avoided initially. Paracentesis may be needed if tense ascites impairs respiratory function. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS guideline)

While paracentesis may be required for tense ascites causing respiratory compromise or refractory oliguria, it is not the immediate first step. Initial management should focus on intravenous fluid resuscitation to correct haemoconcentration and restore renal perfusion. VTE prophylaxis should not be withheld - LMWH is safe to commence and the risk of thrombosis in severe OHSS is significant. Paracentesis is considered after initial resuscitation if symptoms persist or respiratory function is compromised. (Source: FSA OHSS guideline)

While cabergoline has evidence for preventing OHSS when given from the day of oocyte retrieval or hCG trigger, its role in treating established severe OHSS is limited. It is not a first-line treatment for established OHSS. Oral fluid intake should be encouraged rather than restricted, as restriction worsens intravascular depletion. The key management priorities are intravenous fluid resuscitation, VTE prophylaxis, and monitoring, not oral fluid restriction. (Source: RANZCOG OHSS guideline)

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is characterised by painless cervical dilatation leading to mid-trimester pregnancy loss, typically between 16 and 24 weeks. Cerclage indications are classified as history-indicated (placed at 12-14 weeks based on obstetric history alone), ultrasound-indicated (placed when cervical shortening is detected on surveillance), or rescue (placed when membranes are prolapsing through a dilated cervix). This patient ideally should have been offered a history-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks given her two previous mid-trimester losses, but since this was missed, an ultrasound-indicated cerclage at 20 weeks with a cervix of 15 mm remains appropriate and beneficial. Vaginal progesterone is used as adjunctive therapy.
key_points: Ultrasound-indicated cerclage is recommended when cervical length is 25 mm or less before 24 weeks in women with a history suggestive of cervical insufficiency
A history-indicated cerclage should ideally be placed at 12-14 weeks in women with two or more previous mid-trimester losses consistent with cervical insufficiency
Transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or cervical anatomical abnormalities precluding vaginal suture placement
explanation.pearls: McDonald cerclage is placed as a purse-string suture at the cervicovaginal junction using non-absorbable suture (e.g., Mersilene tape) and removed at 36-37 weeks - it should not be placed if there is evidence of chorioamnionitis, active bleeding, or ruptured membranes.

sources.label: FIGO Good Practice Recommendations on Cervical Cerclage
NICE NG25: Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: While vaginal progesterone alone may be appropriate for women with a short cervix but no history of cervical insufficiency, this patient has a classic history of cervical insufficiency (two painless mid-trimester losses) combined with a shortened cervix at 15 mm with funnelling. The combination of this history and ultrasound findings constitutes an indication for ultrasound-indicated cerclage. Waiting for further shortening below 10 mm risks membrane prolapse and loss of the opportunity for cerclage. (Source: RANZCOG cervical insufficiency guideline)

The Arabin pessary has been studied as an alternative to cerclage in some populations, but the evidence does not support its use in preference to cerclage in women with a history of cervical insufficiency and a short cervix. The PECEP trial and subsequent studies have shown inconsistent results. For women with a classical history of cervical insufficiency and a cervical length of 15 mm with funnelling, a McDonald cerclage is the evidence-based intervention. (Source: RANZCOG cervical insufficiency guideline)

Bed rest has no evidence of benefit in preventing preterm birth and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk. Tocolysis is not indicated as there is no evidence of preterm labour (no contractions). Antenatal corticosteroids are not indicated at 20 weeks as the fetus is pre-viable. The appropriate management is cerclage placement to address the cervical insufficiency, not expectant management. (Source: RANZCOG cervical insufficiency guideline)

This patient meets criteria for ultrasound-indicated cerclage: a history consistent with cervical insufficiency (two painless mid-trimester losses) and a cervical length of 15 mm or less on transvaginal ultrasound before 24 weeks. A McDonald cerclage (purse-string suture placed around the cervix) should be performed after excluding infection (normal inflammatory markers, negative vaginal swabs) and active labour (no contractions, intact membranes not prolapsing). Vaginal progesterone is recommended as adjunctive therapy. RANZCOG guidelines support cerclage in this clinical scenario. The cerclage is typically removed at 36-37 weeks or earlier if preterm labour ensues. (Source: RANZCOG cervical insufficiency guideline)

Transabdominal cerclage (e.g., Benson technique) is typically reserved for women in whom transvaginal cerclage has previously failed, or those with cervical anatomical abnormalities (previous trachelectomy, congenital short cervix) that preclude adequate vaginal suture placement. It is a more invasive procedure requiring laparotomy or laparoscopy and mandating caesarean delivery. A cervical length of 15 mm at 20 weeks is amenable to a McDonald cerclage, which is the appropriate first-line surgical intervention. (Source: RANZCOG cervical insufficiency guideline)

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is a severe complication of pre-eclampsia characterised by Haemolysis (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes, elevated LDH and bilirubin), Elevated Liver enzymes (AST and ALT above 70 U/L), and Low Platelets (below 100 x10^9/L). It is a medical emergency that can progress rapidly to hepatic rupture, DIC, renal failure, and maternal death. Definitive treatment is delivery, which should be planned within 24-48 hours after maternal stabilisation. Key differentials include acute fatty liver of pregnancy (characterised by hypoglycaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, and DIC) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (ADAMTS13 below 10%, neurological features).
key_points: HELLP syndrome diagnostic triad: microangiopathic haemolysis (schistocytes, elevated LDH), elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT above 70 U/L), and low platelets (below 100 x10^9/L)
Magnesium sulfate loading dose 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour maintenance is given for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is differentiated by hypoglycaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, and DIC - HELLP typically has normal fibrinogen and INR
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in HELLP syndrome is given as a 4 g IV loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance infusion, with monitoring of patellar reflexes, respiratory rate (above 12/min), and urine output (above 0.5 mL/kg/hour).

sources.label: SOMANZ Guidelines for the Management of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

options.rationale: Delaying delivery until 37 weeks is inappropriate in the setting of HELLP syndrome. HELLP is a life-threatening condition that can progress rapidly to hepatic rupture, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and maternal death. Delivery is the definitive treatment and should be planned urgently after maternal stabilisation. While corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation are appropriate at 34 weeks, they should not delay delivery beyond 48 hours. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

This patient has HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis - elevated LDH, schistocytes; Elevated Liver enzymes - AST/ALT above 70 U/L; Low Platelets - below 100 x10^9/L) in the context of pre-eclampsia (hypertension and proteinuria). Immediate management includes: (1) blood pressure control with intravenous labetalol or hydralazine targeting systolic below 160 mmHg and diastolic below 110 mmHg; (2) magnesium sulfate loading dose 4 g IV over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour maintenance for seizure prophylaxis; (3) antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 11.4 mg IM) for fetal lung maturation at 34 weeks; (4) plan delivery within 24-48 hours as HELLP syndrome does not resolve without delivery. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

While TTP shares features with HELLP syndrome (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia), TTP is characterised by ADAMTS13 activity below 10% and typically presents with neurological features and renal impairment rather than hepatic involvement. The combination of hypertension, proteinuria, epigastric pain, elevated liver enzymes, and thrombocytopenia in the third trimester is consistent with HELLP syndrome, not TTP. The normal fibrinogen also argues against DIC. Plasma exchange would delay definitive treatment (delivery). (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

N-acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol overdose hepatotoxicity and has no established role in the management of HELLP syndrome. While fluid management should be judicious to avoid pulmonary oedema (a known complication of pre-eclampsia), delaying delivery until 36 weeks in the setting of HELLP syndrome is dangerous. HELLP can progress to hepatic rupture, DIC, and multi-organ failure. Delivery should be planned within 24-48 hours. (Source: RANZCOG hypertension in pregnancy guideline)

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP) is an important differential but this presentation is more consistent with HELLP syndrome. AFLP typically presents with hypoglycaemia, hypofibrinogenaemia, elevated ammonia, and leukocytosis, and may cause DIC with a prolonged INR. This patient has normal fibrinogen (3.8 g/L), normal INR (1.1), and the combination of hypertension, proteinuria, and schistocytes with elevated LDH points to HELLP. The Swansea criteria can help differentiate. While both require delivery, the specific management differs. (Source: Queensland Health HELLP guideline)

explanation.summary: Perimortem caesarean section is a resuscitative procedure performed during maternal cardiac arrest when CPR has not achieved return of spontaneous circulation within 4-5 minutes. It serves a dual purpose: improving maternal resuscitation by relieving aortocaval compression from the gravid uterus (significant from 20 weeks gestation), and providing the fetus the best chance of survival. The procedure should be performed at the site of arrest by the most experienced available clinician, without delay for transfer to an operating theatre or arrival of a specialist obstetrician. A midline abdominal incision and classical uterine incision are used for speed. CPR must continue throughout the procedure and after delivery.
key_points: Perimortem caesarean section should aim for delivery within 4-5 minutes of maternal cardiac arrest if CPR has not achieved ROSC
The procedure is performed at the site of arrest by the most experienced available clinician - do not delay for theatre transfer or specialist attendance
Manual left uterine displacement is used during CPR rather than left lateral tilt, as the supine position is essential for effective chest compressions
explanation.pearls: Perimortem caesarean section should aim for delivery within 5 minutes of cardiac arrest onset - it is a maternal resuscitative procedure that improves CPR efficacy by relieving aortocaval compression, not solely a fetal rescue procedure.

sources.label: Queensland Health Maternal Cardiac Arrest guideline

options.rationale: Delaying perimortem caesarean section beyond 4-5 minutes of unsuccessful CPR reduces both maternal and neonatal survival. The gravid uterus at 32 weeks causes significant aortocaval compression that impedes venous return and reduces cardiac output even with manual uterine displacement and high-quality CPR. Perimortem caesarean section is a resuscitative procedure that improves maternal haemodynamics by relieving aortocaval compression, not just a procedure to save the fetus. Waiting 10 minutes significantly worsens outcomes. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10)

Full left lateral positioning makes effective chest compressions extremely difficult and is not recommended during CPR. Manual uterine displacement (already being performed) is the recommended method for relieving aortocaval compression during resuscitation, as it allows the patient to remain supine for optimal chest compressions. After 4 minutes of CPR without ROSC at 32 weeks gestation, perimortem caesarean section should be initiated rather than continuing CPR with positional changes alone. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10)

Perimortem caesarean section should be performed at the site of the arrest (in this case, the emergency department) rather than delaying for transfer to an operating theatre. The critical time window is delivery within 4-5 minutes of cardiac arrest, and any transfer time reduces the chance of both maternal and neonatal survival. The procedure should be performed wherever the patient is located, using whatever equipment is available. CPR must continue throughout the procedure. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10)

While an obstetrician should be called urgently, waiting for their arrival is inappropriate if it delays the procedure beyond the 4-5 minute window. Perimortem caesarean section is a resuscitative procedure that any doctor trained in the technique can perform in an emergency. The procedure should be initiated immediately by the most experienced available clinician - this may be the emergency physician already present. Time is the critical factor, not the specialty of the operator. CPR continues throughout. (Source: RANZCOG maternal collapse guideline)

At 4 minutes of cardiac arrest without ROSC in a 32-week pregnancy, perimortem caesarean section should be commenced immediately. ANZCOR guidelines recommend that the procedure should aim for delivery within 4-5 minutes of cardiac arrest onset. It should be performed at the site of arrest by the most experienced available clinician - in this scenario, the emergency physician if no obstetrician is immediately present. CPR must continue throughout the procedure. The aim is a rapid midline incision and classical caesarean incision for fastest delivery. The procedure benefits the mother by relieving aortocaval compression and improving the effectiveness of CPR, in addition to giving the fetus the best chance of intact survival. Manual uterine displacement, while helpful, cannot fully relieve the compression caused by a 32-week gravid uterus. (Source: ANZCOR Guideline 11.10)
